20955-the-international-monthly-magazine:
The finest portrait yet of Louis Kossuth fronts The International Monthly Magazine for January 1852. Hungary's hero then stood in America, set to mark a bright page in liberty's tale. Taller than most supposed, with a face of piercing intellect, the Tribune's words are quoted.

Kossuth's tour for Hungarian freedom gripped the United States that winter. This monthly mixed portraits, tales, essays, and news for parlour reading. Volume five's first number froze that fever of welcome in print. Readers can feel how a foreign cause fired American crowds before the Civil War split their own house.
addison-steele-spectator-selections-1885:
Joseph Addison and Richard Steele were English writers who changed daily reading in the early 1700s. Together they ran short-lived journals: the Tatler, the Spectator, and the Guardian. Each issue carried brief essays on manners, books, and town life. This volume, published in 1885, gathers a full selection of those papers.

The essays teach through humor, using made-up clubs, letters, and characters like Sir Roger de Coverley. Addison and Steele aimed to make philosophy lively and polite talk smarter. Their clear, balanced prose became the model for modern English essay writing. Students read these selections for over a century as a style guide.
alexander-of-cappadocia-from-the-epistle:
Alexander led the Church first in Cappadocia and then in Jerusalem. He died a martyr in the persecutions of the 250s. His letters survive only in scraps quoted by the historian Eusebius.

An 1885 Fathers volume gathers those fragments under his name. Warm greetings to Origen, once his student, stand among them. Friendship and faith breathe through the brief surviving lines. Brief as they are, the pieces touch readers across the centuries. They keep the voice of a bishop who faced death for his belief. In a shelf of heavy treatises, such small human traces carry a weight of their own.
annals-cakchiquels-brinton-1885:
Daniel G. Brinton edited and translated The Annals of the Cakchiquels in 1885 for his Library of Aboriginal American Literature. The annals, also called the Memorial de Solola, are the chronicle of the Cakchiquel Maya of highland Guatemala. Brinton prints the original Cakchiquel text beside his English, with notes and an introduction.

Cakchiquel lords kept the record from mythic origins through migration, kingship, and war. It runs on through the Spanish conquest, told from the conquered side. Plague, tribute, and forced labor enter its later pages without flinching. Brinton, a pioneer of American anthropology, prized such native histories as primary sources. The annals remain a key voice of the Maya past.
aristides-the-apology-of-aristides-the-p:
Aristides, a philosopher at Athens, presented his Apology to Emperor Hadrian. The presentation came around the year 125, early in the Church's life. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers carries the elegant defense in English.

Aristides sets Christians beside pagans, Jews, and Greek thinkers for comparison. In morals and in worship, he argues, Christians come out ahead. The work then vanished for centuries from Western knowledge. Scholars recovered it only in the 1800s, to wide excitement. It now stands as the earliest Christian apology that we possess whole. Its calm and reasoned tone still impresses readers who expect ancient polemic instead.
artefii-arabis-philosophi-liber-secretus: Artefii Arabis philosophi Liber secretus, 1685. The secret book. This book preserves that work. Later readers can locate it. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Time has kept the file intact.
arxiv-2512-00085:
A robot that must reach many different goals needs policies that adapt to each new objective. Pei Zhou and co-authors introduce Hyper-GoalNet in a 2025 study of goal-conditioned manipulation. Keeping performance steady across diverse goals and settings is the main challenge they address.

Hyper-GoalNet uses a hypernetwork, a network that builds other networks, to generate policy parameters from a goal description. Goal interpretation is separated from state processing, so the goal decides the parameters while current observations are handled by them. The split could help robots switch tasks without retraining a fixed policy for each goal. Manipulation tasks, from grasping to assembly, are the proving ground for the method.
arxiv-2512-00285:
Mixtures of atoms and molecules form a delicate quantum system called an atomic-molecular Bose condensate. Avinaba Mukherjee and Raka Dasgupta study how such a system relaxes under Gaussian white noise in 2025. They describe the dynamics through polarization, the imbalance between atoms and molecules, and through coherence.

Relaxation times for both quantities are computed with a mean-field model and with a hierarchy that keeps higher-order correlations. The authors vary the initial polarization and the Feshbach detuning to see how each steers the decay. The results inform experiments that use noise and resonance tuning to control ultracold gases. Noise is usually the enemy in cold-atom labs, so studying its effects head-on is notable.
arxiv-2512-00385:
Splitting a three-dimensional point cloud into superpoints makes semantic segmentation far cheaper. Louis Geist, Loic Landrieu, and Damien Robert present EZ-SP in 2025, a fast and lightweight superpoint-based segmentation method. Earlier pipelines were bottlenecked by a slow partition step running on the CPU.

The authors propose a learnable, fully GPU partitioning algorithm that produces geometrically and semantically coherent superpoints much faster than prior methods. Speed matters because point clouds from lidar and scanning keep growing. Faster partitioning brings detailed three-dimensional understanding closer to real-time uses like robotics and mapping. A speedup of more than tenfold turns an overnight preprocessing step into an interactive one. Superpoints group nearby points that likely share a label.
arxiv-2512-00485:
Elliptic equations with singular terms model effects from chemical reactions to thin films, but their solutions are delicate. Fessel Achhoud and Hichem Khelifi study a class of anisotropic elliptic equations in 2025, involving unbounded coefficients and a singular right-hand side. Anisotropy means the equation behaves differently in different directions.

The authors address existence and regularity: whether solutions exist at all, and how smooth they must be. Singular nonlinearities can force solutions to blow up or vanish at boundaries, so the analysis needs care. Such results anchor work with numbers, since a computed answer means little if the problem beneath it is not well posed. Wild coefficients describe stuff whose traits can break down or blow up in places. For folks who solve such sums on a grid, the gain is peace of mind. The task they code is known to have a sound base, not just a good look.
arxiv-2512-00585:
Poisson superalgebras blend the geometry of Poisson brackets with the sign rules of supersymmetry. A 2025 study classifies the representations of the Grassmann Poisson superalgebra. The field is assumed to have characteristic different from two, so the sign rules behave normally.

The author proves that every irreducible Poisson supermodule over this algebra is isomorphic to the regular module or to its opposite. Moreover, every unital module over the algebra is completely reducible. Complete classification results like this tidy an entire corner of algebra, giving later researchers a firm list to build on. Complete reducibility means every module splits into the classified simple pieces. Representation theory asks how an algebra can act, and here the answer is short.
arxiv-2512-01085:
Wenjun Zhang, Shekhar Chandra, and Aaron Nicolson generalize medical phrase grounding in a 2025 paper. Phrase grounding links a written finding in a radiology report to the region of the image it describes. Grounded reports are easier to read, especially for non-experts who need to see what a phrase refers to.

Most current systems follow a referring-expression setup and return exactly one bounding box per phrase. Real reports often break that rule, with one finding appearing in several places. The authors' generalized approach allows the output to match how findings actually spread across a scan. Better grounding could make AI reports more transparent.
arxiv-2512-01485:
Jindi Lv and co-authors widen how language models reason through hard tasks. Step-by-step thought chains help a lot. But a single chain tends to lock onto one path. It rarely weighs other fair paths in full.

The team lets many paths grow and aid each other. Reinforcement learning guides that joint search. Soft abstract tokens let paths share sense in a smooth space. Joint search should find better answers on tasks with more than one good route. It may also cut the risk of one early slip ruining a whole chain.
arxiv-2512-01785:
Paul Desmarchelier and co-authors simulate electric double-layer capacitors with tunable electrode metallicity. Brownian dynamics tracks ions near charged electrodes. How metallic an electrode is changes ion layering a lot. Past models fixed electrodes as perfect metals or insulators.

Their description uses the Thomas-Fermi screening length inside the metal. Tuning that length spans real metals in one frame. Better capacitor models guide energy storage design. Supercapacitors need exact ion layer physics to raise density without losing speed. Screening length can be read from metal data, so the model ties to real electrode stock rather than a free fitting knob.
arxiv-2512-02085:
Lithium fluoride is a simple two-atom molecule whose energy levels twist where two electronic states nearly meet, an event called an avoided crossing. V. G. Ushakov, A. Yu. Ermilov, and E. S. Medvedev compute in 2025 how that near-meeting reshapes the molecule's rotation-vibration spectrum.

They follow the spectrum far above the first dissociation limit, into the range where the molecule can fall apart. Their ab initio calculations cover adiabatic potentials and other molecular functions across a wide span of atomic separations. The work also extracts resonances and predissociation lifetimes, telling how long excited states survive before breaking, data that spectroscopy and molecular physics rely on.
arxiv-2512-02185:
Reasoning language models answer hard questions by thinking at length, but their size and long outputs make them costly to run. Ziyan Wang and seven co-authors propose in 2025 a pruning method that trims unimportant parameters, guided by the model's own reflection on what it needs.

Pruning promises relief for deployment in resource-constrained settings, where the newest reasoning models simply do not fit. The twist here is self-reflection: the pruning decision is informed by the model's behavior rather than a blind importance score. Done well, structured pruning could bring multi-step reasoning to hardware that currently cannot afford it.
arxiv-2512-02285:
Drones can film wildlife up close, but flying too near stresses animals and ruins the very behavior researchers want to record. Jenna Kline and three co-authors present in 2025 a drone system designed to run on the aircraft itself and adapt its behavior to the animals' vigilance state.

Human operators face an attention bottleneck: they cannot fly the drone and monitor the whole group's stress responses at once. An edge-native system that watches vigilance and adjusts its approach automatically could gather behaviorally relevant video with less distraction to the animals. Better monitoring serves conservation science, where data quality and animal welfare must be earned together.
arxiv-2512-02585:
Vinod Sarky and co-authors lay out a shared database plan for energy storage materials. Batteries, solid state cells, capacitors, and hybrid devices store and supply power in compact, portable forms. Data about their materials sits scattered across papers and labs, in mixed formats that resist comparison.

A common framework for electrochemical and electrical storage data would let researchers search and reuse results. Standard records make it easier to spot trends and avoid repeating costly tests. Shared data of this kind can speed the hunt for better batteries and capacitors for vehicles and grids. Once records share one form, a search can span years of work by labs that have never met or shared a bench.
arxiv-2512-02685:
Huankun Sheng and six co-authors teach machines to split a scene into its objects without labels. Slot attention methods carve a scene into object slots, learning structure from raw images alone. Many treat foreground and background the same way, so background clutter leaks into object slots.

Their foreground aware design adds pseudo mask guidance to steer attention toward real objects. Cleaner separation improves instance discovery on real world data. Object level representations of this kind can help robots and vision systems reason about scenes as things, not just pixels. Clean splits of this kind are the first step for any tool that must count or track what it sees.
arxiv-2512-02985:
Saaketh Desai, Prasad Iyer, and Rémi Dingreville learn the elastic rules of surfaces from the behavior of the bulk beneath. Surface elasticity governs how surfaces and interfaces carry stress and hold stability. Its key quantities include surface tension, residual surface stress, and surface stiffness.

Closed form expressions for those quantities are hard to derive from atomistic data, and they depend strongly on modeling choices. The authors learn interpretable relations from bulk properties instead. Readable rules, rather than black boxes, let materials scientists design coatings and nanostructures with predictable surface behavior. Rules you can read can be taught, fought, and fixed. Rules in a black box must be taken on faith by each new team that buys in.
arxiv-2512-03085:
Smoothing data on a ring of points is a classic math task. Justin Grieshop studies one smoothing tool for that task in this 2025 work. The tool is of Fejér type, named for a known method in Fourier work, and the ring is a finite cyclic group.

Grieshop gives a self-contained account and proves a bound with clear, exact constants. Exact constants matter because users can see how large the error can be. The result fits work in signal work and number theory. It also gives students a clean path into the proof. The proof style, with all steps shown, makes the result easy to check and teach.
arxiv-2512-03385:
Voyager 1 now samples space beyond the Sun's bubble. T. A. Porter, I. V. Moskalenko, A. C. Cummings, and G. Jóhannesson study its cosmic-ray data in this 2025 work. They ask how the nearby interstellar medium shapes the spectra measured locally.

Using the GalProp code, they vary the local gas and source distributions. They look for signatures of those distributions in low-energy spectral features. Knowing the local setup helps separate true cosmic-ray traits from local effects. That aids models of how cosmic rays spread through the Galaxy. Low-energy features are the most sensitive to local gas, making them the key diagnostic here.
arxiv-2601-06785:
Research by Tadashi Arimitsu and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with conformal preimage decay exponent of the julia sets of rational graph-directed markov systems. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. We define and investigate the conformal preimage decay exponent of the Julia sets of rational graph-directed Markov systems.

The authors show that this exponent coincides with the difference between the topological entropy and upper sequential capacity topological pressure. For the rational skew product map associated with the system S S. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-06885:
Jinwoo Hwang and three co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on protein design done on GPUs. New tools can now run the full design task on a GPU, from start to end. Yet teams know too little about how these tools act as a whole. The paper tests one such tool chain step by step.

The team runs the chain on many kinds of input. They change the length of each protein chain and the way new chains are drawn. They track how much of the GPU the work fills. In most runs, the GPU stays far from full use. The team also finds that run time shifts a great deal with chain length and draw style. The results help labs plan runs and spot waste.
arxiv-2601-07185:
Shawn Li and six co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how large language models fend off prompt attacks. A prompt attack hides a rogue instruction in a user query or in text the model pulls in. The model may then drop its set task and obey the rogue text. Teams train defenses to spot and block such tricks.

Most defenses are trained with fine-tuning on tagged data. Each sample is marked as benign or as an attack. The authors find that such defenses learn shallow clues on the surface of the text. They key on the look of a prompt, not on what the prompt asks the model to do. That habit leaves a gap. A fresh attack in a new style can slip past a guard that learned the old style by rote. The paper urges tests that probe past the surface clues.
arxiv-2601-07285:
Research by Grygoriy Torbin and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with faithfulness and DP-transformations generated by arithmetic cantor series expansions. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. The paper is devoted to the study of conditions for the Hausdorff-Besicovitch faithfulness of the family of cylinders generated by Cantor series expansions.

The authors show that there exist subgeometric Cantor series expansions for which. The corresponding families of cylinders are not faithful for the Hausdorff-Besicovitch dimension on the unit interval. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07385:
Research by Petr Zelina and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with computing patient similarity based on unstructured clinical notes. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Clinical notes hold rich yet unstructured details about diagnoses, treatments, and outcomes that are vital to precision medicine but hard to exploit at scale.

The authors introduce a method that represents each patient as a matrix built from aggregated embeddings of all their notes. Enabling robust patient similarity computation based on their latent low-rank representations. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07485:
R. Poitevineau, E. Tolley, and V. Etsebeth present a machine learning model for radio astronomy images in 2026. Their subject is radio galaxies, galaxies that shine brightly at radio wavelengths. The team trains a denoising diffusion probabilistic model, a generative method that builds images by removing noise step by step. Their version is unconditional yet guided during use.

Training data come from three sources: the FIRST radio galaxy catalog, Radio Zoo, and cutouts from the MGCLS catalog. The model learns both to synthesize new radio galaxy images and to inpaint missing parts of real ones. A masked guided approach steers that filling-in process. Such tools can help astronomers test pipelines and complete damaged survey images.
arxiv-2601-07785:
The Euclid team models a source of noise that galaxy shapes bring to their own survey of the cosmos. Galaxy shapes do not point at random; their alignments track the large scale web of matter. These intrinsic alignments can spoil weak gravitational lensing work. The team builds a semi-analytic model of galaxy shapes and alignments inside the Euclid Flagship run. Their 2026 preprint predicts the contamination in Euclid's lensing observations.

Euclid is a space telescope that scans billions of galaxies to map dark matter and dark energy. Weak lensing reads that map from tiny bends in galaxy shapes. Intrinsic alignments add a false signal on top. A good guess of its size lets the team correct for it. The Flagship run gives a true to life test universe. The paper serves cosmologists preparing Euclid data analysis. This is a check run, done before the real sky data comes in.
arxiv-2601-07885:
Weipeng Jiang and colleagues uncover a safety flaw in how language models read emoticons. Emoticons convey feelings in digital communication, yet their safety implications for large language models are largely unexplored. The authors name the flaw emoticon semantic confusion. Under it, models misread ASCII emoticons and perform unintended, even destructive, actions. Their 2026 preprint documents the vulnerability.

A smiley built from punctuation looks trivial, but models may attach the wrong intent to it. In agentic settings, a misread symbol could steer real tool calls. Finding such flaws before deployment is the point of this research. The study widens the range of inputs safety testing must cover. It serves AI safety scholars and red teams. Small symbols, the authors argue, can carry big risks.
arxiv-2601-08185: Ming-Chiang Chang and co-authors describe self-driving labs that explore new materials with human guidance. Their 2026 arXiv paper combines automated phase identification with AI-assisted human reasoning. Robotic platforms can search huge chemical and processing spaces far faster than manual work. Such labs raise throughput on repeat experiments and can use expert judgment. Human input steers the search toward user-defined goals, such as better performance metrics. The work speaks to researchers building autonomous labs that stay aligned with what scientists actually want.
arxiv-2601-08985:
Julia Sheffler and six co-authors pin down the age of a near group of stars called the Ursa Major group. The group is one of the close star sets to us. Yet past age calls span a wide range, from young to near a billion years. Age sets how we read the past of the group and of its stars.

The team uses the large set of group picks to date. They bring more than one age tool to bear on the same stars. Tools span spin rate, chem marks, and light curves from space scopes. A joint call from all tools is more firm than one tool alone. A reader in star work gets a new age with a clear base in many lines of proof.
arxiv-2601-09285:
Mianzhi Pan and seven co-authors help chat models call the 3D form of metal organic frameworks. Such frameworks are crystal sponges with vast use, from gas trap to drug haul. Their 3D form sets their use. Chat models can draft crystals, but these sponges hold vast counts of atoms in strict plans. A plain model call oft breaks that plan.

The team adds space thought steps to the model. Steps force it to weigh how atoms sit next to each, not just which atoms are there. That care may lift true calls for sponge forms. A reader in stuffs work gets a path to AI calls that respect the hard space rules of real sponges.
arxiv-2601-09485:
Jianhang Ai and Christos Pelekis bound the tail chances of a classic sampling variable. Their 2026 arXiv paper concerns the hypergeometric distribution, which counts black marbles drawn without replacement from an urn. The question is how small the chance of extreme counts can be shown to be.

Tail bounds turn a vague sense of rarity into a hard number. Such bounds back tests in statistics, audits, and randomized algorithms. The authors work on lower bounds, the harder direction, since they must show extreme draws are not too rare. Sharp bounds in both directions make the classic urn model fully quantitative.
arxiv-2601-09585:
J. Jiang and nine co-authors map the light spectrum of a special ytterbium ion. Their 2026 arXiv paper reports high-resolution spectroscopy of the isotope 173Yb+. That isotope has a richer hyperfine structure than its siblings, which favors better clock transitions.

That structure also suits probes of new physics and richer quantum computing designs. Yet the ion's electronic spectrum has stayed poorly characterized until now. The team measures it in fine detail. Precise line positions are the raw material for atomic clocks and for searches that compare spectra against theory to spot cracks in known physics.
arxiv-2601-09785:
Yoav Zigdon solves string theory's low-energy equations to build a ball of strings. His 2026 arXiv paper presents the Superball of Strings. The solution represents a microcanonical ensemble of highly excited superstrings.

The result is a static, spherically symmetric fuzzball made of BPS strings. Its size follows a random walk scaling. Fuzzballs are the leading string-theory picture of what a black hole really is inside. Instead of a smooth hole with a sharp edge, the mass sits in a tangled ball of string. A clean ensemble solution gives that program a concrete case that others can check line by line.
arxiv-2601-10385:
Eliya Blumenthal, Natan Karaev, and Shay Hacohen-Gourgy clear a quantum memory fast with a Rabi drive. High Q cavity modes are a lean way to store quantum states. Their shield from noise is their draw. That same shield makes them hard to clear. A slow clear step caps how fast a chip can cycle.

Past clears use weak links or long measure steps. The team drive the mode with a Rabi tone. The drive cools the mode in a smooth flow. No measure step is used. Their test shows a fast, clean reset on a real rig.
arxiv-2601-10585:
Elizabeth K. Jones, Samuel Hadden, and Daniel Tamayo study mean motion resonances, a key effect in orbital dynamics. A resonance occurs when two orbiting bodies fall into a steady rhythm of periods. Old theory ranks these resonances by strength. First-order ones look strong, while higher orders fade fast as orbits grow round.

The authors show that conjunctions, the close passes of the two bodies, can cancel each other out. Those canceling effects make higher-order resonances weaker than the old ranking suggests. The finding helps explain why first-order resonances rule in practice. It matters for models of planets and moons whose orbits lock into step.
arxiv-2601-10885:
Diogo D. Carvalho, Pablo J. Bilbao, Warren B. Mori, Luis O. Silva, and E. Paulo Alves learn collision operators from plasma data. Collisions set how a plasma transports heat and momentum. Their operator is often guessed or simplified. The team instead infers it from phase space data, the full map of particle positions and speeds.

Their method pairs a differentiable kinetic simulator with gradient-based optimization. The simulator's core is a differentiable Fokker-Planck solver. Because it is differentiable, gradients can steer the operator toward the one that best matches the data. The approach could sharpen plasma models for fusion and space physics, where collision rules are often the weakest link.
arxiv-2601-10985:
Ieng-Wai Un, Subhajit Sarkar, and Yonatan Sivan build a quantum optical theory of how Drude metals respond to few-femtosecond light pulses. Very short pulses slam energy into a material faster than its electrons can settle. Transparent conducting oxides are the test materials here. Their conduction band is curved in a way that bends the usual response rules.

The team's framework works in energy space with a density matrix. It tracks electron populations, the permittivity, and quantum coherences between states. Against older models, it claims much simpler math at the same accuracy. Ultrafast optics needs such tools: experiments now run at time scales where older models strain.
arxiv-2601-11285:
Frank Stefani updates a climate model that splits blame between two drivers. His 2026 preprint weighs solar forces next to human ones. The goal is to count how much each one drove warming. A past work from 2021 made the first such count.

The method joins two predictors in one double regression. One is the log of carbon dioxide levels in the air. The other is the geomagnetic aa-index, a proxy for the Sun. Both are fit to sea surface temperatures since the mid-1800s. The new work refines the fit and the forecast that flows from it. The forecast spans the next 130 years in the earlier design.
arxiv-2601-11485:
S. Chernov studies the phase of the visibility function in radio work. The 2026 preprint takes an analytical route to the problem. In radio interferometry, the visibility function is the core data. It is complex, with both amplitude and phase parts.

Phase holds much of the shape data for a source. Chernov checks how phase depends on the base projection. The setting is radio interferometry with space-based baselines. Those baselines reach up to six Earth diameters in length. Long baselines give sharp views of compact radio sources. Knowing phase behavior helps turn raw data into images. The work serves very-long-baseline methods in radio astronomy.
arxiv-2601-11585:
Hyunjun Kim filters context for LLM agents with information theory. The 2026 preprint names the frame Entropic Context Shaping, or ECS. Context work for agents must sort useful text from distractors. Misleading context can pull an agent's answer off course.

ECS measures context utility by a shift in answers. It checks how the model's answer distribution moves. Useful context shifts the spread toward the correct answer. Distractors shift it away or add noise with no gain. That score lets the system keep what helps and drop the rest. Cleaner context means fewer tokens and fewer errors. The frame gives agents a principled way to pack context.
arxiv-2601-11885:
Zhifei Li, Ziyue Qin, Xiangyu Luo, and their co-authors match entities across two knowledge graphs that hold images and text. The task is to find which nodes in each graph name the same thing. Rich data in each mode should help, but shallow traits can mislead.

Their model, named MyGram in the work, is a graph transformer that is aware of each mode. It also tracks the global spread of traits. By use of form in each mode, it aims for more sound matches. Good matches help merge data from many sources.
arxiv-2601-11985:
M. Shekari Tousi and K. Azizi weigh if baryons with two top quarks could exist. Baryons are parts made of three quarks. Top quarks are the heaviest known quarks, so a pair in one baryon is an extreme case.

They give a full theory check of the masses of such states. The set spans five named forms with unlike light quarks and other heavy quarks. Mass checks show if such states could bind at all. The work guides searches, even if the odds are low.  Even a null result would bound how such states can form.
arxiv-2601-12085:
Yu-Xuan Zhang and Jing-Ling Chen ask if a famed test for entanglement can be stretched to a stronger quantum link. Entanglement, Bell nonlocality, and EPR steering are three grades of quantum link. Peres gave a simple spectral test for entanglement based on partial transpose.

No test of like grace yet exists for steering in a two-qubit system. They explore in a systematic way if such a Peres-type test can be built. A simple steering test would aid labs that certify quantum links. The work maps what such a test can and cannot do.
arxiv-2601-12185:
Mark L. Lewis sharpens a theorem of Artin on characters of a finite group. Characters are traces of group representations, and rational valued ones are a key subset. He shows the dimension of the space they span has a clean count.

That count equals the number of conjugacy classes of cyclic subgroups of the group. A count in terms of group form is easier to use than a span check. The result adds a neat bridge between character theory and subgroup structure. It is classed under representation theory of finite groups.
arxiv-2601-12385:
Feifei Li and seven co authors study how to learn the grammar of a programming language from the outside. In a black box setup, one can run code and watch what works, but the rules stay hidden. Past ways to infer those rules fail to scale. They take too long on the large, real world languages that coders use each day.

Grammar inference matters because a clear grammar is the base for many code tools. Tests, parsers, and safety checks all lean on it. The team takes up the scale problem for complex languages head on. Their work asks how far inference can go when time is tight and the language is large. The paper was set for a major software engineering venue in 2026.
arxiv-2601-12585:
Mengli Dawn Duan, Yuhe Sissi Jiang, Matthew Varona, and Carolina Nobre test how well AI reads charts. Multimodal language models are now used to interpret visualizations of many kinds. Yet little is known about why they fail when they do. The team present the first systematic analysis of barriers to visualization literacy in such models.

They use a regenerated literacy test with synthetic data as their benchmark. They then open code 309 wrong responses from four top models. Their coding uses a barrier centered strategy borrowed from human literacy research. Sorting errors by barrier shows which chart skills models lack most. That map can guide both training and chart design for AI readers.
arxiv-2601-12885:
Shima Sadat Mousavi, Xiao Tan, and Aaron D. Ames certify safety constraints for controlled systems. Control barrier functions keep a system inside a safe set by restricting its inputs. Real systems often carry many such constraints at once. Checking them only at sampled points leaves gaps between the samples.

The team develop certificates that propagate compatibility from sampled vertices to their convex hull. Under mild concavity and affinity assumptions, the whole hull inherits feasibility. They present three sufficient conditions for that step. Feasible inputs can be obtained per coordinate, with a common input, or by convex blending. Set wise certificates could make safety checks both faster and more trustworthy.
arxiv-2601-12985:
Melanie A. Kilian and David Elsweiler build a taxonomy of information request intents in work tasks. Classifying query intents can improve retrieval by aligning results with user motivations. Existing taxonomies come mostly from system log data. They capture isolated information needs, while broader task context often stays unaddressed.

Their taxonomy is task based, organized around rules, resources, and restrictions. Those three lenses describe why a person asks within a larger job. Their paper was set for a 2026 venue on human information interaction. Task aware search could serve professionals far better than keyword matching. The work bridges information science and workplace studies.
arxiv-2601-13285:
Syed Akbar Hussain and co-authors probe thin films that mix niobium with uranium. The films span a set range of uranium share. They were made by DC magnetron sputtering, a spray of atoms in a vacuum, at room terms. Such films join a superconductor base with a heavy actinide guest.

X-ray checks show a steady shift in one niobium peak as uranium grows. That shift fits a clean swap of uranium for niobium in the grid. The team also tracks odd traits in how the films resist current. They tie those traits to spin orbit links born in the film. For matter staff, the films give a tuneable case of how a heavy guest bends a superconductor.
arxiv-2601-13385:
Lavsen Dahal, Yubraj Bhandari, Geoffrey D. Rubin, and Joseph Y. Lo use organ aware focus to triage CT scans. CT is a high load scan kind. Fast and sound triage can lift care and cut doctor strain. A whole study must be tagged with a firm score and with proof set in the scan.

Off the shelf vision language models strain at that task. They cope poorly with 3D body plans, shifts in scan style, and noisy report based teach. The team's focus step makes the model weigh the right organ for each call. That tie of call to place gives proof a doctor can check. For scan teams, a call with proof beats a bare score.
arxiv-2601-13685:
Sin-Yu Huang, Lele Wang, and Vincent Wong study how AI agents can share less data yet plan far ahead in 2026. Agentic AI can sense its surroundings, reason, and act to reach goals. Long-horizon tasks need many steps of planning, which can mean much data traffic. Sending all raw data wastes bandwidth.

Task-oriented communication sends only the data a task truly needs. The team links this lean sharing to hierarchical planning, where big goals split into sub-goals. Lean links could let agent teams work over weak networks. That matters for robots, drones, and far-flung sensors.
arxiv-2601-13885:
Esma Balkır and co-authors adapt a smart testing idea to grade AI models with fewer items in 2026. Computerized adaptive testing picks next questions based on past answers. It has worked well for multiple-choice benchmarks. Modern model evals, though, use generation tasks scored on a continuous scale.

Scores like ROUGE, BLEU, and judge ratings are bounded but not just right or wrong. The team extends item response theory to such scores. They swap the Bernoulli response model for a heteroskedastic normal one. Confident rankings with fewer items would cut the cost of model evals.
arxiv-2601-13985:
Andrea Mazzolini and co-authors ask if simple null models can explain systems built from parts in 2026. Component systems are ensembles built from a shared repertoire of modular parts. They appear in biological, ecological, technological, and socio-cultural domains. Genomes, texts, cities, and software all fit this frame.

Such systems show statistical regularities that can look like laws of physics. A null model is a bare random baseline with the same basic limits. If the baseline reproduces the patterns, no deeper law is needed. The work tests how far that plain account can go.
arxiv-2601-14385:
E. Zackrisson leads a team on lensed star clusters in this 2026 paper. Strongly lensed star clusters have been detected out to redshift ten in galaxy cluster fields with the James Webb Space Telescope. Lensing bends light, so one cluster can appear as mirror images across a critical curve. The standard assumption is simple. Both images should show identical spectral energy distributions.

The team asks what happens when the two images do not match. Their title proposes an answer: a mismatch could signal a top-heavy stellar initial mass function. That means the cluster made more massive stars than usual. Extreme stars in high-redshift clusters could leave the same mark.
arxiv-2601-14585: Vertices sit on a circumference in the plane, and directed line segments link pairs of them. When the segments form closed cycles and each turn runs anti-clockwise, the figure is a cyclic polygon. This 2026 math paper studies star decompositions of such a polygon, ways to split it into star-shaped parts. The evidence pack lists no authors for this entry. The abstract gives definitions only. So the paper's main results cannot be stated from the evidence.
arxiv-2601-14685:
K. Kade and a large team model a distant galaxy in this 2026 paper. The galaxy is the submillimeter galaxy G09v1.97. It is strongly lensed, so its light is magnified and stretched by a foreground mass. The formation mechanisms of intensely starbursting galaxies at high redshift remain unknown. One possible mechanism is mergers and interactions, which can drive intense star formation.

Detecting those mergers at high redshift remains a challenge. Lensing helps by magnifying the view. The team gives detailed lens modeling and kinematics for this galaxy. Kinematics map how its gas moves, which can betray a merger in progress. Readers get a close look at how one extreme young galaxy is built.
arxiv-2601-15085:
Quantum chromodynamics, the theory of the strong force, describes hadrons in two very different ways. A 2026 arXiv review takes up the task of joining those two views. In one view, a hadron at rest is a bound state shaped by confinement and interquark forces.

In the other view, a fast hadron is a swarm of partons. That picture uses parton distribution functions and form factors to state what is inside. The review builds one frame that connects the two domains. It draws mostly on the authors' own studies from the past few years.
arxiv-2601-15185:
L Elliott puts an algebraic topology on the group of homeomorphisms of a space. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with the Zariski topology, a spare topology built from algebraic sets. Here it is placed on a general group of structure-preserving maps.

The topology is the coarsest one with a set property. Sets cut out by word equations in the group must come out open. In such a set, a product of powers of one element with fixed elements stays away from the identity. The paper studies what this topology looks like for homeomorphism groups.
arxiv-2601-15685:
Myong-Hwan Ri presents a bold claim about two classic equations in a 2026 arXiv paper. The Navier-Stokes equations govern fluid flow. The Euler equations govern it without viscosity. Both are famous for open questions about global solutions. Ri shows that any Leray-Hopf weak solution of Navier-Stokes, in dimension three or more, has stronger regularity than first assumed. The initial data lie in a Sobolev space past a threshold.

The title states the payoff: global solvability for the Euler equations follows. Claims of this size draw close scrutiny in fluid dynamics. A full proof would settle questions that have stood for decades. The abstract states the result in direct terms. Readers should treat it as the author's claim, to be weighed by expert review of the full argument.
arxiv-2601-15885:
Chaitanya Gupta and Anthony J. Short study an artifact in quantum walk models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Quantum walks are discrete spacetime models. They can simulate Dirac particles, the relativistic electrons of theory. Fermion doubling is a known flaw in such models. High-momentum states produce extra low-energy solutions. Those extra solutions behave like additional Dirac particles. A simulation then shows particles that should not exist.

Doubling has plagued lattice models for decades. Each new framework must face it in its own way. The authors examine how it arises in Dirac quantum walks. Understanding the artifact's roots points to cures or workarounds. For quantum simulation, faithful particle behavior is the whole point. Spurious copies corrupt predictions, so mapping the flaw is essential work.
arxiv-2601-16085:
Francesco Aprile builds four point links in a strong gravity theory by bootstrap steps. His 2026 preprint works in the AdS and sphere space of string theory. The links join four fields, some with high modes. One field is a pair type field and three are single fields. Past ways to find such links need long direct sums.

Aprile uses the rules of how fields split and join. Those rules, plus a few firm needs, pin the link form down. No long sum over states is then needed. The method is the first in a chain on high mode links. It shows how far pure rules can reach in this theory.
arxiv-2601-16285:
Joel Dahne, Javier Gómez-Serrano and Joana Pech-Alberich prove a tone drop for plain shapes. Their 2026 preprint deals with the first tone of a fixed area shape. Tone here is the first Dirichlet value, a maths mark of how a drum or wave acts. Shapes are plain forms with N sides of same length and angle. The team fixes the area and varies the side count.

They prove the first tone falls as side count grows. They also prove the step ratio falls in the same way. A clean fall was guessed but not yet proved in full. The proof closes that gap for all side counts from three up. It is a neat result in shape maths.
arxiv-2601-16485:
Hiroki Shibata and coauthors sum palindromes and suffix trees on tries as they grow. Their 2026 preprint deals with tries, tree forms of word sets. A trie is a broad form of a lone string in text maths. Tasks span top palindromes and split palindromes in the trie. Online sums must update as new signs join the trie.

Fast online sums serve live text sets that grow by the day. Suffix trees on tries back fast search in those sets. The team gives steps that keep both sums true live. Steps that hold live cut rebuild cost to nil. The work is in the theory of text code steps.
arxiv-2601-16785:
Evgeny Skvortsov loosens a famed frame for field models in physics. The AKSZ frame packs a model's data in one neat math form. That form needs a strict no-gap trait to work. His 2026 preprint drops that strict trait. In its place, a softer form takes the lead. This shift lets the frame hold models that are not purely shape-based.

The action of a model then writes in space-time forms. It reads like a broad kin of the classic action. Such broad frames can hold more real-world fields. They may also join gravity and matter in new ways. Pure math gains a tool with wider reach.
arxiv-2601-17485:
J. J. Segura builds a method to map fractures in rock from sparse measures. Fractured media hide their cracks below ground. Field teams get only sparse point data and traces of cracks in three dimensions. Segura maps those points onto flat fracture planes inferred from trace lines. Each plane gets its own local grid.

A convex objective blends the data with a smooth prior. It adds a sparsity penalty on curvelet terms to keep sharp edges. The result is a sparse-to-dense rebuild of the fracture field. Such maps guide water, oil, and geothermal work. They also help judge where cracks may leak. The method respects the flat, sharp nature of real fractures.
arxiv-2601-17585:
Matija Luka Kukić and co-authors fix a mismatch in sequence labeling with decoder-only models. Labeling tasks tag each token in a sequence. They gain from context on both sides of each token. Decoder models, though, read only the prefix. That one-way view has pushed labeling toward encoder models. The team uses sequence repetition to help.

Repeating the sequence boosts token embeddings in their tests. It gives the decoder a second view of each token. Better labeling serves search, health records, and language tools. If decoders can label well, one model family can do more jobs. The trick is simple, which aids uptake. The work tests it on labeling tasks.
arxiv-2601-17685:
Haixin Jiang, Xinyu Chen, and Liang Chen speed up nonuniform sampling series with a sinh window. Sampling series rebuild signals from uneven samples. Recent window tricks sped the nonuniform Fourier transform and Shannon sampling. The authors bring a sinh-type function to Lagrangian nonuniform sampling. Their goal is faster convergence of the series. Theory gives error estimates for the method.

Numeric tests back the estimates, as the abstract states. Faster series mean fewer terms for the same accuracy. Uneven samples arise in medical scans and sensor nets. A leaner rebuild saves time in all of them. The sinh choice is the novel twist. It shows window design still has room to grow.
arxiv-2601-17785:
Tushar Jain reviews how blockchains can stay safe once quantum computers grow strong. His 2026 preprint looks at digital signature schemes that resist quantum attack. Most coins and chains today rely on elliptic curve methods. Those methods rest on math problems that a quantum method named Shor's algorithm can break. If that break comes, forged signatures could put whole chains at risk.

The paper weighs how well the quantum-safe options perform in real blockchain use. Speed, size, and cost all matter when a chain checks each trade. A scheme that is safe but too slow may not fit live networks. The study gives chain builders a guide for a change they may one day have to make.
arxiv-2601-18185:
Taisuke Hoshino proves structural results about von Neumann algebras built from graphs. His 2026 preprint studies relative bi-exactness. The algebras come from graph products and from graph-wreath products of groups. In a graph product, groups at the vertices combine with commutation rules set by the graph's edges. Hoshino obtains relative bi-exactness for the von Neumann algebras of such products, and for their wreath versions as well.

Bi-exactness is a rigidity trait with strong fallout for an algebra's structure. Extending it to graph-based products widens a key toolkit in operator algebras. The results help classify algebras that arise from groups on graphs. Pure results of this kind often pay off far from their source.
arxiv-2601-18485:
Keyun Su and three colleagues chart the cross shape of long threads of gas and dust in our own galaxy. Such threads are the bones of the star fields where new stars form. Their cross shape, read from the side, can hint at how each thread was made. The team pull two maps for each thread: how thick the gas is, and how warm its dust runs.

They stack those maps for a set of threads and read the trends. Some threads sit in calm zones, and some sit in zones that press on one side more than the next. A lopsided home can bend the cross shape in ways the maps can show. The work gives fresh clues on how the great threads of the galaxy form and change. Those clues feed the tale of how stars are born.
arxiv-2601-18885:
Eugenio Carretta studies old star groups to read what the first huge stars left in them. The groups were born soon past the start of space. Their small stars still live, but their huge stars died long ago. No eye can now see what mix of huge stars the groups were born with. That mix set how much of each kind of stuff the group would hold in time.

Carretta reads the stuff in the groups' stars with fine light tools. He sets the counts for two kinds of stuff side by side: stuff made in calm burn, and stuff made in the blast of a dying huge star. The pair of counts can tell the two paths apart. That split could pin the birth mix of huge stars. Such a pin would feed the tale of how the first stars built the stuff of worlds.
arxiv-2601-19085:
Joshua V. Dillon argues that in brains and in small models alike, speed is a sign of confidence. Living neural systems must act fast on tight energy budgets, and evolution's answer is to act on the first signal. Circuits that crown the first firing cell, and codes based on time to first spike, both treat timing as trust.

Dillon applies the same rule to teams of tiny recursive models. Letting the first model to halt speak for the team gives strong results on a hard Sudoku test set. The trick is cheap: no voting scheme, just trust in the fastest finisher.
arxiv-2601-19185:
M. N. Achasov and a large team measure a basic ratio that describes the neutron's inner makeup. The experiment smashes electrons into their antimatter twins at the VEPP-2000 collider in Russia. Some collisions create a neutron and an antineutron. From those events the team extracts the ratio of the neutron's electric form factor to its magnetic one.

The electric and magnetic factors describe how charge and magnetism are spread inside the neutron. In this time like regime, reached through annihilation, the values can differ sharply from the familiar ones. Such measures test the theory of the strong force where it is hardest to compute.
arxiv-2601-19285:
Xinyu Zhou, Jiawei Zhang, and Stephen J. Wright explain why diffusion models sometimes copy their training data. Diffusion models make strikingly good images and media, yet they can also memorize, spitting out near copies of training items. That behavior is a legal and privacy risk, not just a quirk.

The team builds a theory around the score function, the field that guides the generation. Smoothing that function, they argue, explains and may curb memorization. An optimization based account turns a vague worry into knobs that trainers can turn. They can use them when they set up a run and judge how much copying is too much.
arxiv-2601-19485:
Liang Chang, Yilong Wang, and Saifei Zhai work at the meeting point of topology and algebra. The Kuperberg invariant is a number computed from a three-dimensional shape, built using a Hopf algebra. A basic question is whether that number depends on extra choices made along the way. If it does not, the invariant is called gauge invariant, and it is far more useful.

The authors prove gauge invariance for the Weeks manifold under any framing. The Weeks manifold is a famous closed hyperbolic shape. They also prove the same for the three-dimensional torus. These are the first such examples built from hyperbolic shapes for general Hopf algebras. The results back a program of producing algebraic invariants by topological means.
arxiv-2601-19985:
Jean-François Gonzalez and Stéphane Michoulier study a bottleneck in planet formation: grains must grow, but they drift and shatter. Small dust grains in protoplanetary discs spiral inward and fragment on collision. Two ideas may break the barrier: porous grains, and the streaming instability, which clumps grains together. The streaming instability is currently the favoured route to planetesimals.

The authors examine conditions near the carbon monoxide snow line, where CO freezes out. They ask whether that location favours strong clumping when grains are porous. Snow lines change grain properties, so they are natural places to test formation theories. The results refine where the first planetesimals are likeliest to form.
arxiv-2601-20185:
Husein Zolkepli improves X-Codec-2.0, a neural audio codec used for speech modeling in many languages. The original system runs at a latent rate of fifty frames per second and a sampling rate suited to narrow speech. That setup limits both time efficiency and sound fidelity.

The new version lowers the latent rate and doubles the sampling rate, which should give cleaner audio with fewer tokens per second. Both changes matter for multilingual speech tools, where data rates and quality vary by language. A more efficient codec helps speech models train and run on less hardware.
arxiv-2601-20585:
Aiming Hao and four colleagues present ranking-aware reinforcement learning for ordinal ranking, where labels come in an ordered scale such as star ratings. Ordinal tasks are hard because the labels depend on each other in order, which conventional methods model poorly. Their framework, RARL, learns those relationships explicitly.

At its core is a unified objective that joins regression and learning-to-rank so each improves the other. Regression pins down the level; ranking enforces the order. Ordinal outputs drive recommendations, grading, and medical staging, so respecting order rather than treating labels as plain classes should raise accuracy across those uses.
arxiv-2601-20985:
Abdullah Akgül and four co-authors blend two frameworks for control that must plan far ahead. Their 2026 paper presents distributional active inference. Optimal control of complex environments with robots faces two intertwined challenges. One is organizing sensory state information well. The other is far-sighted action planning. Reinforcement learning addresses only the latter. That leaves it sample-inefficient, the authors note.

Active inference is a leading process theory of how brains handle both problems at once. The paper distributes that theory, tracking full distributions rather than point estimates. Richer state handling should sharpen planning in turn. The work targets robots that must act wisely with limited trials. It offers a brain-inspired route to control that learns faster from experience.
arxiv-2601-21085:
Elias Charnay and six co-authors report the first direct sighting of a predicted pattern in turbulent light. Their 2026 paper observes two-time, ballistic correlations in integrable turbulence. Such correlations describe the emergent statistics of complex systems. Their direct measure in experiments is hard. The team worked with a photonic platform. Its dynamics follow the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation.

Integrable turbulence is disorder that still obeys exact math. Ballistic correlations spread at a steady speed, like a thrown ball. Seeing them confirms a deep prediction about such systems. The platform lets the team watch correlations form in real time. Results like this test whether theory's tidy picture survives the lab. The paper joins optics with the physics of complex waves.
arxiv-2601-21385:
Jakob M. Grzesik and seven co-authors set out a general theory for beams of free electrons meeting quantum optical systems. Free electrons are flexible probes, but their interplay with bound quantum systems lacked a unified frame. The theory covers arbitrary light environments around the target.

The framework widens the quantum optics toolbox to include electron beams. Possible uses include finely tuned quantum control, imaging, and spectroscopy at very small scales. A shared theory lets device builders compare designs on common ground. It also links electron microscopy with quantum light work, two fields that have mostly grown apart.
arxiv-2601-21685:
Jools D. Clarke, Gordon Yip, and Nikolaos Nikolaou explain black-box regression models whose inputs have internal structure. Their framework perturbs the input and watches the output move. Unlike standard tools, it accounts for correlations inside the structured input.

Ignoring those correlations can credit the wrong part of the input. The team demonstrates the method on machine learning retrievals of an exoplanet's atmosphere from transit data. The planet used is WASP-107b, a well-studied case. Trustworthy explanations matter in astronomy, where a model's answer about a distant world cannot be checked by hand.
arxiv-2601-21785:
Minge Liu and co-authors examine a small asteroid that never strays far from Earth. The object, called Kamo'oalewa, is a quasi-satellite of Earth and the first target of China's Tianwen-2 sample return mission. Its reflected light shows distinctive features that hint at an unusual surface and history.

The 2026 study re-analyzes the asteroid's spectrum in visible and near-infrared light. From that spectrum the authors study what the surface is made of. They also study how space weathering has changed it. Space weathering is the slow darkening caused by sun and particles. Knowing the surface in advance helps the mission plan its sampling. And helps scientists judge whether this object is a chip off the Moon, as some have proposed.
arxiv-2601-21985:
Yunyang Li and co-authors improve how generative models build three-dimensional molecules. A good model must respect Euclidean symmetries, since a molecule rotated in space is the same molecule. It should also favor shapes that are stable and low in energy.

In practice, symmetry-respecting diffusion models inherit biases from the rough, semi-empirical data they train on. They copy those errors instead of learning the true equilibrium shapes given by high-quality physics. The team's 2026 preprint, Elign, aligns such diffusion models using foundational machine learning force fields as the reference. Better molecular generators feed drug discovery, where plausible, stable candidate shapes are the starting point for everything else.
arxiv-2601-22085:
Matthew Satriano and Evan Sundbo connect a counting tool to the shape of geometric spaces. They introduce an integral version of the Hodge polynomial. That function encodes the integral cohomology of smooth projective varieties. In plain terms, it counts holes and cycles in a refined way.

The authors prove their polynomial is well-defined on the Grothendieck ring of varieties, a ring built by cutting spaces into pieces and tracking the pieces. As a consequence, varieties that are equivalent in that ring, called K-equivalent, must have isomorphic integral cohomology groups. Their 2026 preprint strengthens a bridge between algebraic bookkeeping and topology, giving geometers a finer invariant to tell spaces apart.
arxiv-2601-22185:
Alberto Maria Mongardini and Alessandro Mei assemble evidence on one of crypto's wildest corners. Meme coins are among the most active, and least observable, parts of the cryptocurrency market. They churn extremely fast, show minimal project commitment, and attract widespread fraud.

Countless meme coins launch across multiple blockchains while relying on off-chain websites and social accounts to look legitimate. The authors' 2026 preprint presents MemeChain, a multimodal, cross-chain dataset built for meme coin forensics and risk analysis. The dataset joins on-chain records with web and social traces. That lets researchers and regulators study how scams are staged. It is a first step toward tools that warn buyers before the collapse.
arxiv-2601-22285:
Luca Zhou, Bo Zhao, Rose Yu, and Emanuele Rodolà ask what makes two trained models safe to merge into one. Merging blends the weights of models tuned for split tasks. Their 2026 preprint tests a common belief: that merge success is a trait of the models alone.

With a frame that works across model shapes, they show success hangs on the merge method and the partner tasks too. They use plain pairwise scores that a user can read. Those scores help predict a good merge before it is tried. The work can save teams much wasted blend work.
arxiv-2601-22385:
Chaoyue He and five co-authors refine how models learn from ranked answers. Direct Preference Optimization steers a model toward the answers people liked more. Their 2026 preprint notes that the method uses one global heat dial for all pairs, as if each pair taught the same amount.

Real pairs differ: some show clear safety or fact fails, others show mere taste. Their variant scores each pair by its sense content and sets the dial per pair. Fairer weighting could yield models that learn the key lessons fast. It may also cut drift from noisy pairs. The work sharpens a core training tool.
arxiv-2601-22485:
Naen Xu and a large team shield language models from fraud with a web of linked facts. Their 2026 preprint, FraudShield, notes that models now run key flows like contract checks and job screens. Fraudulent inputs can bend those flows toward loss or harm.

A knowledge graph gives the model firm facts to check claims against. The shield aims to spot and block the bend before it acts. Such guards matter as models take on money-linked work. The work tests a graph-based defense in real flows. It seeks safety without gutting the model's use.
arxiv-2601-22685:
Su Binyi, Huang Chenghao, and Chen Haiyong teach a detector to say unknown when it sees a class it was never given. Zero-shot detection names known classes in new images, while out-of-vocabulary ones must be refused. Their 2026 preprint, OOVDet, notes that past tools overfit the known set and wave strangers through.

Their method learns a low-density prior: a sense of where known classes live, so stray ones stand out. Honest refusal matters in safety and watch tasks. The work seeks both sharp naming and firm rejection. That pair is harder than either alone.
arxiv-2601-22985:
Pyo Min Hong and Albert No watermark text from diffusion language models, a new target for marking. Unlike standard models, these models can produce tokens in any order. A perfect predictor would not care about that order, but real models depend strongly on the unmasking sequence.

Their method, dgMARK, turns that order sensitivity into a channel for a hidden mark. A reliable mark helps prove where a text came from. Watermarking matters as AI text spreads into news, school, and legal settings. Order sensitivity, a flaw for prediction, becomes the feature here: the watermark rides on how tokens get unmasked.
arxiv-2601-23085:
Mohanna Hoveyda and four co-authors answer complex questions that carry strict logical conditions. A query may demand results meeting several constraints joined by and, or, and not. Neural search often ignores those operators, while purely generative reasoning applies them unevenly.

Their system, OrLog, joins language models with probabilistic reasoning to enforce the logic. Candidate answers are checked against the query's structure in a principled way. Reliable constraint handling matters for legal, medical, and product search, where a missed not changes the answer. Probabilistic reasoning supplies the discipline, so answers must satisfy the query's conjunctions, disjunctions, and negations in a consistent way.
arxiv-2601-23185:
Markus Bachmayr and three co-authors study how pre-scaling affects training neural networks for parametric equations. These networks estimate solutions of partial differential equations that depend on parameters. Training can be slow or unstable when the underlying operators are badly scaled.

Using well-conditioned frame forms of the operators, they show clear gains for standard training methods. They also analyze numeric stability, not just speed. Reliable training matters as neural solvers move into engineering and science workflows. Frame forms are the pre-scaling vehicle, re-expressing operators so standard optimizers see a well-scaled problem. Real improvement in standard training performance is the reported effect, not a marginal gain.
arxiv-2601-23285:
MH Farhadi, Ali Rabiee, and Sima Ghafoori jointly learn user intent and assistance in shared autonomy systems. Shared autonomy blends human control with robotic help, as in assistive arms or wheelchairs. The system must infer what the user wants and choose how much help to give, while respecting user agency.

Older methods used fixed blending ratios or split inference from arbitration. Their end-to-end optimization learns belief and policy together. Joint learning should adapt assistance more gracefully in unstructured, everyday settings. Static blending ratios are the baseline habit being replaced, because fixed help levels cannot fit unstructured environments.
arxiv-2604-01185:
Lea Delance and five co-authors study how charged chain molecules stick to a solid in a liquid. Their 2026 paper links that sticking to a flaw in how drops pull back. Drop control matters for inkjet printing, health care tools, and food work.

Drops that spring and stretch slide more slowly on tilted water-shedding surfaces. They also stretch out more than plain drops do as they slide. Why this happens at the small scale is still not well known. The team works at the surface where a drop meets the solid. What they find there should help explain the slow, stretched slide. The work fits fields that must place small drops with care.
