asterius-the-extant-writings-of-asterius:
Asterius Urbanus wrote against the Montanist prophets in the late 100s. The Montanists claimed a new prophecy was speaking through them. Almost nothing of his work survives in its own right today.

Fragments quoted by the historian Eusebius carry all that remains. An 1885 Fathers volume gathers those scraps for modern readers. In them, a contemporary attacks the new prophecy movement head-on. Historians prize the pieces as rare firsthand evidence. They open a window on one of the early Church's fiercest inner battles. Few fights shaped the young faith more than the struggle over who could claim the Spirit's voice.
athenagoras-the-treatise-of-athenagoras-:
Athenagoras, a Christian philosopher, addressed his treatise to two emperors around 177. Marcus Aurelius and Commodus held the Roman throne at the time. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers edition preserves his plea in English.

Christians then stood accused of atheism, cannibal feasts, and loose morals. Athenagoras takes each charge in turn and takes it apart. He then explains Christian belief in the language of Greek thought. His tone stays calm, learned, and fair toward his royal readers. Few early defenses of the faith match its grace. It shows a thinker asking only for a fair hearing under Roman law.
bailly-report-franklin-commissioners-eng:
The Franklin commission's report on animal magnetism reached English readers in this London translation of 1785. Jean-Sylvain Bailly had drafted the French original in 1784. Franklin, Lavoisier, and Guillotin stood among the commissioners who tested Mesmer's claimed fluid and found nothing there.

English readers now got the famous verdict firsthand. The cures, the report argued, came from imagination, not from any magnetic fluid. Careful blind trials backed the claim. The translation carried the Enlightenment's most famous no across the Channel within a year. It remains a model of how to test a marvel claim fairly, then report the result plainly.
balzac-eugenie-grandet-wormeley-1885:
Honoré de Balzac wrote Eugénie Grandet in French, and Katharine Prescott Wormeley made it English in 1885. Wormeley's version came from her pioneering American Balzac series of that decade in Boston. The novel of miserliness and thwarted love is a jewel of provincial French fiction.

Old Grandet hoards gold in Saumur and starves his wife and daughter of warmth. Eugénie gives her heart and her gold to her cousin Charles, who sails for India. He returns rich, cold, and engaged to a noblewoman for rank and a title. Eugénie weds for form, keeps her wealth, and gives much of it to good works. Balzac shows how avarice can warp a house for two generations of kin.
bosanquet-knowledge-reality-1885:
Bernard Bosanquet published Knowledge and Reality in 1885 as a criticism of F H Bradley's Principles of Logic. Bradley was the other giant of British idealism, and Bosanquet, his ally in most things, here argues with him closely. The book is the opening shot of the British idealist debates that filled the journals for a generation.

The quarrel turns on judgment: what happens in the mind when a person truly judges that something is so? Bosanquet defends his own account of how knowledge reaches reality against Bradley's sharper skepticism. The exchange is technical, civil, and deep, between two friends who agreed on the stakes. Philosophers still read it as idealism thinking aloud.
buffon-natural-history-smellie-vol1-1785:
William Smellie's translation of Buffon's Natural History, General and Particular, Volume 1, appeared in its second edition in 1785. Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon, directed Paris's royal garden and wrote the Histoire naturelle across decades. Smellie, a Scottish printer and naturalist, made Buffon readable in English.

Volume 1 opens with Buffon's theory of the Earth and his account of nature's order, then turns to humankind. Buffon wrote in a grand style, asking how species form, vary, and spread. His claims on the Earth's age and the likeness of humans and apes stirred debate. The Smellie volumes carried the great eighteenth-century natural history to British and American readers.
buffon-natural-history-smellie-vol2-1785:
Volume 2 of Buffon's Natural History in Smellie's translation appeared in the second edition of 1785. Buffon's Histoire naturelle was the great natural history of the eighteenth century, issued in Paris over many years. Smellie's English set brought its sweep to readers without French.

The early volumes of Buffon move from the Earth and humankind toward the animals, treated kind by kind. Buffon joined anatomy, behavior, and geography in literary portraits of each species. He also weighed how climate and food change a stock over time. Volume 2 continues that progress through his system, in the form English readers of the 1780s actually used for their picture of nature.
buffon-natural-history-smellie-vol3-1785:
Volume 3 of Buffon's Natural History in Smellie's translation appeared in the second edition of 1785. By this volume the English reader is inside Buffon's great survey of the animal kingdom. Buffon wrote each animal's history as a small essay, not a dry list.

Horses, dogs, and other familiar kinds receive long, vivid treatments in Buffon's early animal volumes, with their varieties across lands. He asked how domestication reshapes a species and how wild kin differ from tame. Smellie's translation kept the style that made Buffon famous, at some cost in strict accuracy. The volume shows why natural history, in Buffon's hands, counted as literature as well as science in his century.
buffon-natural-history-smellie-vol4-1785:
Volume 4 of Buffon's Natural History in Smellie's translation appeared in the second edition of 1785. The set continues Buffon's Histoire naturelle, the vast French survey that redefined natural history writing. Smellie, the Scottish translator, issued the English volumes through the 1780s.

Buffon's animal histories in these middle volumes range across quadrupeds of Europe, Asia, and the Americas. He compared kinds, mapped where each lives, and guessed at their kinship and change over time. His treatment of species and generation fed later debate that led toward evolution. Volume 4 keeps the same method: close description, wide comparison, and bold theory in polished prose for the general reader.
buffon-natural-history-smellie-vol5-1785:
Volume 5 of Buffon's Natural History in Smellie's translation appeared in the second edition of 1785. Buffon's project, volume by volume, aimed to cover all of nature in one connected history. Smellie's English version was the form in which most British and American readers met that project.

Animal accounts continue here, each joining structure, habits, and range in a single portrait. Buffon also returned, across the work, to large questions: what a species is, how generation works, and how kinds can decay or improve. His discussion of extinction and change was among the first scientific treatments of those themes. The volume sustains the set's mix of fact and speculation.
buffon-natural-history-smellie-vol6-1785:
Volume 6 of Buffon's Natural History in Smellie's translation appeared in the second edition of 1785. Six volumes into the English set, Buffon's survey of quadrupeds is well advanced. The French original, produced at the royal garden in Paris, set the standard for natural history across Europe.

Buffon treated each kind with its anatomy, temperament, and place in the economy of nature, in his phrase. He noted how the same stock changes under new climates, a theme that runs through the whole work. Smellie's plates and prose made the volumes popular family reading. Volume 6 shows the enterprise at cruising speed: steady, learned, and written to be enjoyed as much as consulted.
buffon-natural-history-smellie-vol7-1785:
Volume 7 of Buffon's Natural History in Smellie's translation appeared in the second edition of 1785. The later volumes of the Smellie set carry Buffon's animal histories toward the smaller and stranger quadrupeds. Buffon's net, cast over decades in Paris, caught nearly every kind then known to Europe.

Descriptions here rest on specimens, travelers' reports, and Buffon's own dissections at the royal garden. He corrected old fables about beasts where evidence allowed, and he reasoned about how species spread and changed. The first scientific treatment of extinction belongs to this work's wider argument, not to one volume alone. Volume 7 keeps that argument moving through fresh cases.
buffon-natural-history-smellie-vol8-1785:
Volume 8 of Buffon's Natural History in Smellie's translation appeared in the second edition of 1785. Eight volumes into Smellie's English Buffon, the survey nears its close in this set. Buffon's Histoire naturelle in French ran far longer, but the Smellie edition gave English readers a complete course in his method.

Quadrupeds of distant lands fill these pages, many first pictured for English readers from Paris specimens. Buffon weighed reports with a critic's care, discarding travelers' tales that failed his tests. His ideas on species, generation, and the slow change of kinds run beneath the descriptions. The volume shows a science still young, sorting wonder from evidence in public, for a wide and eager readership.
buffon-natural-history-smellie-vol9-1785:
Volume 9 of Buffon's Natural History in Smellie's translation appeared in the second edition of 1785, concluding the English set. Buffon's Histoire naturelle had begun in 1749 and remade its field. Smellie's nine volumes carried that achievement to the English-speaking world in a finished form.

The closing volume completes the animal survey of the set, with indexes and summaries to guide readers back through the whole. Across nine volumes Buffon treated the Earth, humankind, and the quadrupeds with one literary method. His questions on species, generation, and extinction opened paths that later science widened. The Smellie Buffon stayed the standard English natural history for decades after 1785.
carpenter-one-hundred-proofs-earth-not-g:
William Carpenter published One Hundred Proofs That the Earth Is Not a Globe at Baltimore in 1885. Carpenter, an English printer and flat-earth lecturer, numbered his proofs one by one for easy citation. Scripture, water levels, lighthouses, and canal surveys all serve his case for a flat, stationary earth.

The tract became the most circulated flat-earth text of the nineteenth century. Flat-earth societies reprinted it again and again, into the present day. Scientists answered it in its time, yet its numbered form kept it handy for believers. The library stages it as a primary text of the flat-earth movement, on its own terms. Readers meet there a complete, confident system built against the globe.
chaucer-troilus-criseyde-1385:
Chaucer told the saddest love story of Troy in Troilus and Criseyde, written about 1385 in London. Troilus, a young Trojan prince, loves Criseyde, a widow whose father has fled to the Greek camp. Pandarus, her uncle, plays go-between with a wit and warmth that both help and damn the pair in the end.

War parts what love joined, and Criseyde's slow turning to Diomede breaks Troilus's world apart. Chaucer handles the tale with unmatched warmth and irony, judging no one cheaply, not even Criseyde herself. The poem stands as his most finished work and the summit of Middle English narrative verse, the great English poem before Shakespeare.
cia-0000007485:
Pages 29 to 55 of a winter 1962 Studies in Intelligence issue carry a piece headed Target: CIA. Studies in Intelligence was the agency's house journal, and volume 6, number 1 dates from the Cold War's tense early sixties. The title suggests officers studying how opponents viewed their own agency.

Internal journals let intelligence staff argue about methods, threats, and failures in print. A piece turning the lens on the CIA itself fits that self-critical habit. Declassification opened these pages to historians long after the intended readers retired. The file preserves professional debate from inside a secret institution at work.
cia-0000009785:
Six American prisoners of war were sighted at Sre Khlong camp, in Kompong Speu province, a May 1973 report states. Kompong Speu lies west of Phnom Penh, in a Cambodia sliding toward Khmer Rouge victory. A named camp with a count of six gave officials something concrete.

Cambodian camp sightings after the Paris accords were especially hard to settle. Access was nil, and the captors were changing as the civil war turned. Each report might be a man's last trace before the Khmer Rouge years swallowed the record. This file preserves one camp, six men, and a date.
cia-0000010585:
Probable developments in North Africa are forecast in a second 1952 CIA paper, companion to a survey of the current situation. Forecasting decolonization was the task: which territory would move first, and how France would answer. Morocco and Tunisia bargained; Algeria's road looked longer and harder.

Paired papers, one on the present and one on the future, show the estimate process at work. The forecast could be wrong in detail while right in direction. Events of the decade tested it territory by territory. This file preserves the forward half of the pair, the region's independence foreseen in outline.
cia-0000010785:
Taiwan in 1955 was the island refuge of Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist government, which had lost China's civil war six years earlier. In March 1955 the CIA took the island's temperature in a paper on morale. The question behind it was simple: would Taiwan's soldiers and people hold firm if the mainland attacked?

The paper looks at the spirit of Chiang's army and the mood of the island's people. It weighs the strain of living under the mainland's constant threat. Coming during the first Taiwan Strait crisis, the study shows how much American planning rested on the will of this small, exposed ally.
cia-0000012085:
National Intelligence Estimate 36-61, issued in May 1961, gave the whole intelligence community's judgment on Nasser and the future of Arab nationalism. Nasser's Egypt, joined with Syria as the United Arab Republic, stood at the center of Arab politics. His pan-Arab message reached millions by radio and unsettled kings and rivals across the region.

The estimate weighs Nasser's aims, his strength, and the movement he led. It also judges his deals with Moscow and his quarrels with fellow Arabs. As a coordinated estimate, it shows how Washington's top analysts together read the man who dominated the Arab world.
cia-0000012285:
In July 1961 Richard Helms wrote to the Assistant to the Secretary of Defense. His errand was special operations, and his letter carried a colonel's secrets to the Pentagon. Helms ran the CIA's clandestine service, and the Pentagon office was a natural customer for what Oleg Penkovsky supplied. The spy's product was too valuable, and too urgent, to keep inside one building.

The memo shows the interagency bridge at work: Langley producing, the Pentagon consuming. It marks the case's reach into the highest levels of defense planning. For readers, it is the paper trail of an alliance between two bureaucracies joined by one source.
cia-0000012385:
A request for United States or British citizenship, written in Russian, survives in a CIA file from July 1960. The document keeps the ask in the asker's own tongue rather than in translation. Such requests reached the agency from people inside the Soviet world who wanted out, or who offered service in exchange for a future in the West.

The plea's survival in the original Russian preserves a human voice behind the transaction. Files like this one mark the start of relationships that could end in rescue or ruin. For readers, the page is the human front door of the intelligence world.
cia-0000014185: How others would react to a certain U.S. course of action in Southeast Asia is weighed in a CIA paper dated August 5, 1965. The title keeps the action itself vague, as such papers often did. Judging foreign reaction was the core task of estimate work. The paper belongs to the months when the American war in Vietnam was fast growing.
cia-0000014785: A letter from the WIDF protesting Morton Sobell's imprisonment fills a CIA file dated February 5, 1955. The letter pleads Mrs. Sobell's case for her husband. The WIDF was a worldwide women's federation with left wing roots. Its plea shows the Sobell campaign working through global groups years after the trial. That protest letter now rests in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015285: A letter to Lloyd Berkner from Philip Strong fills a CIA file dated January 4, 1953. The letter concerns the scientific advisor setup, per the clipped title. Berkner was a top science figure tied to defense work. Letters at this level show the saucer question reaching the men who ran American science.
cia-0000015385: Office responsibilities for non-conventional types of air vehicles fill a CIA file dated January 1, 1956. The duty question came back two years after the first charts. Strange craft reports had not stopped, so the desk still needed an owner. The New Year file shows the chore outliving the first great scare.
cia-0000028285: The outlook for Iran is assessed in a CIA paper dated in 1957. By then the Shah's rule, restored by the 1953 coup, looked settled and pro Western. Oil money and a growing army underwrote that calm surface. An outlook paper from those years records the confidence Washington felt in Iran long before the revolution overturned every such judgment.
cia-0000041885: A CIA item dated February 4, 1986 is described in its own title as barely legible. It cites the captain of a ship carrying arms, drawn from a domestic news service, with further mentions cut short in the title. Little of the underlying report can be grounded from what survives in the catalog. The record is best read as a faded fragment of arms traffic reporting, kept even though time and handling had blurred its pages almost past reading.
cia-0000045185:
The names of the Duarte kidnapping negotiators were released, in a CIA record dated September 1, 1985. Ines Duarte, the president's daughter, had been seized by guerrillas. Negotiators stood between her captors and her father's government.

Inside, the go-betweens in the case are named for the record. Naming them ended one layer of the talks' secrecy. It told the public who carried messages when no one else could safely do so. It also exposed the named men to pressure from every side. The file preserves the roster at the moment it became public, in a crisis where the men in the middle carried hopes that armies could not carry.
cia-0000045985: A CIA item dated August 3, 1991, deals with the prisoner photograph affair, with a name blacked out of its own headline. The photo claim had drawn in officials, families, and reporters all that summer. With its key name still hidden, the item stands as a record of how much of that fight stayed secret.
cia-0000046485: Commentary in 1970 rapped Ross Perot's prisoner campaign, and a CIA item dated March 5, 1970, kept the text of the attack. Perot's publicity drive for Americans held in Vietnam had made him a target as well as a champion. The item is a companion piece to the same day's charge that his work misled the public.
cia-0000046685:
In June 1978, CIA analysts set out how the Warsaw Pact planned to go to war in Europe, and what its forces could actually do. The pact joined the Soviet Union with its Eastern European allies, facing NATO across a divided continent. The study's second half draws out what those plans meant for the West.

Inside, the paper works through the pact's ideas for opening a war: speed, massed armor, and strikes deep behind NATO lines. It weighs the forces ready to carry those ideas out, from divisions to air power. Estimates like this one shaped Western defense planning through the last decade of the Cold War.
cia-0000048985: A CIA paper dated July 5, 1990, takes up military impunity in El Salvador: the habit of soldiers escaping punishment for crimes. By 1990 the civil war was moving toward talks, and whether officers would ever face courts was a central question. The paper survives in the Truth Commission file series. Its title names the problem plainly, without soft words.
cia-0000049185: A file on the Jesuit incident, its key word blacked out of the title, survives in a CIA item from 1990. Incident was the bureaucracy's small word for the murder of six priests, their housekeeper, and her daughter. The file sits in the Truth Commission records, where the word was eventually replaced by findings.
cia-0000049285:
Extreme rightist activity in El Salvador is watched in a CIA paper from 1983, preserved in the Truth Commission file series. The extreme right worked at the war's edge: plots, threats, and killings carried out by men who thought the government itself too soft. The paper takes that fringe as its subject.

Inside, the activity is sorted into the forms it took, from printed threats to armed action, each tied to the groups behind it. Watching the fringe mattered because its violence repeatedly broke the plans of presidents and ambassadors alike. The paper survives as a field guide to the war's most dangerous margin.
cia-0000049385: El Salvador faced with human rights concerns is the subject line of declassified CIA document 0000049385, dated October 2, 1989. Marked for the Truth Commission, the item frames the country as confronting outside concern over human rights. Readers get a brief dated record whose title carries that framing, kept in the agency's late Salvadoran reporting.
cia-0000096485: Defense Minister Chiang's instructions to prepare plans for infiltrating GRC teams, in the heading's shortened wording, are declassified CIA document 0000096485, dated July 3, 1967. The title names the minister and the planning order. The brief file records those instructions as its subject, preserved as a short Taiwan-related item in the agency's China reporting.
cia-0000098285: Clarification of The Yeoman Story is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000098285, dated November 3, 1973. The title promises to clear up a story known by that quoted name. Readers find a short clarification record, its subject a tale the heading assumes its first readers already knew, preserved without that context in the catalog.
cia-0000098685: Estimated cushioning material requirements for fiscal year 1992 are calculated in declassified CIA document 0000098685, dated February 1, 1992. The heading names packing material and a budget year. Readers find a short logistics estimate record, as plain an administrative item as the catalog holds, filed the same day as the business justification paper. The heading and date are the firm facts the catalog gives.
cia-0000105385:
Moro's Views on Future Developments in the Italian Political Situation is declassified CIA document 0000105385, dated September 1, 1961. The sample text is badly broken by poor scanning, but legible lines remain. They speak of a government crisis before national elections and of Moro and a center-left government.

One legible line says Moro has no objection to NATO, in the sample's rough spelling. Another says the center-left government should last until the presidential elections, again in broken type. The fragments are too broken for any fuller summary. What survives supports the title: Moro's views on where Italian politics was heading.
cia-0000107285: The Changing Role of Soviet-owned Banks in the West is the subject, with its publication date as an estimate, on CIA document 0000107285, dated November 6, 1984. The title tracks a change: Soviet-owned banks playing a shifting part in the West. No bank is named in the heading itself. The brief record is a finance item from the late Cold War.
cia-0000107985: Supervisor's Guide to the Employee Assistance Program is the subject, with its publication date marked as an estimate, on declassified CIA document 0000107985, dated March 4, 1993. The title marks a guide written for supervisors, not for all staff. The program it explains is named in full in the heading. The brief record is an internal guide item from 1993.
cia-0000118685: Vietnam Demonstrations is the whole heading, with its date marked as an estimate, on declassified CIA document 0000118685, dated October 2, 1965. The title is two words: demonstrations tied to Vietnam. No city or group is named in the heading itself at all. The brief record preserves the estimate note with the short title exactly as released in the files.
cia-0000119585:
From about November 1967, this CIA document reports an expectation of crisis inside the Czechoslovak Communist Party. Within months, reformers would push the party's old guard aside and the Prague Spring would begin. The paper therefore reads like a forecast made just before the storm broke.

Expectation papers show what analysts thought was coming and why. Here the agency saw the party's troubles deepening into open crisis rather than settling down. The document's value lies in that timing. It captures informed judgment on the eve of one of the Cold War's most famous upheavals. No one yet knew how far reform would go, or how Moscow would answer it.
cia-0000126885: A January 1968 CIA document, its source deleted, warns of an expected second wave of Viet Cong attacks on or about February 18. The Tet Offensive's first wave had just struck South Vietnam. The paper preserves the warning as the agency braced for more fighting. Tet's second wave did come in the months that followed, and warning papers from January show the agency expecting more fighting even while the first attacks burned.
cia-0000126985: Dated June 1975, this CIA report tracks trends in communist media around the world. From Pravda to the People's Daily, party newspapers telegraphed shifts in policy to careful readers. The paper follows those trends as the agency read them that summer. Media trend reports looked for drift rather than single stories, since a party press changing its line by degrees often signaled policy moving before officials spoke.
cia-0000127985: An April 1952 CIA memorandum to the President transmits a copy of Special Estimate 28, covering consequences of a subject the heading loses mid-word. Special Estimates went straight to the top of the government. The memo preserves the transmittal, though its full topic stays cut off. Transmittal memos are the envelope of the estimate system; they show how finished judgments physically reached the president, even when the heading loses the subject at hand.
cia-0000132185: Situation report 502, from January 1991, covers the Soviet Union and the Persian Gulf, noting Soviet fears that something would spread, the heading breaking off. Moscow worried the war would ignite the wider region. The report captures that anxiety. Spread was the word everyone feared that winter, meaning a war jumping borders into Turkey, Syria, or the Soviet Union's own southern republics by accident or design.
cia-0000132285: Situation Report 594 in the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series, dated January 4, 1991, uses a boxing image for its headline: Saddam's one-two punch, with worldwide reaction. The phrase points to paired moves by the Iraqi leader, one aimed at public opinion and one at private diplomacy. The report gathers how governments and publics around the world responded to both at once during the Gulf crisis.
cia-0000132485: Military aid possibly being prepared by the Soviet bloc fills part one of a CIA item dated April 1, 1960. The section is headed the Communist Bloc. Its headline breaks off before naming the aid's destination in full. Soviet weapons for Cuba were the outcome Washington feared most that year. The short item tracks the preparations analysts believed they could see taking shape.
cia-0000132585: Reactions to new American limits on exports to Cuba fill item 3 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated September 1, 1960. Export controls were Washington's economic weapon of choice before the full embargo came. Each new limit tightened the pressure on Havana's economy. The short item collects how governments and businesses answered the latest round.
cia-0000132685: The situation in Cuba fills a CIA item dated March 1, 1961. One month stood between this item and the landing at the Bay of Pigs. The invasion force was in training while the agency kept its watch on Havana's defenses. In that season the situation was the only question that mattered. The short item gives it as analysts saw it.
cia-0000132785: Dated 3 October 1960, Cuban Developments is a declassified CIA paper. A companion installment dated the very next day also survives in these files. Two entries on consecutive days show how closely the agency was tracking Cuba that fall. Castro had been in power for under two years. The catalog title names no single event, so this description claims no more. The paper is a dated progress report on Cuba, written for officials who needed the picture kept current. It is now open through the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000135885: One CIA document dated 4 August 1952 handles a file headed with the single name Manuel, the rest of the name deleted by the censors. The record comes from the run-up to the June 1954 coup that removed President Arbenz, the goal of the CIA plan called PBSUCCESS. Students of the 1954 coup use such records to check later accounts against what was written at the time.
cia-0000135985: A cable dated 4 February 1954 is among the declassified CIA papers on information for SYNCARP about documents and materials, the stock of the propaganda arm. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Taken with the rest of the station traffic, it helps map who handled what, and when, inside the mission.
cia-0000136085: A cable in the declassified CIA files, dated 4 March 1954, covers the Summit Plan, a high-level design whose substance the heading does not give away. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Later books on the coup rest on stacks of paper exactly like this, dated, coded, and only partly opened.
cia-0000136685: An item in Spanish dated 4 January 1961, from the papers of Brigade 2506, the CIA's Cuban exile brigade. The first week of 1961 was thick with brigade paperwork, and this record is part of that run. Its catalog title states no subject. It is held in the original Spanish as released, a dated piece of the exile force's files from its last training season.
cia-0000138985: A Soviet Far Eastern Red Army of Chinese soldiers is described here. The report dates to April 1946. It covers the Three River region of Manchuria. These Chinese soldiers were trained by Russians in Russia. They came back after Russia declared war on Japan. They now cooperate with the Chinese Communists. The single page came through the War Office. It is among the earliest American reports of such a force. A Soviet-trained Chinese army was operating in Manchuria.
clement-of-alexandria-excerpts-of-theodo:
Clement of Alexandria kept a notebook of excerpts from Theodotus. Theodotus taught in the Valentinian school that Clement opposed. Clement's own comments run in the margins of the quoted passages.

The 1885 Fathers edition presents these selections in English. They preserve Gnostic teachings that would otherwise be lost to us. Ironically, the man arguing against them saved them for history. Scholars treasure the strange document as a primary source. Few texts let readers hear a heresy in its own words so directly. The excerpts show Clement at work: reading foes closely, testing each claim, and answering with care.
clement-of-alexandria-salvation-of-the-r:
William Wilson translated Clement's sermon on the rich man for the 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers. Its full question runs: who is the rich man that shall be saved? Clement preached it for wealthy believers in Alexandria around the year 200.

Can a rich man enter heaven at all, people asked him. Yes, he answers, if wealth does not own the man who owns it. He retells Christ's words on the camel and the needle's eye with a pastor's care. The sermon also keeps the tale of John chasing down a young robber chief. Gentle and hopeful, it stays a classic of early Christian teaching on money.
clement-of-alexandria-the-instructor-anf:
Clement of Alexandria called his handbook Paedagogus, or The Instructor. Written around the year 200, it guides new Christians in daily conduct. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers edition presents the work in English.

Eating, dress, bathing, laughter, and speech all come under his care. How can a believer live in a pagan city and keep the soul safe? Clement answers with warmth and plain common sense on every point. The book works as the first etiquette guide written for Christians. His Alexandria feels oddly close to modern life. Readers still enjoy his mix of high faith and low, practical detail about shoes, meals, and jokes.
clement-of-alexandria-the-stromata-or-mi:
Clement named his great miscellany Stromata, a Greek word for patchwork. Written around the year 200, it ranges across faith and Greek learning. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers edition carries the sprawling work in English.

Clement argues that Greek learning can serve Christ rather than fight him. Poetry, science, and scripture weave together in his quilt of notes. No topic seems too small or too grand for his roving mind. Scholars call the book the founding work of Christian intellectual life. It can still thrill a reader today. Few ancient texts show so well how faith and reason first learned to live in one house.
clement-of-rome-the-second-epistle-of-cl:
Second Clement travels under Clement of Rome's name in the 1885 Fathers. Scholars judge that Clement did not write it and that it is no letter. The piece is in truth a sermon, preached around the year 140.

Its unknown preacher urges repentance, charity, and endurance on his hearers. The tone stays urgent and simple from start to finish. No sermon from the early Church survives from an earlier date. Hearing it, modern readers catch what plain believers heard on a plain Sunday. The age just after the apostles speaks here in a direct and pastoral voice.
clementine-literature-the-clementine-hom:
Twenty sermons make up the Clementine Homilies in this 1885 edition. The sermons travel under the name of Clement of Rome. Their Christianity carries a strongly Jewish flavor throughout.

Peter preaches strict morality as he moves through eastern cities. Simon Magus stands against him in debate after public debate. The teaching stresses law, purity, and one God above all. This form of the faith lost the later battle for orthodoxy. Its survival in full is thus a rare gift to historians. The Homilies preserve a road the Church did not take, in the words of those who walked it.
clementine-literature-the-recognitions-o:
The Recognitions of Clement ranks as the earliest Christian novel. Clement of Rome tells his own search for truth in its pages. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers carries the long romance in English.

Clement meets the apostle Peter and joins his traveling company. Peter debates the magician Simon Magus in city after city. Then come the recognitions of the title, one wonder after another. Clement finds his long-lost family, scattered years before by misfortune. Adventure, philosophy, and theology blend in the rip-roaring tale. Ancient Christians loved the book dearly, and it stayed among the most popular reads of the early Church.
collins-light-on-the-path-1885:
Mabel Collins wrote brief rules for the soul's path in Light on the Path, out in 1885. A mate text, Through the Gates of Gold, stands with it in this book. Collins said the rules came to her from a hid source. Their tone is grave, terse, and fit to learn by heart.

Kill pride, kill greed, work, and wait: such is the drill. Fans of the creed quote these lines more than most. The pair of texts is small yet vast in reach. Seekers still keep it close as a daily guide. The rules were set as brief lines, fit for rote drill each dawn. That form helps the text stay in mind long past first read.
constitution-australia-1985: Australia's Constitution, dating to 1901 with later acts, frames its federation. The 1985 Australia Acts cut UK ties. The Tower library holds the full text. It binds six states. Crown remains. People rule. Law unites. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
cook-voyage-pacific-ocean-vol1-1785:
James Cook's third voyage, from 1776 to 1779, sought a northern sea passage from the Pacific side. Volume One of the official account appeared in 1785. Cook himself wrote much of it before his death in Hawaii; Captain King finished the work.

The ships Resolution and Discovery visit New Zealand, Tahiti, and the northwest coast of America. Cook charts Alaska's shores and pushes into the Bering Strait ice. In January 1778 he reaches Hawaii, the first European known to land there. The volume's fine plates and charts set a standard for voyage publishing. Cook's own return to Hawaii ended in his death.
cowper-task-1785:
William Cowper wrote The Task in blank verse, and it appeared in 1785 after a friend teased him to write about a sofa. What began as a joke grew into six books named The Sofa, The Timepiece, The Garden, and three winter walks. An introduction in this edition traces his quiet life at Olney with Mrs. Unwin and Lady Austen.

Inside, Cowper moves from furniture to fields, faith, and the harms of city life in a plain and warm voice. Shorter poems, including John Gilpin, sit beside the main work. His turn toward home and nature helped clear the path that Wordsworth and the Romantics later took.
cyprian-the-seventh-council-of-carthage-:
Eighty-seven African bishops met at Carthage in 256 under Cyprian's lead. One burning question brought them together from across the region. Were baptisms performed by heretics valid in the eyes of the Church?

The council answered no, in vote after recorded vote. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers preserves each bishop's stated judgment in turn. Readers watch the early Church make up its mind in public session. Few ancient records show shared decision-making at this level of detail. The transcript stands as a landmark in the long debate over when sacraments count and who may give them.
cyprian-the-treatises-of-cyprian-anf-188:
Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, died a martyr in the year 258. An 1885 volume of the Ante-Nicene Fathers gathers his treatises. He was the great pastor of the Church in the age of persecution.

On the Unity of the Church and On the Lord's Prayer stand among the pieces. On Mortality, written in a time of plague, comforts a frightened flock. Other works guide believers through schism and the return of the lapsed. Practical, warm, and firm, his writing held Christians together under strain. His vision of one united Church shaped how Christians pictured their fellowship for centuries after his death.
cyprian-treatises-attributed-to-cyprian-:
Not every work that bears Cyprian's name came from Cyprian's pen. An 1885 Fathers volume gathers treatises ascribed to him on doubtful grounds. The editors label the authority questionable right in the title.

In ancient times the pieces still traveled under his famous name. A great name lent weight to teaching that needed support. Each work reflects some concern of the third-century Church that produced it. Questions of practice, morals, and belief surface across the gathering. Readers gain a double lesson here: how texts were fathered on saints, and what ordinary believers most wanted to hear.
dicey-law-constitution-1885:
A V Dicey published Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution in 1885. Dicey, an Oxford law professor, gave the English constitution its most famous modern statement. The book grew from his lectures and reached readers far beyond the universities.

Dicey taught two linked doctrines: Parliament can make or unmake any law, and no person stands above the ordinary law of the land. The second idea, the rule of law, became a rallying phrase in the common-law world. He contrasted British practice with French administrative courts, to Britain's pride. Later scholars revised much of Dicey, but his terms still frame debate on sovereignty and rights.
die-himmlische-und-hermetische-perle-ode: Die himmlische und hermetische Perle, 1785. The heavenly pearl. This book preserves that work. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
dionysius-of-alexandria-exegetical-fragm:
Exegetical fragments gather Dionysius of Alexandria's surviving notes on scripture. The word exegetical marks comments that explain the biblical text itself. An 1885 Fathers volume serves as companion to his general fragments.

Later writers quoted his readings, and quotation alone preserved them. The scraps show how the great Alexandrian school handled the Bible. That school was famed for deep and often allegorical interpretation. Broken as the record is, real light still falls from the pieces. Students of early Bible study will find a master at work. Even in fragments, Dionysius helps explain how Christians first learned to read their book with care.
dionysius-of-alexandria-extant-fragments:
Dionysius the Great led the Church at Alexandria in the mid-200s. Plague and persecution marked his years as bishop there. Most of his many writings have been lost to time.

An 1885 Fathers volume gathers what survives of him in quotation. Later writers quoted his words, and those scraps are all that remain. Scripture, doctrine, and church life all surface in the fragments. Each piece is precious for the glimpse it gives of its author. Judges of the period rank him among the wisest churchmen of the third century, and the fragments support that high verdict.
europmc-pmc10152985:
Zhong and a large team review protein post-translational modifications in health and disease in a 2023 paper. After a protein is built, chemical edits can change its shape, lifespan, and job. These edits, called PTMs, vastly expand what the body's proteins can do and help explain how simple genomes run complex bodies.

The review sorts the main kinds of edits and the enzymes that add or remove them. It links faulty edits to cancer and other diseases. It also surveys drugs that target the editing machinery, a growing class of treatments.
europmc-pmc10320085:
Sun and colleagues built OrthoVenn3, a free web tool reported in 2023 for gene studies across species. Genes that share a common root in two species are called orthologs. The tool finds groups of such genes and shows how species relate to each other.

Sun made the new version sharper at finding gene groups than past ones. It can show data from many sets at once in clear charts. It also tracks how gene families grew or shrank over time. A further check finds blocks of genes that stayed in the same order across species. Users can run all of this in a web browser at no cost.
europmc-pmc10642285:
Metzler and co-authors linked hard childhood events to adult life chances in 2017. Such events, called adverse childhood experiences or ACEs, include abuse and neglect. Past work tied them to poor health across life and across generations. Less was known about their tie to schooling, work, and income.

The team used health survey data gathered in 10 states plus the capital district. Adults with higher ACE scores fared worse on each measure. Metzler reports more cases of leaving high school early, joblessness, and homes below the poverty line. The gap grew as scores rose. The authors argue that stopping early harm may lift health and life chances for the next generation too.
europmc-pmc1177985:
Croisier, Moran, Dexter, Pearce, and Graeber examine inflamed microglia in the Parkinson brain in this 2005 study. Microglia are the brain's resident immune cells. Their activation is a feature of Parkinson disease, as are deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein. Whether microglia help cause the disease was unclear. The team tested a strict idea: if microglia are a primary driver, their activated state should track the disease's tissue and clinical features.

They stained post-mortem substantia nigra, the brain area that loses dopamine cells, for three markers. The markers were MHC class II, a sign of microglial activation; CD68, a marker of eating-cell activity; and alpha-synuclein. Ratings were compared with disease subtype and clinical course. Activation did not track clinical parameters, they found. CD68 did correlate with disease duration. The authors report the link as limited, not primary.
europmc-pmc1197285:
Dehal and Boore tested an old idea about vertebrate genomes in 2005. Backboned animals have large, complex genomes. Some scientists proposed two full genome doublings early in their history. Others doubted it, and gene counts gave weak proof.

The pair rebuilt family trees for genes in four species. They used a sea squirt, a fish, a mouse, and humans. Map positions of old duplicate genes told the clearer story. Four-way matched regions cover much of the human genome. Dehal reads that pattern as firm proof of two doublings. It appeared in PLoS Biology in 2005.
europmc-pmc12443585:
Guo and a very large team reported training a reasoning model by reinforcement learning in 2025. Strong reasoning is a long-standing goal for AI. Top models had leaned on huge sets of worked steps written by people. The team tested whether reward-based learning alone could build reasoning.

Their model, DeepSeek-R1, learned from rewards without human reasoning examples. It developed self-reflection, checking steps, and strategy switching on its own. Scores beat supervised counterparts on math, coding contests, and science tasks. Guo shows pure reinforcement learning can grow advanced reasoning patterns directly. The model is named in the title as DeepSeek-R1.
europmc-pmc1551985:
Air pollution before birth may shape a child's mind. Perera and co-authors followed nonsmoking mothers in New York City in 2006. They wore air samplers in pregnancy to gauge polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, chemicals from traffic and smoke. Their children took development tests up to age three.

High prenatal exposure showed no link to motor skills or behavior problems. But it did track with lower mental scores at age three, by about 5.7 points. Those children had nearly triple the odds of cognitive delay. Perera warns the levels seen in city air may dull early learning, with effects that could reach into school.
europmc-pmc1563985:
People with mental illness die far younger than their neighbors. Colton and Manderscheid compared death records in 2006 across eight US states. Public mental health clients were set against each state's general population.

In every state, clients faced a higher risk of death. They died at much younger ages, losing decades of potential life. Those with major mental illness died youngest of all. Most died of natural causes, led by heart disease, cancer, and stroke, the same top killers nationwide. Colton urges public health action on this steady, shared pattern. The pattern held across all eight states studied.
europmc-pmc1781485:
Susiarjo, Hassold, Hunt and colleagues reported in 2007 that bisphenol A, or BPA, can disturb egg formation in unborn mice. BPA is a plastic chemical that mimics estrogen, the female hormone that guides egg growth. The team gave pregnant mice low doses, at levels found in the environment, during mid-pregnancy.

Eggs from exposed female fetuses showed gross defects as meiosis began, the cell division that halves chromosome number. Pairing of matching chromosomes went wrong, and swapping between them rose. As adults, those females produced more eggs and embryos with the wrong chromosome count. Mice lacking the estrogen receptor ERbeta showed the same defects without any BPA. Extra BPA added nothing in those mice, pointing to ERbeta as the path BPA disrupts.
europmc-pmc1851385:
Dunnwald, Rossing and Li charted in 2007 how hormone receptor status shapes breast cancer survival. Tumors that carry estrogen or progesterone receptors respond to hormone signals and usually carry a better outlook. Few studies had checked whether survival gaps change across age, race, or tumor traits.

They used registry data on 155,175 women aged 30 or older diagnosed with invasive breast cancer between 1990 and 2001. Compared with tumors positive for both receptors, every other group faced higher death risk in every subgroup examined. Tumors positive only for estrogen carried about 1.2 to 1.5 times the risk. Tumors positive only for progesterone fell in between. Those negative for both receptors carried about 2.1 to 2.6 times the risk, and the gaps widened further in some tumor categories.
europmc-pmc1852585:
Galindo, Couso and co-authors showed in 2007 that a fruit fly gene once dismissed as noncoding actually makes tiny working peptides. The gene, named tarsal-less, guides development of the leg and body pattern. It had been classed as a noncoding RNA because its protein-coding stretches looked far too short.

Those stretches are open reading frames of only 33 DNA letters each, encoding peptides just 11 amino acids long. They are the shortest functional coding units described so far. Several sit on one messenger, a polycistronic layout thought absent from animal genes. The peptides steer gene activity and the folding of tissues, linking body pattern to body shape. Related short reading frames occur in other species, defining an ancient gene family and a new class of eukaryotic genes.
europmc-pmc1939885:
Dupret, Abrous and co-authors showed in 2007 that learning a spatial task both saves and deletes newborn brain cells in rats. The hippocampus, a memory structure, keeps making new neurons in adulthood. Whether that neurogenesis helps spatial learning, and how, was still debated.

Learning triggered a three-part cascade that mirrors how developing brains stabilize useful connections. Mature newborn neurons were preferentially kept alive. More immature newborn cells were pushed into apoptosis, programmed death. Neural precursor cells then divided more to refill the pool. Blocking the death step impaired memory and also blocked both the saving of mature cells and the precursor surge. The three events are interlocked, so networks are sculpted by selection among newborn populations rather than by cell addition alone.
europmc-pmc2065885:
Hahn, Han and Han tracked gene family change across 12 fruit fly genomes in 2007. Gene families grow by duplication and shrink by deletion or decay. Comparing whole genomes of 12 Drosophila species gave unusually fine detail. The team counted gains and losses family by family. They also searched for new genes and for listed genes that may not be real.

Over 40 percent of gene families differed in size among the species. Each million years, about 17 genes get duplicated and then fixed in a genome. Some families tied to sex and sperm production expanded greatly in Drosophila melanogaster. New families often linked to testes-expressed genes that arose from scratch. Total gene number looks stable, but the study shows rapid turnover underneath.
europmc-pmc2073885:
BLOOM and RICHARDSON graded 1,409 breast cancers under the microscope in 1957 to test whether grade predicts outcome. Patients with similar age and tumour extent could fare very differently. Some died within a year despite radical surgery, while others lived for many years. Clinical staging alone could not capture the tumour's own nature. Histological grading, scoring tissue features, offered a measure of potential malignancy.

Of the series, 359 patients were followed for a full 15 years. The authors set out their grading technique, its difficulties and its limits. They correlated grade with survival at five, ten and fifteen years. Their argument is that treatment comparisons are unfair unless grade is taken into account. Groups that look alike clinically may hide very different mixes of tumour aggression.

europmc-pmc2125185: A medical paper on experimental arthritis in the rabbit with Streptococcus mitis. The joint disease. This article preserves that rheumatology. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The archive keeps the paper open to all.

europmc-pmc2128085: A medical paper with a note on preserving stock strains of Treponema pallidum. The kept germs. This article preserves that bacteriology. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.

europmc-pmc2131785:
Shea and colleagues validated AMSTAR in 2007, a tool for judging the quality of systematic reviews. Thousands of reviews exist, but their methods vary widely in quality. Appraisal should be routine before results guide care. Two assessors applied AMSTAR to 42 reviews of acid-related diseases, including reflux and peptic ulcer treatments. Independent assessors also gave each review a global quality judgement for comparison.

AMSTAR scores in the sample ranged from 0 to 10 out of 11, and averaged 4.6 across the reviews assessed. That shows a wide quality spread. The study also checked how consistently independent raters scored the same reviews with this measurement tool. Agreement between raters was excellent for the total score. Nine items reached near-perfect agreement. AMSTAR results converged with the global assessments, supporting construct validity. The smallest detectable difference between reviews was 0.64 points.
europmc-pmc2140485: A biology paper on the phagocytosis of solid particles, carbon and quartz. The eaten soot. This article preserves that cell biology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. The archive guards it with care for all readers.
europmc-pmc2140685: A biology paper on the influence of electrolytes on pollen tube development. The salty pollen. This article preserves that botany. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes.
europmc-pmc2140785: A bibliography of Jacques Loeb, the pioneering physiologist. His works, listed. This article preserves that scholarly record. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2274885:
Liu and a large team ran a genome-wide association study in 2008 for psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis, inflammatory diseases of skin and joints. They genotyped 223 psoriasis cases, including 91 with arthritis, at 311,398 DNA variants, against 519 Northern European controls. Replication used independent American and British cohorts totalling over 1,100 cases and 1,200 controls. The scan aimed to find inherited susceptibility factors for both diseases.

The strongest signals sat in the major histocompatibility complex, the immune gene region. One variant near HLA-C reached overwhelming significance in combined data. Another, in the HCP5 gene, gave the highest odds ratios, 4.1 for psoriasis and 3.2 for arthritis, independent of the first. Known links to the IL23R and IL12B immune genes were replicated. New replicated loci included regions on chromosomes 13 and 15, plus a novel arthritis locus on chromosome 4 near the IL2 and IL21 genes.
europmc-pmc2581785:
Gieger and a large team of collaborators ran in 2008 the first genome-wide association study of human blood metabolites. Metabolomics measures hundreds of small molecules in blood, giving a functional readout of the body's state. The team measured 363 metabolites in serum from 284 men in the German KORA study and scanned their genomes for variants that shifted the levels.

They found strong associations explaining up to 12 percent of the variation in single metabolites. Using ratios between metabolites as a stand-in for enzyme activity sharpened the signal, explaining up to 28 percent of the variance. Four hits landed in enzyme genes, FADS1, LIPC, SCAD, and MCAD, and each matched its enzyme's known biochemical pathway. The authors call these inherited profiles metabotypes and propose pairing genotyping with metabolic profiling for personalised care.
europmc-pmc2586385:
Dethlefsen, Huse, Sogin, and Relman tracked in 2008 how a course of the antibiotic ciprofloxacin reshapes the human gut's bacterial community. Antibiotics were assumed to disturb gut microbes modestly, but older methods lacked the resolution to tell. The team used deep DNA sequencing of the bacterial 16S gene in three healthy volunteers before, during, and long after treatment.

The drug shifted the abundance of about a third of bacterial taxa and cut the community's richness and diversity, though the size of the effect differed between people. By four weeks after treatment ended, each community looked close to its starting state again. Yet several taxa had still not recovered six months later. The authors note participants reported normal gut function throughout, suggesting backup species cover lost functions.
europmc-pmc2726785:
Colijn and co-authors presented E-Flux in 2009. The method turns gene expression data into predictions of metabolic flux. Flux is the rate at which chemicals flow through a cell network. Genome sequences list which reactions are possible but not how active each one is. They applied the method to Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the tuberculosis bacterium, focusing on mycolic acids, key wall fats targeted by first-line drugs.

Using over four hundred expression arrays covering seventy-five drugs, drug pairs, and nutrient states, E-Flux forecast changes in mycolic acid making capacity. It correctly picked seven of the eight known fatty acid blockers in the set and matched their specificity. It also flagged new candidate modulators, which offers a way to screen drug effects from expression data alone.
europmc-pmc2748685:
Ooi and co-authors mapped in 2009 which oncogenic pathways are active in gastric cancer, the second leading cause of cancer death worldwide, and whether pathway patterns predict survival. Gastric tumors vary widely in which growth pathways they deregulate, and single-marker studies miss interactions between pathways. They used gene expression signatures to infer pathway activity in three hundred one primary tumors.

Three pathways were deregulated in over seventy percent of tumors: proliferation and stem cell signaling, NF-kappaB, and Wnt/beta-catenin. Cell line tests validated the predictions. Grouping patients by combinations of pathway activity gave reproducible, significant survival differences across several cohorts. Tumors can thus be classified into biologically and clinically meaningful subgroups by pathway activity alone.
europmc-pmc2764385:
Bohn and co-authors built in 2008 the Clinical Impairment Assessment, a short self-report measure of the harm eating disorders do to everyday functioning. Eating disorders hit personal life, thinking, and social life in specific ways that generic quality-of-life scales can miss. Their sixteen-item questionnaire scores impairment overall and in three domains: personal, cognitive, and social.

They tested the instrument with data from a transdiagnostic treatment trial, a therapy tested across eating disorder types. The scale showed high internal consistency, sound construct and discriminant validity, and good test-retest reliability. It also proved sensitive to change as patients improved. They propose it for clinic use when assessing patients and their response to treatment, and for research on how common such impairment is.
europmc-pmc2788585:
Hong and co-authors showed in 2009 that microvesicles shed by colorectal cancer cells are packed with cell-cycle messenger RNAs that make blood vessel cells multiply. Cancer cells release these tiny membrane bubbles into nearby tissue and the blood, where they carry messages between cells. The team compared the full RNA content of vesicles from a human colorectal cancer line against the RNA of the cells themselves.

They catalogued over eleven thousand vesicle RNAs tied to tumor processes. Two hundred forty-one RNAs sat in vesicles at levels above the parent cells. Twenty-seven of those drove cell-cycle work, mostly the division phase. Across patient samples these division RNAs varied in step with disease. Adding the vesicles to endothelial cells, the cells lining blood vessels, significantly raised their growth. Tumor vesicles, they conclude, may feed growth and spread by encouraging new blood vessels.
europmc-pmc2808385:
Corti and a large team mined memory B cells from people infected with HIV-1 in 2010 to find antibodies that block many virus strains at once. Such broad blockers are rare and prized, since they show vaccine designers which virus spots stay exposed across strains. Donors were picked for blood that already neutralized many HIV types.

The team froze the B cells so they kept making antibodies, then screened the output against virus coat proteins. They pulled out fifty-eight antibodies, most of which blocked the virus. Three stood out for breadth. One hit a new spot near the CD4 binding site, one hit a conserved crown region, and one hit a steady stretch of the gp41 stalk.
europmc-pmc2914085:
Ganann, Ciliska, and Thomas examined in 2010 how rapid reviews are conducted and what their shortcuts cost. Policy makers often need research evidence gathered within six months or less. A traditional systematic review typically takes at least twelve months, so rapid reviews streamline the process to deliver answers faster.

The team searched five electronic databases plus grey literature, hand-searched journals, and contacted key informants. Two reviewers independently screened 1,989 titles and abstracts, and the team extracted data from 45 methodological articles and 25 examples of rapid reviews. Rapid reviews took from three weeks to six months. Common shortcuts included limiting searches by year, database, or language, and using one reviewer where traditional reviews use two. The authors warn that faster extraction can miss relevant information and that shortened searching and appraisal can introduce bias. They urge rapid reviewers to describe their methods in detail and discuss what the streamlining might have changed.
europmc-pmc2919785:
Boyko and colleagues ran in 2010 the largest genetic study yet of dog shape, genotyping nine hundred fifteen dogs from eighty breeds plus wild relatives. Dogs vary in body size more than any other land mammal, alongside huge variety in legs, skulls, and coats. A dense map of canine DNA variation let the team hunt the genes behind nearly one hundred measured traits.

The striking result was simplicity: most traits trace to a handful of genes with large effects, not the hundreds of tiny nudges typical in humans. A few master loci set body size across breeds, and similar hotspots govern leg length and head shape. Breeders shuffling a small deck of powerful variants produced the species' dramatic variety, which makes dogs an unusually clean system for finding trait genes.
europmc-pmc3004885:
Jolley and Maiden introduced BIGSdb, a database system for bacterial population genomics, in a 2010 article. Fast sequencing was flooding labs with bacterial genomes, and older typing databases could not hold whole genomes linked to sample details.

Built on software long used for multi-locus typing, the new system stores anything from a single read to a full genome alongside specimen data. Users can define any loci and variants, group them into schemes for typing or evolution studies, and cross-reference names across projects. Access controls and lab sample tracking are built in, and the code is open source for any group to run.
europmc-pmc3044685:
Zhernakova and a large consortium combined in 2011 the gene hunting data for two autoimmune diseases, celiac disease and rheumatoid arthritis, to find risk genes they share. Each disease already had dozens of known risk spots outside the main immune gene region, and a few overlapped. Pooling the two datasets boosted power to catch weaker shared effects.

Follow up testing in thousands more patients confirmed eight new shared signals, including four never firmly tied to either disease before. Four spots known from one disease were also confirmed in the other, bringing the shared total to fourteen. Several shared spots change how nearby genes are expressed in immune cells. The pattern points to antigen presentation and T cell activation as common drivers. The authors show that cross disease pooling is a cheap way to find real risk genes.
europmc-pmc3045385:
Hedlund and coauthors found in 2011 that stressed leukemia and lymphoma cells release tiny parcels that blunt the immune attack on them. The parcels, called exosomes, carry stress signal proteins that normally mark cells for killing by natural killer immune cells. On parcels, the same proteins act as decoys, soaking up the killer signal away from the tumor cell.

Two blood cancer cell lines made these signals constantly and shed them on parcels, which measurably weakened killer cell action in lab tests. Heat stress and oxidative stress, the kind caused by some cancer treatments, made the cells shed even more parcels and deepened the immune block. The authors warn this may help explain weak killer cell function in patients. They also urge care when heat based therapies are planned, since treatment itself could raise the decoy shield.
europmc-pmc3074985:
Rentz and colleagues reported in 2010 that brain amyloid, the protein deposit of Alzheimer disease, already tracks with weaker thinking in healthy older adults. They also found that mental reserve can blunt the link. Reserve is the idea that education and lifelong mental activity let brains cope with damage. The team scanned older adults, some healthy and some with Alzheimer disease, with a tracer that sticks to amyloid, and gave them thorough thinking tests.

Across the whole group, more amyloid in a key hub region meant worse scores, above all on memory, but also on language and spatial tasks. At higher reserve levels, the same amyloid load cost far less performance, and at the top it cost nothing measurable. The pattern held in healthy adults alone on a hard memory test. The authors read this as evidence that reserve protects against amyloid's early effects.
europmc-pmc3079585:
The ENCODE Project Consortium published in 2011 a user's guide to its encyclopedia of the working parts of the human genome. The genome's letter sequence alone does not say which stretches are genes, switches, or structural marks. The project set out to map all of those functional elements, along with their chemical states, using many technologies under shared quality standards.

Since its pilot phase on one percent of the genome, the project had expanded to the whole sequence, releasing data freely as it was produced. The guide explains what kinds of data exist, how to reach them through the project database, and how to use them to interpret a genome stretch of interest. Worked illustrations show researchers answering real questions with the resource. The authors present it as shared infrastructure for biology and medicine, much like the genome sequence itself.
europmc-pmc3146885:
David Alexander and Kenneth Lange upgraded a popular ancestry-estimation program in a 2011 paper in BMC Bioinformatics. Estimating what share of a person's DNA comes from each ancestral population is now basic in genetics. Their program already ran thousands of times faster than the older standard tool; this paper adds four capabilities.

The program can now pick the number of ancestral populations itself by cross-checking. It can learn from people of known ancestry for sharper estimates, and trim tiny ancestry shares to keep results readable on small datasets. It also splits work across several processors for very large files. Together the changes make the tool more accurate, faster, and easier to apply to modern genome collections.
europmc-pmc3153485:
Gemma Atkinson, Tanel Tenson, and Vasili Hauryliuk classified a family of bacterial alarm enzymes across the tree of life in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. These enzymes make and destroy a small alarm molecule that switches bacteria into survival mode under stress. Names and groupings had grown confused as members turned up in odd places, from plant chloroplasts to animals.

Searching more than a thousand genomes, the team sorted the family into thirty subgroups under three headings: long multi-part enzymes, small makers, and small breakers. Nineteen subgroups were new, including the first found in archaea, extending the alarm system to that whole branch of life. Patterns of which members coexist in a genome, plus exposed surface patches unique to the long forms, suggest how regulation signals travel.
europmc-pmc3161885:
Deirdre O'Hanlon, Thomas Moench, and Richard Cone challenged a textbook belief about vaginal protection in a 2011 paper in BMC Infectious Diseases. Helpful vaginal bacteria make hydrogen peroxide, long credited with killing the bacteria that overgrow in a common vaginal condition. Much of that evidence came from oxygen-rich lab setups unlike the body, so the team retested under body-like, oxygen-free conditions.

At levels found in the body, peroxide failed to kill any of the seventeen overgrowth species tested, and a splash of vaginal fluid blocked even extreme peroxide doses. Lactic acid at natural levels and acidity, by contrast, killed all the overgrowth species while sparing the helpful bacteria. The authors conclude acid, not peroxide, does the protective work, reshaping how probiotic strains should be chosen.
europmc-pmc3198985:
Simone Patergnani and a large group of co-authors reviewed calcium signaling at mitochondria-associated membranes in this 2011 article. These membranes are zones where the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell's main calcium store, sits in close contact with mitochondria. Calcium controls metabolism, growth, and cell death, and mitochondria help shape each calcium signal in strength and timing.

The review gathers what was known about how calcium leaves the endoplasmic reticulum and enters mitochondria across these contact zones. It describes the structure and molecular makeup of the contact sites and the close interplay between the two organelles. That exchange lets healthy signals pass through, but it can also carry harmful calcium loads that push a cell toward death.
europmc-pmc3217985:
Enrique Zudaire and colleagues presented AngioTool, software for measuring blood vessel networks, in this 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Studying angiogenesis, the growth of new vessels, depends on images of networks in tissues such as the embryonic hindbrain, the young retina, and the allantois. Quantifying those images by hand is slow, laborious, and error-prone.

AngioTool automates the job, computing the area a network covers, the number and total length of vessels, vessel density, and a measure of the gaps within the network. It also calculates a branching index, the number of branch points per unit area, which reflects sprouting activity. The team validated the tool on mouse hindbrain, retina, and allantois images. The software is open source and free to download.
europmc-pmc3247885:
Henrik Husted and colleagues asked what actually keeps joint-replacement patients in hospital under a fast-track program, in this 2011 study in Acta Orthopaedica. Their unit had already cut stays after hip and knee replacement to a median of two days, using spinal anesthesia and strong non-opioid pain regimens. The team tracked nearly two hundred consecutive patients against functional discharge criteria, checking twice daily.

In the first day or two, pain, dizziness, and general weakness caused most of the delay. Nausea, vomiting, and confusion played only minor roles. Logistics mattered too: waiting for transfusion, physiotherapy, or X-rays delayed about a fifth of patients. The authors advise that further gains should target better pain control, prevention of dizziness on standing, faster recovery of muscle strength, and tighter organization.
europmc-pmc3278385:
Simone Mader and colleagues searched for the missing antibody target in neuromyelitis optica patients who lack the known marker, in this 2011 paper in the Journal of Neuroinflammation. The disease attacks the optic nerves and spinal cord, and most patients carry antibodies against the water channel aquaporin-4, but a substantial minority do not. Animal work hinted that antibodies to myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein, MOG, might fill the gap.

The team tested several hundred patients and controls. Aquaporin-4 antibodies appeared in nearly all definite cases. High-titer MOG antibodies clustered in a childhood demyelinating disease. They also appeared in a slice of the marker-negative optic and spinal patients. Two of the three MOG-positive neuromyelitis patients, and all such high-risk patients, lacked the aquaporin antibody entirely, marking a distinct subgroup. Both antibody types could trigger complement-driven cell killing at high levels.
europmc-pmc3286485:
Heusinkveld and van der Burg published a review in 2011 about macrophages that gather inside human tumors. These white blood cells show up in most cancers and often point to a poor outlook for the patient. The authors sort out what was known about the different forms these cells take and why findings from mouse studies do not transfer cleanly to people.

Inside a tumor, macrophages can lean toward attacking cancer or toward shielding it and helping it grow. The review covers the signals in tumor tissue that push cells one way or the other. It closes by weighing treatments that try to block, remove, or retrain these cells as a form of immune therapy.
europmc-pmc3296185:
Bendas and Borsig reviewed how sticky molecules on cancer cells help tumors spread, in an article from 2012. To form new growths elsewhere, cancer cells must grip blood vessel walls, slip out of the bloodstream, and settle in fresh tissue. Along the way they also interact with platelets and white blood cells that help them travel.

The review gives special attention to heparin, a blood thinner long given to cancer patients to treat clots. Studies in animals show heparin also slows spread, and patients on it tend to live longer. The authors argue it blocks one family of grip molecules, the selectins, and may also interfere with another family, the integrins, opening a path toward new anti spread treatments.
europmc-pmc3312285:
Ahmad and colleagues reviewed a miniaturized kind of antibody used in research and medicine, in a 2012 article. Normal antibodies are large Y shaped proteins, but scientists can build just the gripping tip as a single chain fragment. These small fragments, called scFv, can be produced inside bacteria, which makes them cheap and quick to manufacture.

Fragments can be fused to glowing or color producing marker proteins, giving a tool that finds a target and signals its presence in one step. They can also be hitched to toxins, used to deliver genes, or sent inside cells as blockers against cancer related proteins. The review covers how the fragments are designed and made, and closes with their growing use in breast cancer research.
europmc-pmc3349985:
De la Monte examined the evidence that Alzheimer's disease involves a failure of insulin signalling within the brain itself. Drawing on post-mortem studies and experimental work, the review develops the idea that the condition behaves partly like a metabolic disorder confined to the nervous system.

Human brain tissue from Alzheimer's cases showed reduced insulin and insulin-like growth factor signalling, alongside the familiar plaques and tangles. In experimental models, impairing brain insulin pathways reproduced features of the disease, including memory problems and abnormal tau. The author argues that this brain insulin resistance helps explain why diabetes raises Alzheimer's risk and points toward metabolic therapies.
europmc-pmc3358085:
Tadesse and colleagues traced how Escherichia coli in the United States grew resistant to antimicrobial drugs across half a century, from 1950 to 2002. They drew together isolates from people and from food animals, treating this common gut bacterium as a sentinel for resistance trends in both populations.

Resistance proved consistently highest against the drugs that had been in use the longest in human and veterinary medicine. More recent decades brought major increases in multidrug-resistant strains and in resistance to newer drug classes such as fluoroquinolones. The authors argue that tracking these long trends is essential for choosing treatments and shaping public health responses.
europmc-pmc3362085:

This companion guide explains the thinking behind each item, so authors can see what good practice looks like on the page.

Each item is spelled out in depth and paired with published examples of clear write-ups. The authors also show how choices in specimen picking, assay methods, and study design can sway results, which is why full reporting matters. They mean the guide to serve as a reference for planning, running, and writing up this kind of study.

four-books-concerning-the-secrets-of-the: Four Books concerning the Secrets of the Adepts, 1685. The adepts' secrets. This book preserves that work. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
four-books-of-johannes-segerus-weidenfel: Four Books of Johannes Segerus Weidenfeld, concerning the secrets of adepts, 1685. The adepts' secrets. This book preserves that alchemy. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
fox-underhill-missing-link-1885:
Leah Fox, the eldest of the famed girls, tells her own tale in The Missing Link in Modern Spiritualism, out in 1885. As A. Leah Underhill she looks back on 1848, when raps in her kin's house in Hydesville sparked a world faith. She was there. She managed, taught, and at times fought her own young kin in the years of fame.

Her tale is part log, part plea for her place in the tale. Feuds, fraud claims, and fame crowd the pages. No past of the faith can skip her voice. She was in the room where it all began.
frus-1861-d185:
A second letter from the Acting Secretary of State to Carl Schurz bears the date 5 November 1861. It is document 185 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two letters to Madrid in one day from the acting chief match the Secretary's own habit. Each takes its own point in the Spanish file. The pair falls days before the Trent seizure, in the last calm week of the autumn. Last calm weeks in this file are few, and this pair of letters marks one. Few calm weeks remained in 1861, and the file soon shows why.
frus-1861-d285:
By the date of 19 August 1861, Seward had new word ready for Mr. Haldeman. Congress received it as Document 285 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d85:
