Martyr never crossed the ocean, yet his decades became the first history of the New World. Eden's version was also the first English book on America, feeding English hunger for the western seas. Court gossip, explorers' tales, and hard news mix in its pages. The work shows Europe learning, letter by letter, what Columbus had found.
phileas-fragments-of-the-epistle-of-phil:
Phileas, bishop of Thmuis in Egypt, wrote to his people under fire. The great persecution of the early 300s was then raging around them. He himself would suffer martyrdom soon after writing the letter.

Fragments of the letter survive in the 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers. They call his flock to endurance in the face of torment. The tortures Christians faced are described with unflinching honesty. No soft words hide the price of holding the faith in those years. The voice is that of a pastor writing what may be his last words. A suffering flock heard them then, and they still carry weight now.
phileas-the-epistle-of-the-same-phileas-:
Phileas of Thmuis wrote this second surviving letter to a fellow bishop. Meletius, bishop of Lycopolis, received it during the persecution years. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers preserves the short piece in English.

Questions of church order stand at the center of the letter. Persecution had thrown normal discipline into deep confusion across Egypt. Bishops had to hold their scattered people together under imperial violence. The letter shows that hard work being done in real time. Brief as it is, historians count the piece precious evidence. Few texts show so plainly how the early Church kept its structure when the state tried to crush it.
pierius-a-fragment-of-a-work-of-pierius-:
Pierius led the school at Alexandria around the year 300. Later ages called him the younger Origen for his learning. Nearly all his many writings have vanished from the record.

One fragment of his notes on Paul's first letter to the Corinthians survives. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers preserves that lone piece in English. Its subject is among the richest letters in the New Testament. Small as the scrap is, the voice in it is genuine and early. It speaks from the last generation of the old Church. Soon after, Constantine would change the Christian world beyond recognition forever.
plos-pone-0000085:
Jeffery P. Demuth, Tijl De Bie, Jason E. Stajich, and their team traced gene families across mammals in PLOS ONE in 2006. A gene family grows when genes are copied and shrinks when copies are lost. Comparing family sizes across mammal genomes shows which families expanded in which lines.

Some families ballooned in just one branch, often those tied to smell, immunity, or reproduction, where fast change pays. Others stayed near constant for a hundred million years. That mix reveals the tempo of genome change: mostly slow drift, with bursts where life history demands. The mammal-wide map gives later studies a baseline for judging whether any one family's change is special.
plos-pone-0000185:
Krishna Jafa, Pragna Patel, Duncan A. MacKellar, and colleagues published this HIV testing study in PLOS ONE in 2007. In 2004 the OraQuick test became the first rapid HIV antibody test approved in the US for oral fluid. It gives results in 20 minutes without a blood draw. The authors investigated false positive results reported with it from August 2004 to June 2005.

A false positive tells a healthy person they may have HIV, so clusters of them demand investigation. The team traced where and why the errors occurred. Their report helped testing programs judge when a rapid result needs lab confirmation, protecting trust in a test designed for fast, wide use.
plos-pone-0000285:
Jenny Fredriksson, Dragi Anevski, Peter Almgren, and colleagues published this human genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. GYS1 is a gene for making glycogen, the stored form of sugar in muscle. The authors report that variation in GYS1 interacts with exercise and gender to predict cardiovascular mortality, the risk of dying from heart and vessel disease.

A gene's effect may only appear in people who exercise, or in one sex. Testing for such interactions keeps researchers from missing real risk factors by averaging everyone together. The finding is a case study in why genetic risk cannot always be read from DNA alone.
plos-pone-0000385:
Dirk Taubert and colleagues studied a molecular gateway in human cells in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. OCT2 is a transporter, a protein that carries small charged molecules across cell membranes. It is known for handling drugs and waste, but the team asked which of the body's own chemicals it normally carries.

Identifying OCT2's natural substrates showed a link to dopamine-using nerve cells, the kind lost in Parkinson's disease. A transporter that moves dopamine-related chemicals could affect how those neurons handle their signals and toxins. The work connects a kidney-and-liver transport protein to brain chemistry, widening where researchers might look for disease mechanisms.
plos-pone-0000485:
Soon-Lim Shin and colleagues found rhythm in the firing of cerebellar neurons, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Purkinje cells are the main output neurons of the cerebellum, the brain structure that fine-tunes movement. Their simple spike trains, the streams of signals they emit, were long read as irregular; the team reported regular patterns in them.

Regularity in a spike train can carry information that average firing rates miss, such as precise timing for coordinating muscles. Showing that cerebellar output has pattern challenges models that treat it as noisy. The work supports a view of the cerebellum as a timing machine, where when a cell fires matters as much as how often.
plos-pone-0000585:
Adrienne Anginot and colleagues showed how immune cells and one adaptor protein govern bone-eating cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Osteoclasts dissolve bone, and their overactivation causes bone loss. The team found that lymphocytes and the Dap12 adaptor are key regulators of osteoclast activation. The activation studied was the kind linked to gonadal failure. That is the hormone drop that drives postmenopausal bone loss.

Bone biology and immunology meet in this finding: immune cells help set how aggressively bone is resorbed when estrogen falls. Dap12 is a signaling adaptor in immune cells, making it a possible drug handle. The work helps explain why menopause thins bone and where treatment might intervene.
plos-pone-0000685:
Andrew Orr, Marie-Pierre Dubé, Julien Marcadier and colleagues pinned a rare eye disease on one gene, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Schnyder crystalline corneal dystrophy is a rare inherited disease passed in dominant fashion. The cornea slowly clouds as lipids build up locally. Some cases also come with abnormal blood lipids across the body.

Earlier studies had narrowed the search but not closed it. The title states the conclusion: mutations in the UBIAD1 gene, which encodes a possible prenyltransferase, are causal for the disease. Naming the gene enables genetic testing for families, and it directs research at the lipid chemistry that clouds the cornea.
plos-pone-0000785:
Shripad D. Tuljapurkar, Cedric O. Puleston and Michael D. Gurven argued that men's mating patterns help explain why humans live so long. Evolutionary theory predicts senescence, declining survival with age, because selection acts more strongly on genes affecting early fertility and mortality than on late ones. Hamilton had quantified that argument: a rare mutation reducing late survival spreads easily because selection barely notices it.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE title flips the lens: mating patterns drive the evolution of human lifespan, and men matter in that math. If older males can still reproduce, selection keeps working on late-life survival. Long human life, including post-reproductive years, may partly be a by-product of male fertility.
plos-pone-0000885:
Maira Goytia, Nathalie Chamond, Alain Cosson and co-authors compared two closely related enzymes from harmful germs, in PLOS ONE in 2007. One enzyme, proline racemase, comes from the parasite that causes Chagas disease. It is a confirmed drug target because the parasite needs it to live and spread in its host.

The puzzle is that a near twin enzyme, hydroxyproline epimerase, does a slightly different job. Mixing the two up could mislead drug design. The team set out the molecular and structural marks that separate them. Clear marks like these help chemists aim at the parasite enzyme without hitting the wrong target.
plos-pone-0000985:
Suresh Gopalan described controls acting across cells that limit a plant virus in Arabidopsis, in a solo PLOS ONE article from 2007. Viruses infect many hosts, and how hosts and viruses signal during infection is still being mapped. That mapping should help design ways to prevent disease.

Gopalan reports a multidirectional non-cell autonomous control, meaning resistance signals act beyond the infected cell, plus a genetic interaction that restricts tobacco etch virus susceptibility. Plants cannot run from infection, so internal signaling is their whole defense strategy. Work in Arabidopsis, the standard lab plant, often transfers to crops. A control that works across cells is a promising kind of resistance.
plos-pone-0001085:
Jing Qu, Guang-Hui Liu, Kaiyuan Wu and colleagues showed that nitric oxide destabilizes a protein that controls sumoylation, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Sumoylation is a tagging system that adjusts how proteins work after they are built. How the tagging pathway itself is regulated was largely unknown.

The team report nitric oxide causes global hyposumoylation, a broad drop in SUMO tags, by destabilizing Pias3. Nitric oxide is a gas cells use as a quick signal, so linking it to a whole tagging system gives it wide reach. One small molecule turning down a general adjustment system could reshape many proteins at once during inflammation or nerve signaling.
plos-pone-0001185:
Pitcher plants of the genus Nepenthes catch insects in jug-shaped leaves filled with digestive fluid. Laurence Gaume and Yoel Forterre studied a surprising property of that fluid in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The plants, widespread in the Asian tropics, live on nutrients from the arthropods they trap.

The authors describe the fluid as viscoelastic. It acts partly like a liquid and partly like an elastic solid, and they show it is deadly to prey. That stickiness helps explain why insects that land in the fluid fail to escape even when it is diluted by rain. The work reveals a trapping mechanism quite different from a simple drowning pool.
plos-pone-0001285:
El Niño events periodically warm the Pacific and starve the Galápagos of food, and marine iguanas suffer heavily. Sebastian Steinfartz and colleagues measured the genetic impact of a severe El Niño on these iguanas, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The El Niño-Southern Oscillation is a major source of climatic disturbance for ecosystems worldwide.

The authors examined how a severe event reshaped the genetic makeup of Amblyrhynchus cristatus populations, through deaths and breeding skews. Models predict stronger and more frequent El Niño events as greenhouse gases rise. Genetic data from past events show what future ones may do to island species.
plos-pone-0001385:
Stephen Welle, Rabi Tawil, and Charles Thornton published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on why men's muscles are larger than women's. The gap in muscle mass is plain to see, but its gene basis was not clear. The team set out to find genes that might drive the gap. They compared gene use in muscle samples from men and women.

By reading which genes were on or off in each sex, they built a list of leads. Some genes stood out as much more active in one sex than the other. The list gives a base for work on muscle growth, loss, and sex based gaps in muscle ills. It may also inform care for weak or wasting muscle.
plos-pone-0001485:
David Allen and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on norovirus, a top cause of stomach flu in all ages. Human noroviruses come in many types, and one type rules world wide. The team read changes in one part of its shell protein. They asked which changes mark each strain and draw immune attack.

Their map of change in that shell region flags spots that likely act as strain marks. Antibodies aim at those spots, so change there lets the virus dodge past defense. Tracking such spots helps labs spot new strains early. It also informs the hard quest for a norovirus shot.
plos-pone-0001585:
Amelia Turagabeci, Keiko Nakamura, and Takehito Takano published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on healthy habits and youth harm in Japan. Bullying, violence, and injury are grave school ills for teens. Daily habits such as sound food, hygiene, and exercise anchor school health plans. The team asked whether those habits track with less harm.

They found teens with healthier daily habits faced lower risks of being bullied, of violence, and of injury. A habits link gives schools a low cost lever beyond rules and guards. It also ties body health to social safety in a way plans can use. The data come from a broad youth survey.
plos-pone-0001685:
Elza Rakhimova, Antje Munder, Lutz Wiehlmann, and their co-authors studied shape-changing bacteria in infected airways for a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Pseudomonas aeruginosa causes chronic lung infections, above all in cystic fibrosis. During long infections, one founding clone splits into niche specialists and varied colony shapes, a pattern called dissociative behavior.

The authors tested how fit these isogenic colony variants are, meaning strains that differ only in colony form. They used a mouse airway infection model to compare them. The full text gives the variant types, the infection results, and which forms held up best in the lung. Knowing which shapes thrive in airways helps explain how this germ settles in for years despite treatment.
plos-pone-0001785:
Keith W. Sockman examined how hatching order shapes a young bird's chances in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Dependent siblings compete for food their parents provide, and that competition can kill. The probability of death may depend partly on production order: eggs laid later hatch later, leaving chicks smaller than their siblings. In altricial birds, chicks hatch helpless and stay in the nest.

Sockman reports that ovulation order mediates a trade-off between survival before hatching and survival after it. The full text gives the nest records and the survival patterns by laying position. The trade-off shows parents and evolution balancing two risks at once, and it explains why laying order effects differ among bird studies.
plos-pone-0001885:
Hanna Maenpaa and co-authors ran a trial on thyroid cancer care in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. After surgery to remove the thyroid, patients often get radioactive iodine to burn away any tissue left behind. How much iodine to give was unsettled, so the team set up a randomized test of a low dose against a high dose.

The trial enrolled one hundred sixty adults whose cancer was of the papillary or follicular type. Each person got one of the two dose levels, and the team judged how well the leftover tissue was cleared. Dose choice matters: too much adds risk and cost, too little may leave tissue behind. Trials like this set the dose on proof, not habit.
plos-pone-0001985:
Wei Li and co-authors tracked a pro-inflammatory signal switched on by flu, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The signal, interleukin-32, is a cytokine, a small protein that spreads immune messages. It had lately been described, and was known to rise when cultured cells met bacteria. But its role in real viral infection in people was little known.

The team found that levels of this signal rose with influenza A infection. As the title states, infection activates this pro-inflammatory pathway. A signal that flares in flu may help explain why some cases turn severe. It also gives drug work a new point to calm the response.
plos-pone-0002085:
Patrick McGowan and co-authors found heavy gene tags in the brains of people who died by suicide, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Shifts in gene expression in the suicide brain had been reported for several genes. DNA methylation, a chemical tag that mutes genes, was thought to play a role. Ribosomal RNA genes encode the backbone of the protein-making machinery.

The team report promoter-wide hypermethylation of the ribosomal RNA gene promoter in suicide brains: dense tags across the switch region. If protein output is damped in the brain, many systems could drift. The study links an epigenetic mark to a tragic outcome, with care.
plos-pone-0002185:
Luís Bettencourt and Ruy Ribeiro built a fast way to judge the threat of a new disease outbreak, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Crowding, travel, and land-use change keep raising the risk of emerging infections. At the time, officials worldwide feared that H5N1 bird flu might learn to spread between people as easily as seasonal flu.

The authors present a real-time Bayesian method, a way of updating odds as fresh case data arrive. It estimates an outbreak's epidemic potential while events are still unfolding. Early, honest numbers on how fast a disease can spread are among the most useful tools health officials can have.
plos-pone-0002285:
Sarra Jamieson, Lee-Anne de Roubaix, Mario Cortina-Borja, and co-authors studied why congenital toxoplasmosis harms some children more than others, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A Toxoplasma gondii infection during pregnancy can pass to the fetus. Infected babies may show brain calcification, fluid on the brain, and eye disease, and new eye lesions can appear at any age.

Not all infected children suffer the same outcome. The team examined genetic and epigenetic factors at two genes, COL2A1 and ABCA4, and found they influence the clinical course. Knowing which children carry the risky variants could guide closer monitoring of sight and development from birth.
plos-pone-0002385:
Kishida, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Its subject is pattern of the Divergence of Olfactory Receptor Genes during Tetrapod Evolution. The olfactory receptor (OR) multigene family is responsible for the sense of smell in vertebrate species.

OR genes are scattered widely in our chromosomes and constitute one of the largest gene families in eutherian genomes. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002485:
Taylor and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Jordan A. Taylor, Kurt A. Thoroughman, among others. Its subject is motor Adaptation Scaled by the Difficulty of a Secondary Cognitive Task. Motor learning requires evaluating performance in previous movements and modifying future movements.

The executive system, generally involved in planning and decision-making, could monitor and modify behavior in response to changes in task difficulty or performance. The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002585:
Si and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Xiaoning Si, Guang Gao, Jerry Wong, among others. Its subject is ubiquitination Is Required for Effective Replication of Coxsackievirus B3. Protein ubiquitination and/or degradation by the ubiquitin/proteasome system (UPS) have been recognized as critical mechanisms in the regulation of many key cellular functions.

The importance of the UPS in viral pathogenesis has become increasingly apparent. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002685:
In 2008, Bingke Bai and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was Virus-Like particles of SARS-Like coronavirus formed by membrane proteins from different origins demonstrate stimulating activity in human dendritic cells. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Bingke Bai, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The pathogenesis of SARS coronavirus (CoV) remains poorly understood. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002785:
Laurent Mereghetti and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of remodeling of the streptococcus agalactiae transcriptome in response to growth temperature. The catalog record names Laurent Mereghetti first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. To act as a commensal bacterium and a pathogen in humans and animals, Streptococcus agalactiae (group B streptococcus. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002885:
George Zogopoulos, Claus Jorgensen, Julinor Bacani and colleagues looked for inherited variants in the EPHB2 receptor gene in 2008. Colorectal cancer clusters in families in about 15 to 20 percent of cases, yet known syndromes explain only a small share. The genetic basis for most family cases was still unknown.

EPHB2 had lately been tied to this cancer, so the team checked germline variants, meaning changes passed down through families, in people with familial colorectal cancer. Published in PLOS ONE, the work tests one candidate gene in detail. It helps narrow where the missing family risk for bowel cancer may lie.
plos-pone-0002985:
Hongjie Yu, Zhancheng Gao, Zijian Feng and colleagues summarized 26 human cases in China. The cases were of highly pathogenic avian influenza A, subtype H5N1. Their article appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The catalog record gives the title, authors, and year. Its abstract snippet repeats the title instead of adding methods or results. On that evidence, the article is a clinical summary of confirmed human H5N1 cases in China.

It was written for clinicians and public health readers tracking severe bird flu infections in people. No further detail is given in the record beyond that summary.
plos-pone-0003085:
Anton Dluzewski, Irene Ling, John Hopkins and co-authors studied food vacuole formation in the malaria parasite in 2008. Plasmodium falciparum makes merozoite surface protein 1 during schizogony as a large precursor cut into four fragments. A second cut during red cell invasion sheds most of it, leaving a 19 kDa fragment.

That fragment may play a role in forming the food vacuole, the chamber where the parasite digests hemoglobin, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, the vacuole is the target of several malaria drugs, so its assembly is worth close study. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003185:
Babacar Faye and co-authors study a fly virus-like element in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Its integrase is the protein that cuts host DNA and inserts viral DNA into it. Most such elements land in varied spots, but a few hit one exact site each time. ZAM, from the fruit fly, is one of those rare precise cases.

The team describe how the ZAM integrase works and why it is so exact in its choice of site. Readers see a natural tool that puts DNA in one set place. Gene work needs that kind of care, since stray inserts can break host genes.
plos-pone-0003285:
Jun Qin, Ming-Jer Tsai and Sophia Y. Tsai study a nuclear receptor in male fertility in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Chicken ovalbumin upstream promoter-transcription factor II, or COUP-TFII, also known as NR2F2, is an orphan nuclear receptor of the steroid and thyroid hormone receptor superfamily. Mice lacking COUP-TFII die during early embryonic development due to angiogenesis and cardiovascular defects.

The authors report essential roles of COUP-TFII in Leydig cell differentiation and male fertility. Readers learn how a broadly acting receptor has a specific testis role. Leydig cells make testosterone, so their development links gene control directly to male reproduction.
plos-pone-0003385:
Carine Poussin and colleagues compared two kinds of body fat in mice in this 2008 study. Fat around the organs, called visceral fat, differs from fat under the skin. The two types expand in distinct ways when an animal grows obese. The team fed mice a high-fat diet for six months and tracked gene activity.

Some mice also got rimonabant, a drug that cuts weight. Gene patterns for metabolism and for the tissue frame differed between the two fat types. The drug changed those patterns too, and not in the same way for each type. The work helps explain why deep belly fat harms health most.
plos-pone-0003485:
Chris Finan and co-authors measured newborn vaccine responses in Gambia for this 2008 study. Babies there receive the BCG vaccine against tuberculosis at birth. The shot protects children from severe, spread-out forms of TB. Yet it often fails against adult lung disease.

The team followed a cohort of Gambian infants after vaccination. Immune responses varied naturally from baby to baby. Mapping that variation helps explain why protection is uneven. Better TB vaccines will need to beat the responses BCG gives. BCG has been given for decades, yet its limits still shape TB policy.
plos-pone-0003585:
Juan Carlos Pizarro and Lori Stevens read insect blood meals with DNA in this 2008 paper. Chagas disease is a leading cause of heart disease in Latin America. The parasite Trypanosoma cruzi spreads through blood-feeding insects. Knowing what those insects feed on is key to its epidemiology.

Their new forensic method analyzes the blood meal inside the vector. It was demonstrated with Triatoma infestans from Chuquisaca, Bolivia. Feeding patterns reveal which animals keep the parasite circulating. The bug's gut becomes an informant on transmission routes. The same DNA tricks now serve wildlife crime labs in many countries.
plos-pone-0003685:
Pierre M. Durand, Kubendran Naidoo, and Theresa L. Coetzer published this malaria study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Malaria is the deadliest protozoan disease of humans, and drug resistance keeps shrinking the drug supply. Most new drug programs fail along the way. The authors looked for better targets in the parasite Plasmodium falciparum.

Their approach, called evolutionary patterning, compares parasite proteins across species. Sites that evolution kept unchanged stand out as spots a drug might strike with less risk of quick resistance. The method turns the parasite's own history into a guide for drug hunters.
plos-pone-0003785:
Jessie McGowan, William Hogg, Craig Campbell, and colleagues published this primary care trial in PLOS ONE in 2008. Family doctors face clinical questions all day with little time to search for answers. A just-in-time librarian service was built to supply rapid information during patient hours. The team tested whether it helped.

In a randomized controlled trial, doctors got librarian answers to their clinical questions as they worked. The study evaluated whether that information improved their decision-making. The results support feeding timely evidence into everyday practice rather than leaving doctors to search alone.
plos-pone-0003885:
Emmanuelle Bille, Roisin Ure, Stephen J. Gray, and co-authors probed meningococcal disease in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns Neisseria meningitidis, the germ behind severe meningitis. The germ often lives in the nose and throat without causing harm. Only at times does it turn deadly, and the reasons were not fully known.

The team searched for genetic factors that push the germ toward disease. They report a link between a bacteriophage, a virus that infects bacteria, and illness in young adults. That link offers a fresh clue to why some carriers get sick. It may point to new ways to flag risky strains.
plos-pone-0003985:
Yasuharu Tokuda, Masamine Jimba, Haruo Yanai, and co-authors surveyed trust and life quality in Japan in 2008. Psychosocial factors like trust are gaining attention in health research. Japanese people live long yet report modest subjective well-being. They also report lower interpersonal trust than many nations.

Their PLOS ONE article links interpersonal trust with quality of life. The cross-sectional survey measured both in a Japanese sample. Higher trust tracked with better reported quality of life. The findings support social connection as part of public health. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004085:
Noha Sharaf Eldin, Soheir Ismail, Hala Mansour, and co-authors studied acute hepatitis C care in Egypt in 2008. Some people clear hepatitis C on their own after symptoms start. Others keep the virus and face chronic liver disease. Knowing the clearance rate guides when to start treatment.

Their study estimated spontaneous clearance after symptomatic acute infection. Patients who did not clear received twelve weeks of pegylated interferon alfa-2a. Short treatment worked as the tested strategy for non-clearers. The results help clinics time therapy instead of treating everyone at once. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004185:
David Marshall and Kathy Hill published this field study in PLOS ONE in 2009. In aggressive mimicry, a predator copies another species' signal to exploit the animal that answers it. Some of the most striking cases involve a predator breaking into a complex signal system of an unrelated species.

The authors describe an Australian predatory katydid that mimics cicadas in a remarkably versatile way. The katydid copies cicada calls to lure its prey within reach. Their account ranks among the most elaborate known cases of a predator faking its way to a meal.
plos-pone-0004285:
Deirdre Cunningham and colleagues published this malaria study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The pir multigene family, found in several Plasmodium malaria parasites, encodes variant antigens that the immune system may target. In the rodent malaria Plasmodium yoelii, the yir branch of this family is large and variable.

Starting from single parasites picked out by micromanipulation, the team tracked how yir transcription profiles change in clonal populations. They report rapid changes and question whether epigenetic memory holds the pattern steady. Fast switching would help the parasite stay ahead of immune recognition.
plos-pone-0004385:
Antarctic shelf waters have stayed too cold for many shell-crushing predators. Crabs and similar hunters are kept out by the chill. Richard Aronson, Ryan Moody, Linda Ivany, and co-authors studied the bottom-living animals there. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper asks what warming seas will do to that balance. Local species evolved with few such predators.

As Earth warms, species from milder waters shift toward the poles. The authors weigh how invading predators could reshape feeding links on the Antarctic shelf. Native bottom fauna could face hunters they never evolved to escape. The study frames climate change as a biological invasion risk. It gives a baseline for watching southern seafloor life.
plos-pone-0004485:
Two polarity proteins share a job in guiding one-sided cell division in fruit flies, show Jose-Eduardo Gomes, Maria Corado, and Francois Schweisguth in PLOS ONE in 2009. Sensory organ precursor cells in the fly divide along the body's head-to-tail axis. The two daughter cells are different, so the division must be aimed with care.

A system called planar cell polarity sets that aim. Two of its proteins, Van Gogh and Frizzled, sit at opposite ends of the cell. The team shows they act redundantly, backing each other up, to orient the division. Redundancy makes the system robust: losing one guide does not fully break the aim. The work adds detail to a steering system used across the animal kingdom, including in our own tissues.
plos-pone-0004585:
The same cortical areas handle two kinds of visual judgment, show Marc Tibber, Elaine Anderson, Dean Melmoth, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. One judgment is visuospatial interpolation: seeing a contour continue across a gap. The other is orientation discrimination: telling which way lines tilt. Much was known about short-range interactions between local visual filters in perceiving broken contours.

Less was known about how spatial information is integrated across distant parts of the visual field. The team found common cortical loci, the same brain spots, activated during both tasks. Shared ground suggests the brain reuses one integration system for both jobs. Findings like this help build a unified account of how scattered visual fragments become whole scenes.
plos-pone-0004685:
Mohamed Abdelkarim and colleagues made new forms of a bone drug that may fight breast cancer, for PLOS ONE in 2009. Drugs called bisphosphonates show promise in cancer care. Their flaw is that they stick to bone and reach soft tissue poorly, which limits their use in breast tumors.

The team masked parts of the drug to help it slip into soft tissue. They then tested the new forms on breast cancer growth and spread. Better reach could turn a bone drug into a wider cancer tool. The work is an early step that still needs much more testing.
plos-pone-0004785:
Lutz Jäncke and colleagues compared brain architecture in golfers of differing skill, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Several studies show that intense practice can reshape brain structure in humans. Cross sectional studies of expert performers suggest long term structural adaptations tied to years of demanding, specific training in a skill domain.

Golf at a high level is one of the most demanding sports for fine control. The team compared golfers across skill levels for brain differences. Skill linked structure can show where practice leaves lasting marks. It also informs training science beyond sport. Taken together, the findings mark a useful step for research in this area.
plos-pone-0004885:
Sjoukje Kuipers and colleagues studied selective survival and maturation of adult born dentate granule cells expressing Arc, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Progenitor cells in adult dentate gyrus provide constant neuronal precursors, yet only a small fraction survive and develop into mature granule cells. Understanding stringent selection is a major challenge, and expression of the immediate early gene Arc marks cells engaged by experience during critical periods.

Experience activated cells preferentially survive integration. Use it or lose it governs adult neurogenesis. Enrichment may boost successful integration. New neurons support pattern separation in memory. Later work can build on these findings and test them in broader settings.
plos-pone-0004985:
Teeth are built by a signal chain called Eda-Edar. Breaking either link causes defects. Cyril Charles and colleagues compared two mouse mutants in PLOS ONE in 2009. One lacks the signal, Eda. The other lacks its receptor, Edar. Their adult dentitions had classically been described separately.

The comparison showed distinct impacts for the two losses. Losing the signal is not the same as losing the receiver. Each shapes the teeth in different ways. That distinction refines how the pathway is understood. It also matters for human conditions where this pathway fails. Teeth, hair and glands all depend on the same signal chain.
plos-pone-0005085:
Prepulse inhibition is the brain's startle filter. A weak sound before a loud one normally softens the flinch. That filter weakens in schizophrenia and related disorders. Motoko Maekawa and colleagues studied a fatty acid's role in PLOS ONE in 2009. The fatty acid is arachidonic acid. Earlier work had tied a fatty-acid binding gene to the filter in mice.

Arachidonic acid drove new neuron growth after birth. It also improved prepulse inhibition in the animals. The fatty acid links brain growth to a psychiatric trait. The finding points to a role for nutrition in brain wiring. It does not promise a treatment. It does show that a dietary molecule can touch both neurogenesis and behavior.
plos-pone-0005185:
Proteins can be joined together with the help of inteins, protein pieces that cut themselves out and link their neighbors. Split forms of the DnaE intein are a popular tool for that joining work. Aranko and colleagues compared natural and built versions of these inteins in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The team tested protein joining both in living cells and in lab mixtures outside cells. Shorter tail pieces of the intein are in demand, since they are easier to make and use. The results show which versions work best in each setting, helping labs pick the right tool for building custom proteins.
plos-pone-0005285:
As bacteria grow resistant to standard drugs, interest in antimicrobial peptides has risen. Short peptides are cheap and stable but often too weak to kill bacteria well. Pasupuleti and colleagues strengthened ultra-short peptides in PLOS ONE in 2009 by tagging their ends.

The tags are stretches of the amino acids tryptophan and phenylalanine, written as W and F. Adding them to the ends helped the peptides kill bacteria while aiming to spare human cells. End-tagging is a simple design trick that could yield a new class of germ killers.
plos-pone-0005385:
Facial clefts are among the most common birth defects and have a strong genetic component. Jugessur and colleagues ran a large candidate gene study in PLOS ONE in 2009, using two national cleft studies from Scandinavia.

The team genotyped over fifteen hundred variants in three hundred fifty-seven candidate genes. Samples came from Norwegian and Danish case-parent and control-parent triads. Searching fetal genes at that scale can separate real risk factors for clefting from the many near misses. Cleft lip and palate can be fixed by surgery, yet the cause hunt still counts. Since a known gene risk could guide care in the womb and in the first days of a child's life.
plos-pone-0005485:
Kenia Whitehead and co-authors reported daily timing behaviour in archaea in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Many living things use cues such as light to expect changes that come later in the day. Expecting change in advance helps them be ready when it arrives.

Archaea are tiny single-celled organisms quite unlike bacteria, and their daily rhythms were little known. The team found signs that these organisms entrain to a daily cycle and act ahead of coming change. If tiny archaea keep time this way, the roots of biological clocks may be older and wider than thought.
plos-pone-0005585:
Julien Muzard and co-authors developed a scan method for scarring in tissues, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Fibrosis is the build-up of collagen that stiffens organs in many chronic diseases. It is a huge health burden, yet doctors lack gentle ways to spot it early and track it.

The team built a probe shaped like a natural collagen binder, attached to a tracer for imaging. In tests, the probe found collagen in scarred tissue without surgery. A scan for fibrosis could change how diseases of the liver, heart, and lungs are managed.
plos-pone-0005685:
Marc Thilo Figge built a math model in 2009 to fine-tune antibody replacement therapy. Some people are born with parts of the immune system missing or broken. One such fault, X-linked disease, leaves patients short of the antibodies that fight germs.

Doctors replace those antibodies with regular doses from donors, but the best dose and timing are hard to set. Figge models the immune response as a system shaped by chance, then uses it to tune treatment. A better-tuned plan could cut infections while using less of a scarce, costly product. The model gives clinics a test bed before changing real care.
plos-pone-0005785:
Ulrich Leischner, Walter Zieglgänsberger, and Hans-Ulrich Dodt measured in 2009 how sharp a whole-sample microscopy method really is. Ultramicroscopy images large, cleared samples in three dimensions, whole organs at once. But users need hard numbers on its resolution and field of view.

The team analyzed those limits directly, so researchers know what the method can and cannot show. Clear samples plus light-sheet views offer a new scale of anatomy, between cell and organ. Honest specs keep the method from being oversold. The paper serves as a reference card for labs adopting the technique.
plos-pone-0005885:
Anna Skoglund and co-authors tracked in 2009 how a stomach germ adapts its coat as the stomach around it changes. Helicobacter pylori infects half of humanity and can cause ulcers and stomach cancer. In chronic gastritis, the acid-making cells of the stomach are lost.

As the gastric environment shifted, the germ's surface sugar variants changed with it, the team found. Variants of its lipopolysaccharide coat likely tune how it grips and hides. That adaptability helps explain infections that last a lifetime. It also complicates vaccine design, since the target keeps changing.
plos-pone-0005985:
When insulin reaches a fat cell, its receptor does not stay on the surface. Siri Fagerholm, Unn Örtegren, Margareta Karlsson and colleagues timed that exit in rat fat cells in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper asks whether the receptor leaves through caveolae, tiny flask-shaped pits in the cell surface where the receptor is known to sit.

The title gives the answer: uptake is fast, insulin-driven, and runs through caveolae. How a receptor leaves the surface shapes how long its signal lasts, so this route helps set the strength of insulin action. The finding adds fine detail to the picture of how fat cells answer insulin, a core question in diabetes research.
plos-pone-0006085:
Shipworms bore through wood at sea with help from a tenant germ. Joyce Yang, Ramana Madupu, Scott Durkin and colleagues read that germ's whole genome in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper reports the complete genome of Teredinibacter turnerae, a marine bacterium living inside cells in the gills of wood-boring bivalves of the shipworm family.

The strain studied is the only cultured member of its kind, which makes its genome a key reference. Genes for digesting wood and fixing nitrogen can be hunted in its sequence. Beyond sea biology, such a genome interests biofuel work, since few creatures break down wood as well as the shipworm and its partner.
plos-pone-0006185:
Touch a hidden real hand and a visible rubber hand at the same time, and people soon feel the fake is theirs. Sotaro Shimada, Kensuke Fukuda, and Kazuo Hiraki studied this rubber hand illusion in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Earlier work showed the illusion fades when the two touches fall out of sync.

The team added delayed visual feedback, so sight lagged behind touch. The sense of owning the rubber hand weakened as timing slipped. The study shows that body ownership depends on senses agreeing in time, not just in place. That insight matters for prosthetic design and for virtual reality, where delays are common.
plos-pone-0006285:
A natural defence peptide made in the gut is tied to inflammatory bowel disease. Marian Aldhous, Colin Noble, and Jack Satsangi studied human beta-defensin-2 in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. People with fewer copies of its gene, and thus lower message levels, are more prone to Crohn's disease of the colon.

The team investigated how the protein itself is dysregulated in bowel disease patients. Gene dose and protein behaviour together shape the gut's antimicrobial shield. Understanding the fault sharpens the search for causes of Crohn's. It may also point to treatments that restore the gut's own defences.
plos-pone-0006385:
Some tumors hide from T cells by dropping the machinery that displays antigens. Xiao-Lin Li and colleagues tested a workaround in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Tumors lacking the antigen transporter TAP usually fail to induce T-cell immunity and resist T-cell killing. Adding the costimulator gene B7.1 changed that picture.

B7.1 costimulation enabled T-cell based immunity against TAP-negative cancer, and TAP1 expression facilitated the effect. Giving tumors a louder activation signal compensates for their dim display. The combination points toward vaccines for hard-to-see tumors. Antigen presentation faults are common in advanced cancer.
plos-pone-0006485:
Baptiste Faure, Didier Jollivet, Arnaud Tanguy, and colleagues studied deep-sea species formation for PLOS ONE in 2009. Rebuilding the history of divergence and gene flow between close relatives is a long-standing hard task in evolutionary genetics. New approaches have made it more tractable. The team applied multi-locus analysis to two hybridizing species from the deep sea.

Where the two species meet, they still interbreed, blurring their boundary. Many genes together can separate true divergence from shared ancestry. The deep sea is a striking test case, since its barriers are invisible. Their work shows how species can split even while genes still flow.
plos-pone-0006585:
Adolfo Sequeira and co-authors analyzed brain gene expression in suicide and depression in PLOS ONE in 2009. Most studies of the neurobiology of depression and suicide focused on the serotonergic system. While serotonergic alterations clearly play a role, they are not the whole story. The team ran a global brain gene expression analysis.

Their title links glutamatergic and GABAergic alterations to suicide and major depression. Those are the brain's main excitatory and inhibitory systems. A global scan can reveal systems that focused studies miss. The results widen the search for antidepressant targets beyond serotonin.
plos-pone-0006685:
Jai S. Rohila and colleagues mapped protein partners of rice kinases in PLOS ONE in 2009. Kinases are enzymes that switch other proteins on or off. Rice leaf cells contain many kinases whose partners were unknown. Knowing the partners reveals how signals move through the plant. The team studied eighty-eight rice kinase genes expressed in leaves.

Each kinase was fused to a tandem affinity purification tag. The tagged proteins were produced in transgenic rice plants. The researchers then purified the kinases along with proteins bound to them. Offspring of the transgenic plants supplied the material for testing. The resulting interaction map gives rice biology a firmer base for studying signaling and stress responses.
plos-pone-0006785:
Ilana Kolodkin-Gal and colleagues compared bacterial self-poison systems in liquid and in biofilms in PLOS ONE in 2009. Toxin-antitoxin modules are gene pairs encoding a poison and its antidote. Many bacteria, including pathogens, carry them on their chromosomes. E. coli carries five such systems. Their effects on cell death were the focus.

Each system affected death differently in liquid media. Effects also differed during biofilm formation. Biofilms are the surface communities bacteria build together. A system harmless in liquid might matter greatly in a biofilm. The contrast shows context decides what these modules do. That matters for efforts to disrupt biofilms in medicine and industry.
plos-pone-0006885:
Randi Sørby and colleagues tracked prion protein in sheep spleens after scrapie infection in PLOS ONE in 2009. Scrapie is the sheep prion disease. Spread of infectivity to the brain requires prion protein in peripheral tissues. The spleen participates in that neuroinvasion process. Exactly how it participates was not known.

The team examined normal prion protein expression in spleen compartments. They also mapped accumulation of the abnormal form, PrPSc. Innervation of those compartments was recorded as well. Nerves may carry the agent from spleen toward the brain. Mapping the spleen's role clarifies the long silent phase of prion disease.
plos-pone-0006985:
Angela Cannas, Glendah Kalunga, Clare Green, and colleagues studied stored urine samples in PLOS ONE in 2009. Doctors increasingly read DNA from urine to diagnose infections and tumors. Samples are often stored first, whether collected at home or kept in biobanks. No best practice for that storage had been set.

The team tested how storage affects urinary DNA from different populations. Sample quality after storage decides whether later tests can be trusted. Their guidance matters for large studies that bank samples for years. Poor storage quietly ruins data long before anyone runs the analysis.
plos-pone-0007085:
Bérengère Vire, Stéphane de Walque, Audrey Restouin, and colleagues tested a leukemia drug in PLOS ONE in 2009. Histone deacetylase inhibitors had shown promise against blood cancers in trials. One such drug, MS-275, kills leukemic blasts by triggering apoptosis. The killing was thought to run through death receptor pathways.

The team linked MS-275's activity to an immune pair, 4-1BBL and its receptor 4-1BB. That pair usually helps coordinate immune cells. If a cancer drug also wakes immune signaling, its benefits may be double. The finding suggests combining such drugs with immune therapies for leukemia.
plos-pone-0007185:
Subramani Poongothai, Rajendra Pradeepa, Anbhazhagan Ganesan, and colleagues measured depression in a large South Indian city population in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper draws on the Chennai Urban Rural Epidemiology Study, known as CURES. India had very few population-based figures for depression when they began.

The authors recruited subjects from that large Chennai study, which involved tens of thousands of people. They report how common depression was in this urban population. Public health readers get a rare local baseline for planning mental health services and outreach across urban India today.
plos-pone-0007285:
Benjamin P. B. Downing, Andrew D. Rutenberg, Ahmed Touhami, and colleagues used bacterial oscillations as a drug sensor in 2009. In Escherichia coli, a protein called MinD sweeps rapidly from pole to pole. That oscillation helps the cell divide in the middle, and it can be watched with fluorescent tags.

The authors expose bacteria to charged molecules including protamine and gentamicin. Gentamicin is a common antibiotic. They use Min oscillations as a single-cell reporter of drug action. Changes in the rhythm reveal how these polycations affect living cells, offering a fast screening readout.
plos-pone-0007385:
Joshua M. Stomel, James W. Wilson, Megan A. León, and colleagues tested a man-made protein inside living bacteria in 2009. Advances in de novo protein evolution let researchers create synthetic proteins from unbiased libraries. Those proteins can fold into stable structures with predefined functions, even though nature never made anything quite like them before.

Whether such proteins work inside living cells was unknown. The authors express a synthetic ATP-binding protein in bacterial cells. They report it causes abnormal growth. Their PLOS ONE result is a caution and a proof: artificial proteins are active in cells, sometimes unexpectedly.
plos-pone-0007485:
Anshuman Dixit and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the spots in proteins where cancer mutations cluster. Protein kinases are the protein family most often implicated in cancer. Resequencing projects have catalogued many mutations across their ranks. Certain positions mutate again and again, forming hotspots. The team compared the sequence and three-dimensional structure around those hotspots to find what marks them.

They identified signature patterns shared by the danger zones. Those signatures combine local spelling with structural context, such as where the spot sits in the folded protein. Recognizing the pattern helps predict which new mutations are likely to drive tumors. It also guides drug design toward the most dangerous variants. The work turns a catalogue of mutations into something closer to a warning system.
plos-pone-0007585:
Marija Zanic and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on EB1, a protein that rides the growing ends of microtubules. Microtubules are the cell's internal rails, and their fast-growing plus ends host tracking proteins. EB1 forms comet-like tails at those tips. How it knows where the tip is was the puzzle. The answer lies in the chemical state of the tubulin building blocks in the lattice.

Freshly added tubulin still carries its energy tag, called GTP. Older lattice has spent it. EB1 recognizes that nucleotide state, so it gathers where the rail is new. That recognition explains the comet and how ends link to other structures. The finding is a neat piece of cellular bookkeeping. It shows the cell reading the age of its own construction material to find the frontier of growth.
plos-pone-0007685:
Sylvain Lacomble and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns Trypanosoma brucei, the parasite behind sleeping sickness. Its swimming tail holds a stiff rod-like structure called the paraflagellar rod. Around forty protein parts of that rod were already known.

The authors mapped how those parts interact with each other, protein by protein. An interaction map shows which parts bind directly and which sit in shared groups. That kind of map helps researchers work out how the rod is built. It also shows where drugs might disrupt the parasite.
plos-pone-0007785:
Holger Mitterer and James McQueen published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests how subtitles affect the understanding of foreign speech. Foreign speech is hard partly because its sounds map oddly onto words. Native listeners can use word knowledge to learn odd pronunciations.

The authors asked whether subtitles give learners the same kind of help. Foreign-language subtitles helped listeners perceive the speech. Subtitles in the listener's own language hurt instead. The result is practical for language learners and teachers alike. Watching foreign films with original-language captions may train the ear better than translated ones.
plos-pone-0007885:
Ashwin Kelkar and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It reads the layered history written into the human X chromosome. One X chromosome in women is largely switched off, a process called inactivation. The chromosome was also built up in layers over evolutionary time.

Those layers are called evolutionary strata, and their boundaries are hard to draw. The authors used Markov segmentation, a method that finds stretches of differing composition in a sequence. They mapped inactivation domains and strata together. The combined map sharpens the picture of how the X chromosome evolved and how it is silenced.
plos-pone-0007985:
Xiao-Xing Li and colleagues counted the germs living in sore stomachs in PLOS ONE in 2009. Two usual suspects were ruled out first: the ulcer germ H. pylori and pain drugs of the NSAID kind. What was left was gastritis with no clear cause.

Gene-based profiling showed the stomach lining still held a rich mix of bacteria. The stomach, long thought nearly sterile, hosts a crowd even in illness from other causes. A full census is a first step toward learning which of those germs soothe the lining and which stir up pain.
plos-pone-0008085:
Wenli Pan and colleagues compared two skin tests for tuberculosis in South African children for PLOS ONE in 2009. Both tests plant a germ protein in or on the skin and read the bump that follows. All the children had the BCG vaccine, which can blur test readings.

More than fifteen hundred children took both the Mantoux injection test and the Tine prick test. The two agreed only in part, and the team weighed what drives a positive read. In places where BCG is routine, picking the truer test shapes how many children get treated or watched.
plos-pone-0008185:
Philipp Schoenenberger, Daniela Gerosa, and Thomas G. Oertner described a light-based tool in PLOS ONE in 2009. Channelrhodopsin-2 is a light-gated channel that lets scientists fire neurons with light. Changes to one part of the protein, at position 128, greatly extend its open state. That offers finer temporal control over gene switches in cells.

The team used this control to turn on immediate early genes with light. These genes switch on fast when cells are active. Precise timing helps researchers link a burst of activity to later cell changes. The method sharpens a widely used tool in brain research.
plos-pone-0008285:
Tania Maffucci and colleagues studied vessel formation signals in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Fibroblast growth factors guide embryonic development and tissue balance. They also drive tumor angiogenesis, the growth of vessels into tumors. When these factors bind their receptors, several signaling cascades start. Two of them involve PI3K and phospholipase Cgamma1.

The team traced a pathway joining those two cascades. That pathway regulates how capillary tubes form after growth factor stimulation. Tube formation is a step toward working blood vessels. Knowing its controls could help limit tumor blood supply.
plos-pone-0008385:
Marco Domingues and his team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about a small protein that kills germs. Such germ-killing proteins may one day stand in for the usual drugs that germs now resist. Their test case, rBPI21, is based on the front part of a protein from white blood cells. It is picky, and harms the coats of germs while it spares our own cells. How it strikes was the point of the study.

The protein made a germ surface fat clump up in heaps. It also forced the coats of germ-like sacs to merge and leak. These two moves spell out how it kills. A clear view of the strike can guide new germ drugs.
plos-pone-0008485:
Anna Corcione and co-authors study a chemokine receptor on B cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The chemokine is called fractalkine, or CX3CL1. It sits on cell surfaces and guides immune cells. Its receptor, CX3CR1, is found on several lymphocyte types. Fractalkine appears in germinal centers, where B cells mature in lymph tissue. The team ask if human B cells bear the receptor and use it.

They find CX3CR1 on human B lymphocytes. They also show it drives movement of tonsil centrocytes toward fractalkine. Centrocytes are B cells in a key stage of maturation. The path may help position them in germinal centers.
plos-pone-0008585:
Margaret Clarke and co-authors image a proton pump in living cells in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The vacuolar H+-ATPase, or V-ATPase, moves protons across membranes using ATP. The resulting proton gradient serves many essential functions. Among them is energizing transport of small molecules such as neurotransmitters. Immune cells use phagosomes to engulf and digest microbes. Acid in those compartments helps kill the prey. The team use live cell imaging to track the pump.

They reveal how the V-ATPase is retrieved from phagosomes after use. Retrieval recycles the pump for new rounds of work. That step had been hidden before live imaging could capture it. The work clarifies how immune cells manage their digestive compartments.
plos-pone-0008685:
Kevin Wanner, Andrew Nichols, Jean Allen, and colleagues chased a scent puzzle in a farm pest. Their 2010 PLOS ONE paper covers the European corn borer, a moth whose caterpillars damage corn. The moth exists in two races that use near-opposite blends of female scent. Males of each race follow only their own blend.

The team hunted for the nose proteins that tell the two blends apart. They tested how each candidate receptor reacts to the scent parts. A sharply tuned receptor would explain how males stay loyal to one race. The findings could help design scent traps that lure this pest away from crops.
plos-pone-0008785:
E. Camilla Forsberg, Emmanuelle Passegué, Susan Prohaska, and colleagues captured gene signatures of blood stem cells in three states. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hematopoietic stem cells build all blood cell types. Resting cells stay quiet, mobilized cells enter the blood, and some rogue cells start leukemias. Keeping the quiet state working for life is vital. The pathways guarding each state were incompletely known.

Profiles of the three states revealed signature gene sets for each. Comparing them highlights what changes when stem cells wake or turn rogue. Those signatures can guide safer stem cell transplants. They also expose early steps toward leukemia.
plos-pone-0008885:
Aristeidis Parmakelis, Marina Moustaka, Nikolaos Poulakakis, and colleagues scanned the genes that help a mosquito fight germs. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. To beat malaria, some plans aim to change wild mosquito groups so they can no longer pass the germ to us. Such plans need a deep grasp of the genes the bug uses to fight off germs. Some genes change much faster than chance would allow. Fast change is a sign that germs and the bug are locked in a long arms race.

The defense genes of these mosquitoes bore clear marks of that fast change. Even one small spot in a gene could show the push. The fast spots show just where germs press the bug most. That map can help us breed or build bugs that block malaria well.
plos-pone-0008985:
Guoliang Li, Jian Ma, and Louxin Zhang tackled how to pick species for rebuilding family-tree history, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Biologists reconstruct what ancestors looked like by comparing living species on a tree. Which species you sample changes how accurate the reconstruction is. Picking well matters when sequencing or measuring species costs money and time.

The team compared two greedy strategies for choosing the sample set. Dropping species that add little beat adding species that look promising. Elimination, in their analysis, reached better reconstructions than insertion. The rule gives genome projects a smarter way to spend a limited sampling budget.
plos-pone-0009085:
Nadja Larsen and co-authors compared gut bacteria in adults with and without type 2 diabetes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fresh evidence was then linking metabolic disease to gut microbes. The gut community helps digest food and trains the immune system. Whether its makeup differs in diabetes was the study's question.

Stool samples from diabetic and non-diabetic adults were profiled. The proportions of major bacterial groups differed between them. Some groups tied to gut health were reduced in the diabetic gut. Differences like these raise the question whether microbes help drive diabetes.
plos-pone-0009185:
Robert van Woesik, Kazuyo Shiroma, and Semen Koksal published this modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It concerns reef corals and the tiny algae that live inside them. Those algae, called Symbiodinium, feed the coral and vary from host to host. The question was whether that variety helps corals cope as oceans warm.

Using a mathematical model, the authors tested whether differences among symbionts predict how many of them live in a coral. They also asked whether specialist types would grow more common under warming. The model links the spread of traits in the symbiont population to coral survival. That link offers a way to forecast which reefs may adjust to hotter seas.
plos-pone-0009285:
Eulalie Buffin and Michel Gho published this methods study in PLOS ONE in 2010. In the fruit fly Drosophila, each bristle and sense organ grows from one special cell. That sensory organ precursor is chosen from a cluster of equal cells. Studying the chosen cell alone is hard because it sits among its near-identical neighbors.

The authors used laser microdissection to cut out single precursor cells cleanly. The method isolates the cell without disturbing its state. With pure samples, researchers can read which genes the chosen cell uses. That opens a window on how one cell wins the contest to become a sense organ's founder.
plos-pone-0009385:
Brigitte van Cleef and co-authors published this public health study in PLOS ONE in 2010. A drug-resistant staph germ, MRSA type CC398, had been found in farm animals. It also appeared in farmers and even in shop-bought meat. The worry was whether it spreads to neighbors who never touch livestock.

The team surveyed communities in the Netherlands with very dense pig farming. They measured how common the livestock strain was in people without direct animal contact. Knowing the true reach of the germ guides policy on farms and clinics. The study separates farm risk from neighborhood risk for a resistant bacterium.
plos-pone-0009485:
Volkhard Rippe and a team of co-authors studied benign thyroid tumors in PLOS ONE in 2010. Such tumors are common, found in about one adult in twenty. Many of them carry a shuffle of DNA on chromosome 19. The team asked what that shuffle turns on inside the tumor cells. They focused on two clusters of tiny RNA genes.

The shuffle switches both clusters on, so the tumors make large amounts of those small RNAs. Those RNAs can change the output of many genes at once. The finding gives these common tumors a clear molecular mark. It also shows how a DNA shuffle can rewire a cell without breaking a protein gene.
plos-pone-0009585:
Tiphanie Gomard and co-authors traced an alarm signal in immune cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dendritic cells sense germs and then rally the rest of the immune system. When they meet bacterial toxin, called LPS, they mature and release inflammatory messengers. A protein named JunB is part of that response. The team tested its role in dendritic cells grown from mouse bone marrow.

JunB drove the making of several pro inflammatory messengers. It did so in a way that depended on the NF-kappaB pathway. The study maps one control point in the first response to infection. Tuning such points could help calm harmful inflammation without silencing defense.
plos-pone-0009685:
Melanoma is the deadliest form of skin cancer. Mitchell Stark and colleagues set out to list every microRNA active in melanoma cells, using deep sequencing to do it. Their catalog appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. MicroRNA changes are known to shape how cancers behave.

MicroRNAs are tiny molecules that tune how strongly genes are switched on. A complete list shows which of these regulators melanoma leans on as it grows. Some entries in the catalog were new, and others matched patterns seen in healthy skin. The map gives cancer researchers fresh targets for tests and possible treatments.
plos-pone-0009885:
A mushroom used in East Asian traditional medicine may help fight prostate cancer. Takanori Tsuji and colleagues tested an extract of Phellinus linteus on advanced prostate cancer cells. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The extract sensitized the cancer cells to apoptosis, the orderly self-destruction of damaged cells. Cells that resist apoptosis are a hallmark of advanced cancers. The tests used athymic nude mice, animals bred without a working thymus for tumor studies. Making stubborn cells die more easily could support future therapies. Advanced prostate cancer has few good options.
plos-pone-0009985:
The genes for one cellular power machine are not scattered at random through the genome. Yael Garbian and colleagues found those genes arranged in clusters. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The machine sits in mitochondria, the cell's power stations.

Oxidative phosphorylation is how cells make most of their energy currency. Complex I is the first and largest machine in that chain, built from many subunits. The expression patterns of its subunit genes were organized in clusters. Clustered control may help the cell build the machine in balance. Order, not scatter, turned out to rule their control.
plos-pone-0010185:
The authors were Irini Tossidou, Beina Teng, Jan Menne, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study covered kidney damage in diabetes, in mice and humans. An early sign is microalbuminuria, small amounts of protein leaking into urine. That leak ties to loss of slit diaphragm proteins, which form the kidney's fine filter in podocyte cells.

The team studied an enzyme, PKC-alpha, inside podocytes under diabetic conditions. They showed it mediates the uptake and loss of nephrin, the filter's main protein. Blocking that route could protect the kidney filter earlier in diabetes.
plos-pone-0010285:
The authors were Boris Malyarchuk, Miroslava Derenko, Tomasz Grzybowski, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study traced early Europeans through one maternal lineage. Haplogroup U5 is generally accepted as the most ancient European mitochondrial lineage. It is thought to have evolved largely within Europe itself, making it a window on the continent's first settlers.

To resolve its family tree, the team fully sequenced 113 mitochondrial genomes. Samples came from central and eastern Europeans, including Czechs and Slavs. The tree they built sharpens the timeline for how U5 spread across Europe. Those genomes anchor the haplogroup's deep history in Europe.
plos-pone-0010385:
Taylor Cohen and colleagues examined stretched lung cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Breathing machines can injure the lung while keeping patients alive. Part of that injury involves the thin cell sheets lining the air sacs. The team grew rat air-sac cells for five days, then stretched them repeatedly. They stretched by two amounts, at a steady rhythm, to mimic machine breathing.

They tracked a signaling system called MAPK as the stretching proceeded. That system helped decide how leaky the cell sheet became. A leakier sheet lets fluid flood the air sacs, worsening injury. Knowing which signals control the leak points to protective settings or drugs. The work links a machine's physical push to a cell's chemical answer.
plos-pone-0010485:
Rui Sousa-Neves and Alexandre Rosas analyzed genetic changes as fruit fly species split apart in PLOS ONE in 2010. Speciation reshapes bodies and builds barriers between populations. Those barriers can be genetic, developmental, or behavioral. Which changes come first, and in what order, was poorly known. The authors mined fly data to trace the sequence of divergence.

Fruit flies are ideal for this because their genetics are so well mapped. Comparing sister species shows which differences accumulate early or late. A clearer sequence could reveal what actually drives splits. That question sits at the heart of evolutionary biology. The study uses a classic model animal to attack a classic unsolved problem.
plos-pone-0010585:
Michael Washburn and colleagues used mice to study a stubborn liver problem, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A harmless virus vector can place a foreign protein in liver cells for months. The immune system often ignores it, which limits some gene therapy plans.

A signaling protein called LIGHT changed that picture. Giving LIGHT helped the immune system clear the lingering protein from the liver. The same treatment also caused liver inflammation. So one signal drove two outcomes: useful clearance and harmful swelling. Separating those two effects is the next challenge for using LIGHT in therapy.
plos-pone-0010685:
D. Lys Guilbride and colleagues asked why malaria vaccines that fully protect some volunteers fail in the field, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Trial vaccines sometimes shield people under lab conditions. In places where malaria is common, the same shots protect poorly, and infants gain the least.

The team reviewed close to two thousand immunization studies spanning decades. They kept only cases of full protection and compared them with field results. From that contrast they built a new model of how anti-malaria immunity works. The model blames a mismatch between what shots train and what real infection demands, and it points trials toward better targets.
plos-pone-0010785:
David Nelson and colleagues found signs of gene swapping inside marine iguana guts, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bacteria trade genes sideways, without reproduction, a process called lateral gene transfer. The trade is well documented in mammal guts. Whether it shapes the gut microbes of wild marine reptiles was unknown.

Gene family trees from iguana gut bacteria showed mismatched branches. Some genes had plainly arrived from unrelated microbes. The iguana gut, fed on seaweed, is thus another marketplace for bacterial genes. Gene trading speeds adaptation in gut communities, letting microbes pick up new food skills from neighbors instead of evolving them slowly.
plos-pone-0010885:
Nickolai Titov, Gavin Andrews, Alice Kemp and co-authors published this mental health study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Internet clinics for anxiety and depression were growing, but critics worried their users might be milder cases who differ from typical patients. If so, results from online trials might not apply to ordinary care.

The authors profiled more than seven hundred applicants to an Australian internet clinic and compared them with patients at a specialist outpatient clinic and with cases from a national survey. The groups were compared on background details and symptom severity measured with standard scales. Titov and colleagues test whether online patients are a fair stand-in for the wider anxious and depressed population. Their answer matters for how much weight health systems should give to evidence from internet treatment trials.
plos-pone-0010985:
Junhong Gui, Tao Wang, Richard Jones and co-authors published this heart genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sick sinus syndrome is a failure of the heart's natural pacemaker. A rare inherited form is tied to mutations in SCN5A. That gene builds a sodium channel that carries the heart's electrical signal. The team tested thirteen such mutant channels to learn how each one fails.

Expressed in human cells and frog eggs, the mutants fell into distinct groups. Some reached the cell surface normally and passed normal amounts of current, but opened and closed with altered timing. Others were mistargeted or produced weak currents. Gui and colleagues show that one syndrome can arise through several distinct molecular failures. That variety explains why the same diagnosis can behave differently across families, and why treatment may need to match mechanism.
plos-pone-0011085:
Pulford, Reim, Bell and colleagues described a drug delivery test in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their target was prion disease, the fatal brain illness linked to a misfolded protein. A major hurdle is the blood brain barrier, a tight wall that keeps most drugs out of the brain.

The team built tiny fat bubbles linked to short RNA pieces and a peptide. These packages crossed the barrier and lowered prion protein levels in nerve cells and in infected cultures. Lowering that protein strikes at the root of the disease process. The result points toward a possible path for treating illnesses like Creutzfeldt Jakob disease.
plos-pone-0011185:
Volkova, Howey, Savill and colleagues modeled sheep trade in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sheep move between farms for sale and breeding, and infections can travel with them. The team built networks of those movements to see how disease could spread through the farm system.

The network view revealed which links and farms matter most for spread. Control that targets the highest risk movements first can slow outbreaks with less disruption. Blanket bans cost farmers heavily, so sharper tools matter. The work informs livestock disease planning in Britain and in other trading systems.
plos-pone-0011285:
Wu, Sercu, Van De Werfhorst and colleagues surveyed coastal city waters in PLOS ONE in 2010. Urban watersheds carry runoff into bays where people swim and fish. The team characterized the bacterial communities living in those coastal waters, looking beyond the standard germ counts used to judge safety.

From those communities they derived new indicators of water quality based on whole community patterns. Richer indicators could catch pollution that single germ tests miss. That aids monitoring programs that keep managed waters safe for swimmers. The approach treats the whole microbial community as a fingerprint of watershed health.
plos-pone-0011385:
Lisa Davenport documented in 2010 a rare case of care for an aging leader in a wild giant otter group. Giant otters live in close family groups led by a dominant breeding pair, and they hunt and defend territory together. What happens when the female leader grows old and weak had barely been recorded in the wild.

Davenport watched younger group members support the declining matriarch, sharing food and staying near her as her condition worsened. Such help is costly for the helpers, so its presence says much about the strength of family bonds in this species. The account adds otters to the short list of wild animals seen aiding an aged leader. For biologists, it raises fresh questions about how social care evolves in group-living predators.
plos-pone-0011485:
Isabelle Lesur and co-authors profiled in 2010 how gene activity changes stage by stage in acute lung injury in mice. The injury floods the lungs with inflammation that rises, peaks, and resolves, and a treatment that helps at one stage can harm at another. Without a molecular clock for the stages, doctors must guess where a patient stands.

Reading gene activity across the injury timeline, the team characterized the signature of each inflammatory phase. Those signatures turn a blur of inflammation into named stages with marker genes. Clinicians and researchers can use the map to match therapy to the moment in the disease course. The work also helps animal studies speak to human care, by letting researchers check that they are treating the same stage they intend to treat.
plos-pone-0011585:
Rodrigo Aldecoa and Ignacio Marín introduced a software tool named Jerarca in PLOS ONE in 2010. Biologists increasingly map complex networks, such as links between genes or proteins. Pulling clear patterns from such tangled maps is hard, yet it is central to genomics and the study of proteins.

Jerarca sorts network members into nested groups, step by step, building on an earlier program called UVCluster. The authors show the method finds layered structure in large networks quickly and reliably. For researchers facing huge interaction maps, the tool offers a practical way to reveal groups within groups instead of one flat list.
plos-pone-0011685:
Daniel Acuña and Víctor Parada studied how people solve a classic hard problem, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The traveling salesman problem asks for the shortest tour through many stops, and the number of possible tours explodes so fast that even computers cannot check them all. People, oddly, do well at such hard problems in daily life.

Given tour problems to solve, participants explored the options efficiently and found near-optimal routes. Their strategies avoided wasting effort on hopeless regions of the search space. Understanding these mental shortcuts can inspire better algorithms and explain how humans handle intractable choices.
plos-pone-0011785:
Erin Koen, Colin Garroway and Paul Wilson tested a hidden flaw in wildlife movement models, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Models estimate how hard a landscape is for animals to cross, guiding corridor planning. Maps, however, end at artificial boundaries that do not exist on the ground, and those edges might bias the results by acting as fake barriers.

The authors show map boundaries do shift estimates of landscape resistance. Model animals pile up or turn back at edges that are pure artefacts. Planners are warned that the map's rim can lie, and that study areas should extend beyond the region of real interest.
plos-pone-0011885:
Min Sung Choi, Andrew Yoo, and Iva Greenwald reported in 2010 on two genes that hold back a key development signal in the roundworm C. elegans. The signal runs through LIN-12, the worm version of the Notch pathway, which guides cell fate choices as tissues form. When Notch signaling cannot be turned down, development and, in humans, cancer risk suffer.
