The team identified sel-11 and cdc-42 as negative modulators that restrain LIN-12 and Notch activity. Brakes like these are as important as the accelerator, since they decide how long a fate signal lasts. Working out the brake system in a simple worm gives clues that carry into the much-studied Notch pathway in human disease.
plos-pone-0011985:
Edgar Deu and co-workers showed in 2010 how to run drug screens in messy, realistic cell mixtures instead of purified proteins. High-throughput screening is the workhorse for finding enzyme inhibitors, but it usually needs targets that can be made in bulk or purified. Many interesting enzymes fail that requirement.

Their method uses activity-based probes, molecules that tag only the active form of an enzyme, to build screening assays that work in complex cell extracts. Screening where the enzyme sits among thousands of other proteins is closer to how a drug will meet it. That widens the list of enzymes that drug hunters can realistically pursue.
plos-pone-0012085:
I-Jong Wang and co-workers coated in 2010 a gene-delivery virus with chitosan to change how well it enters eye cells. The study's purpose was to modulate adenovirus transfection of the cornea, useful for treating eye disease with genes. Chitosan, a sugar polymer from crustacean shells, was attached to the virus capsid by a chemical thioether link.

Testing the modified virus on bovine corneal epithelial cells showed how the coating alters delivery efficiency. A tunable virus matters because raw adenovirus enters some eye cells too poorly and others too eagerly. Surface chemistry like this chitosan coat is one of the few dials available for aiming gene therapy at the cornea.
plos-pone-0012185:
Xianfeng Chen, Xinlei Li, Ping Wang, and co-authors built a new statistical strategy for disease gene hunting, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their quarry was copy number variation, places where people carry extra or missing chunks of DNA. Such chunks clearly cause some human diseases, but no good statistical model existed for testing them across large patient groups, so they were often skipped.

Their integrated strategy makes that testing systematic, opening a class of variation that studies had left in the dark. New risk sites found this way could explain cases that ordinary gene scans missed. Method papers like this widen the net for every disease study that follows, from rare disorders to common ones.
plos-pone-0012285:
Michelle Nerandzic and Curtis Donskey proposed waking a hospital pathogen's spores in order to kill them, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Clostridium difficile causes the most common healthcare-linked diarrhea in rich countries, and its spores shrug off alcohol hand rubs and many disinfectants that kill the active form easily. That toughness is why the bacterium keeps returning to cleaned wards.

Triggering the spores to germinate turns them into the vulnerable active form at a moment of our choosing. A wake-and-kill strategy could finally clear spores from surfaces and hands instead of waiting them out. In infection control, a genuinely new angle on an entrenched problem is rare and valuable.
plos-pone-0012385:
Philipp Antczak, Fernando Ortega, Kevin Chipman and colleagues linked drug chemistry to cell pathway changes in a 2010 PLOS ONE study on toxicity. Modern safety testing needs early signs that a compound will harm the liver or other organs. Past methods used either the drug's chemical features or its effects on cells, rarely both together.

The authors mapped chemical features onto pathway activity and found networks that connect a compound's structure to harmful outcomes. Those networks can flag risky drugs earlier, before animal tests or human harm. The approach points toward safety screens that read both what a drug is and what it does to cells, saving time and failed trials.
plos-pone-0012485:
Direk Limmathurotsakul, Kris Jamsen, Arkhom Arayawichanont and colleagues estimated the true accuracy of culture tests for melioidosis, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Melioidosis is a severe tropical infection, and growing its bacterium in culture is the standard test. Culture is perfectly specific — growth means disease — but how many true cases it misses was unknown, precisely because it is the standard.

Using Bayesian latent class models, which infer truth without a perfect reference, the team estimated culture's real sensitivity. Knowing the miss rate tells doctors how hard to keep looking when cultures stay negative. In regions where the disease is common, that number shapes lab investment and treatment decisions.
plos-pone-0012585:
Patrick Schulz, Johannes Werner, Tobias Stauber and colleagues dissected a disease mutation in a cellular transporter, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. ClC-7 moves chloride and protons across compartment membranes and is found throughout the body. Its failure causes lysosomal storage disease and osteopetrosis, a disorder where bone becomes too dense and brittle; one mutation, G215R, appears in the ADO II form.

The team found the mutant transporter still works chemically but suffers a severe trafficking defect, never reaching its proper post. A routing fault, not a broken engine, calls for different therapy ideas — such as helping the protein fold and travel — than an activity fault would.
plos-pone-0012685:
Hauri, Fabricius, Schaffelke and co-authors measured the water chemistry under seaweed mats on damaged coral reefs. Hurt reefs often end up covered by thick mats or canopies of macroalgae. Their 2010 study asked how that cover changes the light, flow and chemistry felt by corals beneath.

They recorded conditions under the algae and watched effects on understorey corals. A changed microclimate can starve corals of light or alter the water they need. Knowing this helps reef managers judge when clearing algae truly aids recovery. The study separates shade effects from chemical effects with care.
plos-pone-0012785:
Shin and Bleris borrowed tools from engineering to model gene networks. Linear control theory was built to steer machines with feedback loops. Their 2010 paper shows the same maths can describe how genes turn each other up and down inside cells.

A control view lets biologists predict how a network answers a push, and where it stays stable. That is the kind of prediction drug designers need before touching a living system. The paper builds a bridge between two fields that rarely share methods.  The authors test the idea on known network examples first.
plos-pone-0012885:
Chen, Strand, Norenburg and co-authors used network methods to sort ribbon worm samples into likely species. Ribbon worms of the cephalotrichid group are hard to tell apart by eye. Statistical parsimony networks, which link DNA sequences by small changes, had been suggested as a way to spot species in sequence data.

Their 2010 study put that suggestion to the test on real nemertean samples. A method that works could speed species discovery in groups where experts are few. It also gives a check on species named by looks alone.  Worm samples came from several collection sites and hosts.
plos-pone-0334585:
Samuel Abie and co-workers trace drug-resistant staph bacteria along the beef line in two Ethiopian slaughterhouses. This germ spreads between animals and people and shrugs off many antibiotics. Their 2026 study swabs carcasses, tools, surfaces, and workers' hands and clothes, then tests the bacteria found against ten drugs and reads the gene behind methicillin resistance.

A quarter of swabs carried the germ, with workers' hands and hooks the most contaminated spots. Every isolate resisted penicillin and methicillin, and most resisted several drug families, though one drug still worked on all. The resistance gene in these isolates clustered oddly with relatives from milder staph species. Cleaner hands and tools could cut spread to meat and workers.
plos-pone-0336185:
Naji Alyami tested a teaching method that pairs mind mapping with the chatbot ChatGPT to help Saudi university students read English more deeply. Sixty male students in a preparatory year were split into two groups for ten weeks. One group built mind maps with the chatbot's help, while the other learned mapping in the usual way, and both took reading tests before and after.

Students in the chatbot group scored clearly higher on the final reading test. In interviews they said the tool helped them break hard passages into parts and see how ideas connect. They also flagged real problems, including wrong answers from the chatbot and patchy access to technology. Alyami advises teachers to use the method with guidance rather than leave students alone with it.
plos-pone-0338885:
Mikayla Cutler, Nicholas Baker, and co-authors compared how people and computer vision systems tell objects apart when shape and surface pattern disagree. Humans lean heavily on shape, while neural networks lean on texture. Their 2026 study built a huge set of images from three-dimensional models, swapping textures onto objects and varying shading, shadows, and viewing angle.

People classified the swapped objects by shape far better than any network tested. Adding shading and shadow cues narrowed the gap by helping networks, yet the benefit landed differently: people gained most from unusual viewpoints, networks from standard ones. The authors argue that humans use such cues to grasp an object's solid structure, while networks treat them as just more surface information.
plos-pone-0341285:
Hamunakwadi and Smith, in a 2026 study, examine how Malawi's news media covered long-term diseases such as heart disease and diabetes in the years before COVID-19 and during the pandemic. These diseases cause a growing share of early deaths in poorer countries, yet their place on the public agenda was unclear. News coverage shapes what the public and leaders treat as urgent.

The team read headlines and selected stories from two Malawian outlets across nearly a decade. Before the pandemic, coverage heavily favored HIV, tuberculosis, and malaria over ten long-term diseases. During the emergency, COVID-19 took over, and mental health stories surged past the older infections. Coverage levels matched the true burden of disease only patchily. Stories usually framed charities, not the government, as responsible for acting on these diseases. The authors doubt such coverage will push leaders to give these diseases the weight their toll deserves.
plos-pone-0342085:
Luciana Carla Martins de Aquino and co-workers set out a plan to review research on immune cells found inside a hard-to-treat breast cancer. This cancer type lacks the hormone targets many drugs aim at, so treatment choices are few. Their 2026 protocol describes a planned review of whether patients whose tumors hold more of these immune cells live longer and stay free of returning disease.

Searches will cover eight major databases with no language limits, and two reviewers will screen studies on their own. A standard tool will grade how trustworthy each study is, and results will be pooled with statistics software. As a protocol, the paper reports no findings yet. Its planned summary could help doctors judge who may need closer follow-up.
plos-pone-0343185:
Clement Parfait Ndengue and colleagues ran a careful single specimen experiment on how lab handling before testing changes breast cancer marker readings. Tissue came from one untreated patients surgical sample, split into fifty tiny cores. Fixing time up to six days, delay before fixing up to eight hours, and buffered versus unbuffered fixative were varied in set groups.

Hormone receptor and growth marker stains were scored across all handling paths. In low resource labs where standard buffered fixative and tight timing are hard, small handling shifts can move marker scores and thus treatment choices. Full results guide which corners can be cut safely and which cannot, a practical question for labs far from rich centres.
plos-pone-0343485:
Emyo Fujioka and five colleagues watch bats hunting over a pond in this 2026 study. Japanese large-footed bats skim the water for insects. Hunting together could help bats find prey faster. It could also spark costly competition. Thermal cameras and a microphone array tracked every arrival, attack, and exit. The whole pond served as one natural foraging patch.

Attack rates fell by about a quarter when two bats hunted together. Paired flights also ended sooner than chance predicted. A null model, built from random independent events, expected longer overlaps. Real bats cut their shared time short. The pattern amounts to quiet coordination without any obvious signals. By limiting time spent sharing a patch, each bat protects its own catch rate. The study shows how to weigh cooperation and conflict in fully natural settings.
plos-pone-0347485:
Jennifer Shelton and colleagues describe a national monitoring scheme that turns honeybees into environmental samplers across the United Kingdom. Bees forage over wide areas and bring traces of the landscape back to the hive, including DNA from the plants they visited, captured in honey. Since 2018, more than thirty-five hundred volunteer beekeepers have sent in nearly six thousand honey samples.

Most samples come from farmland and from towns between May and October. Reading the environmental DNA in each jar maps what bees are eating, where, and how that shifts over years, at a scale no professional survey could afford. The platform shows how citizen science, organized well, can watch a whole country's ecology continuously.
plos-pone-0347585:
Swati Srivastava and colleagues map women's money access across India, district by district. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. National surveys sample too few people per district. So the team used small-area methods, which borrow strength from census data. They modeled three measures for two survey rounds. The map covers six hundred forty districts.

The gaps are wide. Women's bank account ownership ran from just over half in one Nagaland district to near total in a Tamil Nadu district. Knowledge of microcredit loans swung just as wide. Actual use of such loans stayed low in most places. Fine-grained maps like this aim help at the districts truly left behind.
plos-pone-0347785:
Abdulhameed N Hameed, Mohammad Tariqul Islam, and co-authors built a small antenna meant to serve three generations of wireless bands at once. Modern 5G devices need to work across lower microwave bands, mid-range Ku bands, and very high millimeter-wave bands, usually with several antennas working together. Their 2026 design packs that multi-antenna setup into a square only a few centimeters across.

Slots cut into the front and an L-shaped piece on the back widened each band's reach. Built and measured prototypes reached solid signal strength in all three ranges, and the separate elements barely interfered with each other, a key test for this kind of antenna. The team presents it as a compact option for future phones and other 5G gear that must cover many bands in little space.
plos-pone-0348285:
Miaolu Tang and colleagues used genetically engineered mice to watch benign vessel growths tip toward cancer. Human vascular malformations, tangles of abnormal vessels, usually stay harmless, but rare cases become angiosarcoma, a deadly vessel cancer. The mice carried a switched-on growth gene found in these malformations, with or without loss of a key tumour suppressor.

Almost every mouse with the growth gene developed blood-blister-like skin lesions, showing the gene alone starts the malformation. Losing the suppressor did not create more lesions but changed their character: some grew atypical, fast-dividing, infiltrating tissue resembling the human cancer. The model now offers a way to study warning signs and prevention.
plos-pone-0348585:
Hannah Mary Louise Young and colleagues set out the plan for a systematic review on easing fatigue in people with chronic kidney disease. Fatigue is among the most crushing symptoms of kidney disease, affecting daily life at every stage, yet treatments range from drugs to exercise with little guidance on what works. Their 2026 paper is a protocol describing how the review will be run.

The team will search six databases plus grey literature, accept studies of many designs in any language, and judge quality with standard checklists. Findings will be pooled where possible and graded for certainty. The finished review is meant to feed directly into United Kingdom kidney symptom guidelines.
plos-pone-0348785:
Qing Zhang and co-workers study why young Chinese travelers book tea-culture homestays, guesthouses wrapped in tea traditions. Generation Z guests increasingly seek stays with cultural depth. Their 2026 study surveys these consumers and models how personal involvement with tea culture feeds a sense of cultural identity, and how both shape the wish to book.

Deeper involvement raised both cultural identity and booking interest. Cultural identity itself also lifted booking interest. Part of involvement's effect ran through identity: feeling the culture as one's own turned interest into intent. Homestay hosts who stage real tea rituals, stories, and hands-on picking or brewing may convert curious browsers into guests more effectively than price cuts.
plos-pone-0348885:
Nathan Fortier, Gabe Rudy, and Andreas Scherer benchmarked the leading computer tool that predicts whether a DNA change will break the splicing step of gene reading. They set it against two free reimplementations and an older combined tool. Licensing on the original restricts hospital use. Six datasets, from a thousand hand-checked variants to a hundred thousand research records and tricky deep-intron cases, formed the test bed.

All three modern tools beat the older ensemble and matched each other closely on common variants. On deep intron variants, the original tool kept a clear lead, and the team found that the usual decision threshold is about ten times too high there. At default settings, most such harmful variants would pass unnoticed. The authors give clinical labs a practical map of where each tool can be trusted.
plos-pone-0349085:
Jian Guo and co-authors upgraded a scene text recognition system in 2026, the technology that reads signs and labels in photos for cars and apps. Light models falter on rotated, warped, or oddly styled text, a common real world case.

Three additions drive the upgrade. A jumbling step shuffles image patches to break the model's reliance on fixed layout. Self teaching passes knowledge from deep layers to shallow ones. A mixture of expert paths handles varied styles. Together they aim at robustness without a heavy model. The design accepts that street text is unruly and trains for that directly.
plos-pone-0349285:
Thirupathi Rao N and colleagues built a hybrid deep learning model for finding and outlining kidney lesions in CT scans. Kidney disease varies widely and lesion edges can be faint, so radiologists face a slow, error-prone task. Their model, GDT-SwinKid, marries a transformer that grasps the whole scan's context with a decoder that restores fine detail, tuned by a statistical distribution step.

On clinical datasets, the model outlined lesions with overlap scores up to the mid-ninety percent range. It sorted cases with near-perfect discrimination, beating leading transformer and convolutional rivals by several points on overlap. Accurate kidney lesion maps support surgical planning and treatment tracking, so gains of this size are clinically meaningful if they hold in new hospitals.
plos-pone-0349385:
Babar Hayat and co-authors built a deep learning framework in 2026 for diagnosing faults in industrial plants. Missed faults threaten safety and quality, yet many systems ignore how a plant is wired and which sensors can be trusted.

Their design reads plant data with layered networks, then aims attention using process structure and a running estimate of each sensor's reliability. A sampling trick attaches honest confidence to each call, and twin outputs handle detection and diagnosis together. On a standard chemical plant benchmark the framework reported strong, interpretable results. Knowing when a diagnosis is unsure is as valuable as the diagnosis itself.
plos-pone-0349585:
Michele Petkovski, Johannes Steinrücke, and Alejandro Dominguez-Rodriguez surveyed three hundred eleven adults in the Netherlands and Germany about climate emotions and green behavior. Eco-anxiety, eco-guilt, and eco-grief had each been linked to action separately, but never modeled together. Both countries face real flood risk, making the emotions concrete rather than abstract.

All three emotions correlated positively with pro-environmental behavior. Anxiety's link to action ran through guilt, but guilt also carried a suppressive twist, weakening the pathway in a nonlinear way, while grief did not mediate at all. Only age changed the pattern, strengthening or weakening the anxiety-to-guilt step. Campaigns that simply raise guilt may therefore misfire; the emotional plumbing is more complicated than one lever.
plos-pone-0349685:
Yucai Jiang and co-authors built a learning system for networks that never sit still, such as social platforms where users and connections appear and vanish daily. Most graph learning tools assume a fixed structure, so they miss how relationships shift over time. Their 2026 study proposes a network that pays selective attention to neighbors and then updates that attention as the graph changes.

A memory component carries the attention weights forward, letting the model adjust which neighbors matter as ties form and fade. In tests on standard benchmark datasets, the system beat leading rival methods at predicting future links. The authors present it as a step toward tools that treat change itself as part of the data, useful wherever networks grow and rewire constantly.
plos-pone-0349785:
Teresa Molohan and co-authors fitted young female Gaelic football players with GPS trackers to map the running demands of county-level matches. Ladies Gaelic football is fast and physical, but its under-sixteen and under-eighteen games had never been profiled this way. Their 2026 study covered one hundred thirteen players across twenty-one championship matches over two seasons, breaking results down by half, position, and age grade.

Running output fell in the second half for every position and age group. Midfield and half-line players covered the most ground and at the highest speeds, forming a distinct workload group. Older players outran younger ones in total and high-speed distance. The authors offer the profiles as reference data for training loads, talent development, and managing young players' progression.
plos-pone-0349885:
Siobhan Hinchy, Anna Beug, and co-authors reviewed what happened when a general practice in a deprived Dublin area offered half-hour mental health appointments, double the usual time. Standard slots squeeze the wide emotional problems patients bring to family doctors. Their 2026 review covered charts for one hundred ninety-five patients seen in these extended consultations over two years.

Patients were young, with a median age of twenty-nine, and most lived in areas of above-average deprivation. Anxiety and low mood dominated the complaints. Doctors adjusted or started mental health medicines for about thirty-eight percent, referred about a quarter to psychiatry, and pointed more than half toward community supports. Much care stayed entirely in the practice. The authors argue the model shows what primary mental health care can do when given time.
plos-pone-0350085:
Hong Li, Zhiming Li, and co-authors tested whether patterns hidden in breast MRI scans can predict if a cancer has invaded nearby vessels, a sign that guides treatment choices. Checking for this invasion normally requires tissue after surgery. Their 2026 study used scans from one hundred sixty-six women with operable invasive breast cancer, extracting hundreds of image features from different scan types.

Four prediction signatures were built and compared. The winner used change features, calculated as the difference between scans before and after contrast dye was given, and it clearly beat two of the other signatures. A signature from a standard anatomical scan also performed respectably. The authors propose the change-based signature as a possible non-invasive marker to flag vessel invasion before surgery.
plos-pone-0350185:
Richmond Owusu Ateko, Nicholas Ekow Thomford, and co-authors gathered all available research on abnormal blood fats among adults in Ghana, a quiet driver of heart disease that is rising with urban lifestyles. Their 2026 systematic review searched six databases for Ghanaian studies published since 1980 and brought together twenty-four studies covering roughly eleven thousand people.

Reported rates of the disorder varied enormously, from three percent to over seventy percent, reflecting different populations and definitions. The commonest problem was low levels of the protective cholesterol type, while high triglycerides were rarest. Southern and middle regions showed higher rates than the north. Because studies differed so much in methods, the authors summarized rather than pooled the results, and they call for standardized national measurement.
plos-pone-0350385:
Pengliang Zhang, Xianmin Liu, and colleagues studied a cell surface protein called THY1 in mouse colitis in 2026. Inflamed gut blood vessel growth feeds inflammatory bowel disease, and THY1's part in that process was unclear.

Using viruses to raise or silence the protein in mice with chemically triggered colitis, the team found THY1 made inflammation, oxidative stress, and vessel growth worse. Silencing it reversed those effects. The protein worked partly by blocking a calming type of immune cell and by pushing cell death pathways. Blocking THY1 is a candidate idea for calming inflamed bowel, at least in animal work.
plos-pone-0350585:
Shivani Singh and co-authors compared three drugs for agitation after traumatic brain injury in 2026. Agitation is common and dangerous during recovery, and the drugs compared are better known for preventing seizures, so clear evidence on calm and safety was needed.

Nearly two hundred adults were followed for a week with a standard agitation scale. Sodium valproate calmed the most patients and worked fastest, with relief in a median of three days. Levetiracetam was slowest. Side effects were also kinder for valproate and levetiracetam than for phenytoin. The observational design limits certainty, but the ranking gives treating teams a practical starting point.
plos-pone-0350885:
Sanghun Lee, Jeongsup Song, and Yangseon Kim prospect a cow's stomach for fungus-fighting bacteria. Their 2026 study isolates a Paenibacillus strain from the bovine rumen. Relatives of this species are famous biocontrol agents, but nearly all studied strains come from soil. The rumen strain's genome was fully sequenced: one circular chromosome of about five and a half million letters. Genome mining looked for machinery to make antimicrobial compounds. Culture tests then challenged the bacterium against real fungi.

Thirteen biosynthetic clusters turned up. They include blueprints for fusaricidin and other known antifungal weapons. Chemical analysis confirmed at least one such compound is genuinely produced. In dish tests the strain suppressed a broad range of plant-pathogenic fungi and mould relatives. It also hit selected fungi and yeasts troubling clinics and vets. A rumen microbe armed for chemical warfare could seed greener crop protection, once its products are purified and proven.
plos-pone-0350985:
Roads and runways bend under moving traffic, and Chun-li Zhang and colleagues worked out the mathematics for a stiff plate resting on layered, direction-dependent soil. Their 2026 PLOS One paper builds a three-dimensional model of how the plate and ground respond together as loads travel across.

Equations from elasticity and thin-plate theory were solved with transform methods, linking each soil layer into one system. Computer simulations checked the answers and varied the inputs. Layering of the ground changed bending the most, and the top layer's directional stiffness mattered far more than uniform soil would suggest. Engineers designing pavements on layered ground, the authors say, ignore that direction effect at their peril.
plos-pone-0351085:
Md Mirazul Islam and colleagues pulled active compounds from flowers of water hyacinth, an invasive water plant, and tested the flower extract for healing effects. Lab separation found five compounds, including two well known plant flavonoids. Extract tests covered germ killing, clot dissolving in a dish, and diarrhoea control in mice, plus computer checks of drug likeness.

Germ killing was moderate, strongest against a common skin and food germ. The extract dissolved about fourteen percent of lab clots. In mice, higher doses cut diarrhoea counts by close to forty percent, nearing a standard drug. Computer models showed plausible target binding. A pest plant may yield useful leads, though purity and safety work lie ahead.
plos-pone-0351185:
Outward Bound schools run outdoor courses meant to build character, and Jim Sibthorp and colleagues studied eleven schools across cultures to find what actually does that building. Their 2026 PLOS One paper distills an evidence-based framework from the comparison.

Five levers appeared everywhere: the school's educational philosophy, service to others, genuine adventure, the teaching model, and how instructors behave. Each lever looked different in different countries, yet character gains seemed strongest when the five were deliberately aligned into one coherent experience. The framework gives schools a shared language for design while keeping room for local flavor, a balance global education networks often struggle to strike.
plos-pone-0351885:
Capodici and colleagues reviewed reviews on remote medical care around the world in a 2026 paper. Video and phone care spread fast during the pandemic, yet uptake stayed uneven between rich and poor health systems. The team grouped reported barriers and helpers by theme and compared them across country income levels.

Poorer settings most often reported basic barriers such as weak infrastructure and high costs. No evidence at all came from the lowest-income countries. Several common barriers had no matching solutions in print. The authors warn that a research base drawn mostly from rich countries can deepen the very gaps remote care was meant to close.
plos-pone-0351985:
Ricardo Veiga and Bonifacio Zanutto introduce a new pattern-recognition method in this 2026 paper. The problem is untangling two patterns printed on top of each other. Ordinary classifiers see only the confusing mixture. Their framework, called CROP, alternates between two kinds of attention. Bottom-up steps guess which pattern is present, and top-down steps rebuild it.

Each round, the method names the most likely pattern and reconstructs its clean form. A mask then removes that pattern from the mixture. The leftover becomes clearer, so the next round can name the second pattern. Training needs only clean examples, never labelled mixtures. On overlapping handwritten digits, the procedure separated and labelled both numbers successfully. The design mimics how human attention picks one object out of a cluttered scene.
plos-pone-0352185:
Md Mamun and three colleagues engineer a cooling system for desert electronics in this 2026 study. Remote sensor nodes bake by day and freeze by night. Fans clog with dust and compressors guzzle power. Their design pairs a solid-state thermoelectric module, which can heat or cool on command, with fanless heat spreaders. Solar power and smart energy management keep it running around the clock. The sealed box has no moving parts in its thermal path.

Simulated desert tests showed brisk performance. The system pulled temperatures from about forty degrees down to twenty within five minutes. Efficiency beat expectations for a thermoelectric design. Energy use ran about ten percent below forced-air equivalents. Desert monitoring, from pipelines to wildlife sensors, depends on electronics surviving unattended for months. A dust-proof, maintenance-free thermal system removes one of the commonest reasons such nodes die young.
plos-pone-0352585: UAV-assisted sparse ground networks — modeled and analyzed. This paper did so. The analysis revealed how drones fill connectivity gaps. The findings guided the aerial infrastructure — wings as network towers.
plos-pone-0352785:
Nesreen Alqaissi and seven colleagues survey health sciences students in Palestine about artificial intelligence. Their 2026 study covers six hundred sixty-six undergraduates in nursing, medicine, health sciences, and dentistry. A structured questionnaire measured what students know, how they feel, and what they actually do with AI tools. The setting matters. Palestinian universities teach under real resource limits, so the results speak to similar schools elsewhere.

Knowledge lagged behind enthusiasm. Students answered barely forty-three percent of knowledge questions correctly. Machine learning and deep learning concepts were the weakest ground. Attitudes, by contrast, were clearly positive. Ethical awareness earned especially high endorsement. Practice questions mapped how far AI had entered daily study habits. For curriculum designers, the gap is the story: willing students, thin technical grounding. Teaching can build on the goodwill while repairing the concepts students will need as AI enters their clinics.
plos-pone-0352885:
Alžběta Danielisová leads an archaeology team tracing how bronze ornaments changed along a major Iron Age trade corridor in Central Europe. In the fourth and third centuries before the common era, a new lead-rich bronze suited bold, high-relief ornament styles. The team analyzed metal from cemetery finds in Bohemia and Moravia and compared it with material from a large open production site, using isotope and element fingerprints to source the metal.

Fourth-century alloys proved mixed and varied, while third-century recipes settled into a more standard leaded mix with better casting behavior. Danielisová and colleagues tie the shift to wider social and economic change, as new centers and networks reshaped craft production. The metal record thus tracks rising elites as much as workshop skill.
plos-pone-0352985:
Adem Gok, Kubra Bilge, and Tuba Gok tested dental sealants in a 2026 laboratory study. Sealants fill the deep grooves of molars to block decay. The team wanted to know how material choice, an adhesive step, and saliva contamination each affect performance. They used one hundred sixty extracted human molars split into eight groups.

Resin-based sealants and flowable composites leaked least and bonded most strongly. Glass ionomer materials performed worse on both counts. Adding adhesive raised bond strength but slightly increased leakage. Saliva contamination clearly weakened bonds and opened gaps at the edges. Re-etching the enamel after contamination restored a good seal. Microscope images confirmed tighter margins for the resin materials, giving dentists clear guidance on technique.
plos-pone-0353185:
Goran Erfani and five colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One survey of how much people of different ages use digital technology at home in a district of North East England. Households across the district received the survey in early 2022, and more than nine thousand people replied, spanning six generations from the oldest adults to Generation Z. Respondents estimated their weekly time with digital tools and the internet.

Younger generations reported the most time online, while the two oldest generations reported the least, and this district's residents spent less time online than comparable British groups. Baby Boomers and Generation X stood out as statistically distinct from every other group. The authors suggest pairing tech-savvy younger people with older adults for training, and designing health platforms that welcome users at every skill level.
plos-pone-0353385:
Andrey and colleagues tested whether game data alone can set fair speed limits for young elite soccer players in a 2026 study. Coaches often draw a personal line linking how hard a player can speed up with starting speed, then judge game efforts against it. The question was whether tracking data from matches could replace a short lab-style sprint test.

Game records came from more than one hundred fifty players over a season, with a smaller group also doing the standard test. Errors stayed large no matter how many games were added, and links with test results were too weak for personal use. The authors conclude that teams still need the direct test, and that better tracking gear matters more than more matches.
plos-pone-0353485:
Douglas Seiler led a team of six authors working on the Herculaneum scrolls, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. These papyrus scrolls were carbonized when Vesuvius erupted, and many may hold lost classical texts. The hard question is which fragile lumps are worth the effort of virtual unrolling and reading.

Seiler's group built a model scroll, carbonized in the same way, to learn what readable scrolls look like under scanning. That model opens a way to sort real scrolls by their chance of holding legible text. Scholars could then focus costly imaging on the best candidates. The prize is large: texts lost for nearly two thousand years.
plos-pone-0353685:
Wondwesen Tafesse and three colleagues analyse more than two hundred and thirty thousand tweets about generative artificial intelligence in education, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Most earlier research asked small groups of students or teachers directly. Topic modelling of this huge public conversation sorted it into seven themes, from the tools as learning assistants and research helpers to worries about exams, policy, and resources.

Sentiment scoring then showed which themes drew disproportionate praise and which drew disproportionate complaint. The authors frame the results through stakeholder theory: universities do not adopt such tools in a vacuum, but amid a loud public negotiation among students, teachers, vendors, and regulators. Knowing where the argument stands helps leaders govern adoption rather than chase it.
plos-pone-0353785:
Wasifa Orthy and co-authors charted how folks differ in the way frustration hits them. Frustration is felt by all, but labs tend to study it in tight, fake settings. Their 2026 study ran one hundred forty-five folks, from teens to folks in their sixties, through a task built to vex: time squeeze, ping alerts, vague marks, and a rigged keyboard.

Self-reports split the group into high, mid, and low frustration types. The high type leaned to tense traits, weak grip on feelings, and low ease with discomfort. The low type leaned to sharp emotional sense and high self-set bars. Gaps were soft at this size, not firm proof. Orthy and colleagues say research should start from such personal types.
plos-pone-0353885:
Vauthier and Kabuth interviewed endurance runners who live with type one diabetes in a 2026 study. Thirteen French-speaking runners described how they work with doctors while training for extreme events. Managing blood sugar through long runs takes daily trial and error that clinic visits rarely capture.

Runners said respect from doctors often depended on keeping blood sugar in a good range, a pattern the authors name as a kind of merit test. Skilled runners built strong know-how of their own, yet clinic routines still limited how fully that know-how counted. Talks with doctors mixed teamwork with quiet bargaining. The study asks care teams to value lived skill even when numbers slip.
plos-pone-0353985:
Sreelakshmi K. V and colleagues, in a 2026 computer study, mine the sea life off India's coast for new germ-killing peptides, small protein chains that punch holes in bacterial membranes. Drug resistance is outpacing new antibiotics, and the microbes of the Indian Ocean are barely explored. Their quarry is the group of hard-to-treat hospital germs known by the acronym ESKAPE.

From ocean microbe DNA, the team assembled genomes and predicted tens of thousands of candidate peptides, then filtered by shape and chemistry down to ten finalists. Two leads were simulated atom by atom against the membranes of three resistant germs. One settled flat on the surface in a stable coil, while the other flexed and dug in. Their different styles suggest different killing modes worth testing. The authors present the ocean microbiome as a stocked shelf for antibiotic discovery, with lab tests as the necessary next step.
plos-pone-0354185:
Yua Okano and three colleagues demonstrate a cheap optical sensor that detects tiny changes in how much a liquid bends light, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Such refractive index readings help identify chemicals and biological samples. Their device uses a patterned grating whose reflected colour is deliberately lopsided, paired with a simple blue-green LED rather than costly laboratory lasers or spectrometers.

When the liquid above the grating changes even slightly, the overlap between the LED's light and the grating's reflection shifts, and the reflected brightness swings sharply. The measured sensitivity was high and the detection limit fine. A sensor this simple could suit field testing, food checks, and bedside diagnostics.
plos-pone-0354385:
Chenhao Sun and co-authors investigate in 2026 how hot springs form around Wenquan County in Xinjiang, China, where geothermal heat could be developed further. Their work combined satellite reading, ground heat checks, geophysical surveys, drilling, and chemical and isotope tests on the water. Fault lines in the rock turned out to guide where warm zones appear.

plos-pone-0354485:

Between 2015 and 2018, patients aged eighteen to sixty-five arriving with mono-like illness or community pneumonia were offered an HIV test, since both conditions can signal undiagnosed infection. plos-pone-0354585:
Hayat Khan's 2026 study looks at how to clean an antibiotic called spiramycin out of water. Antibiotics used in medicine and farming often end up in rivers and wastewater, where they can harm people and wildlife. Khan uses light together with a catalyst powder, tungsten trioxide, to break the drug down, a process that is normally slow and costly to fine-tune by trial and error.

To speed things up, Khan trained a machine learning program on a small set of experiments and let it sort out which settings mattered most. The program predicted results with high accuracy and showed that the acidity of the water mattered more than anything else. Under the best settings found, close to nine tenths of the antibiotic was destroyed, mostly by highly reactive hydroxyl radicals.
plos-pone-0354885:

They analyzed over a hundred thousand lab-confirmed cases from 2020 to 2025, typed by viral variety, across more than fifteen hundred municipalities. A scan method hunted for clusters of each of the four dengue types in space and time.

One type, DENV-3, dominated after a long absence, and the 2024 to 2025 season fired nationwide at once. Hundreds of municipalities saw all four types cluster together. Mendoza-Cano offers the fine-grained maps for targeting mosquito control where mixed dengue circulates.
plos-pone-0355285:

Traces of medicines, farm chemicals, and care products now show up widely in rivers, and plain enzyme treatment breaks only some of them down. The team tested the hybrids against more than twenty such pollutants, with and without a helper compound.

Results varied sharply by pollutant. A few were wiped out almost fully, others only partly, and a couple resisted entirely. Anchoring the enzyme often beat the free enzyme by wide margins, and the helper lifted some stubborn cases. Al-Maqdi and colleagues say tuned enzyme hybrids could form one layer of future water cleaning, matched to the pollutants present.
plos-pone-0355385:

The design bans direct left turns and routes them through a U-turn opening down the road. Their 2026 study modelled thirty real junctions and six U-turn layouts, running thousands of simulations across traffic levels.

The U-turn design beat the conventional junction whenever traffic stayed at or below a mid-level threshold. Best opening distances shifted with demand: nearer for moderate flows, farther for heavy directional splits and the busiest approaches. Above the threshold, the classic four-way signal won consistently. Badwes and Alarifi give road planners a demand-based rule for choosing between the designs.
plos-pone-0355485:

plos-pone-0355685:

Low birthweight drives newborn deaths and lifelong harm, and over ninety-five percent of cases occur in poorer countries. Pooling fifty-two national health surveys covering some three hundred seventy thousand women, the team used a matching method that pairs women with similar backgrounds who did and did not receive adequate care.

Women who completed at least four prenatal visits delivered babies averaging modestly heavier than matched peers; those reaching the World Health Organization's recommended eight visits gained roughly a third more again. Population-level estimates told the same dose-response story, and sensitivity checks suggested the findings were sturdy. The authors urge expanding not just access to prenatal care but continuity, so women complete the full schedule.
plos-pone-0356285:

Diabetic nerve damage dulls and distorts feeling in feet and hands and is among the earliest harms of the disease. Mice ate the fatty diet for four months while the team tracked weight, blood measures, feeling tests, and the nerve fibers in foot skin.

The mice grew obese with the expected blood problems, including poor sugar control and insulin resistance. Feeling changed from about the third month, with odd mixes of dullness and oversensitivity, and by the end the skin had lost nerve fibers and their helper cells. Rastoldo and colleagues judge the model faithful enough for testing how the damage starts.
plos-pone-0356385:

Soft silicones mimic living tissue and are widely used as cell culture surfaces in mechanics research. Their 2026 study pressed a tiny probe into two soft silicone types before and after light treatment, working in a soap solution to stop sticking.

After exposure to deep UV in air, both surfaces grew clearly stiffer while the bulk material stayed unchanged. Chemical checks showed added oxygen at the surface, matching the stiffening to surface oxidation. The treated surfaces also attracted water more strongly. Wilder and colleagues note the effect matters wherever deep UV is used on soft silicone labware.
plos-pone-0356485:

These apps, reimbursed by the national system, must prove they help patients, but real-world studies battle dropout and patchy data, making single-item scales tempting shortcuts whose use has never been mapped.

The planned scoping review will catalogue every study of a listed health app that used single questions, recording what was measured, why the shortcut was chosen, and what limits the authors admitted. Two reviewers will screen independently under standard reporting rules. No findings exist yet; the map should help regulators judge when one question is a fair measure and when it is a fig leaf.
plos-pone-0356685:
Haolun Xu and seven colleagues model a hidden flaw in the cables that carry high-voltage direct current across long distances, in this 2026 simulation study. These cables are wrapped in insulation bounded by shielding layers, and tiny bumps on that interface can concentrate the electric field, aging the insulation and shortening the cable's life. The team built a three-dimensional model of a very high-voltage cable and varied the bumps' size, shape, and the material's temperature behavior.

Height mattered far more than shape: taller protrusions distorted the field dramatically, with distortion rising roughly tenfold across the range tested. Distortion near a bump also grew as the insulation's conductivity became more temperature-sensitive. The findings give makers a clear priority, keep interface protrusions low, and offer designers a way to judge how much imperfection a cable design can tolerate.
plos-pone-0356785:

Four traits anchor the study: emotional intelligence, flexible thinking, soft skills, and self-directed learning, with digital transformation of the university as a fifth force. A structural modeling method suited to tangled predictions tested how the traits lean on each other.

Emotional intelligence tied strongly to both flexible thinking and soft skills. Flexible thinking fed soft skills and fed self-directed learning directly, and soft skills in turn carried a substantial push toward self-directed learning. Digital change also tied to self-directed learning on its own. AlMuhaysh argues universities should train these human capacities alongside platforms, since tools alone do not make independent learners.
plos-pone-0356885:

plos-pone-0357185:

Interviewing nineteen adolescents and parents across several centers in 2023, the team coded hundreds of statements into themes about how the suspected illness is lived, not just treated.

Three themes emerged. The experience was filtered through family history, including relatives' own encounters with the disease. Families felt ambivalence toward medical discourse, grateful and doubtful at once. And they hungered for clearer knowledge to fend off misinformation. Teenagers voiced confusion about what the disease even is, some indifference toward it, and a specific fear: that it lies dormant in them and might resurface to harm them later. The authors argue care pathways must explain themselves, not just prescribe.
plos-pone-0357285:

plos-pone-0357385:
