It also shows Scotland answering the skeptics in kind, story for sworn story.
spr-proceedings-vol3-1885:
Parts eight and nine make up volume three of the SPR Proceedings, issued in 1885. The Society for Psychical Research printed its findings here for members and critics alike. Telepathy tests continue from the earlier volumes, with tighter controls. Cases of apparitions and haunted houses enter with sworn statements.

Investigators weigh each report for error, fraud, and coincidence before printing. Trance mediumship receives long, careful write ups from sittings. The society's habit of publishing doubts beside wonders marks every part. Volume three deepens the archive of the great evidential debate of the era. Researchers still mine it for early cases. Its caution is as notable as its claims.
stanley-congo-free-state-vol1-1885:
Henry Stanley returned to the Congo in 1879 in the service of King Leopold of Belgium. Volume One of The Congo and the Founding of Its Free State, from 1885, tells of his five years there. Stanley had traced the Congo River to the sea two years earlier.

He built stations, cut a road around the falls, and signed treaties with hundreds of chiefs. Steamers were hauled in pieces past the rapids to the upper river. Stanley presents the work as commerce and civilization. Later history judged Leopold's Free State a horror, which gives this proud volume a grim second meaning today.
stanley-congo-free-state-vol2-1885:
Volume Two of Stanley's Congo narrative, also from 1885, continues the founding of the Free State. Stanley's crews were opening the upper Congo to steamers and trade posts. The volume runs to the year the Berlin Conference blessed Leopold's claim.

Stanley describes new stations, river surveys, and his dealings with Arab traders and local rulers. He also argues Europe's case for taking the Congo basin, in the blunt language of the Scramble for Africa. The Emin Pasha relief trip, his last great expedition, lay just ahead. Read now, the volume documents both exploration and the start of a catastrophe.
stevenson-childs-garden-verses-1885:
Robert Louis Stevenson had been a sickly child, kept in bed for long stretches in Edinburgh. As an adult he turned those years into A Child's Garden of Verses, published in 1885. The book holds sixty-four poems, complete, and it has never been out of print since.

The poems see the world at a child's height: a bed becomes a ship, a shadow follows like a friend, and trains and foreign lands feed daydreams. Stevenson remembers both the fun and the loneliness of childhood without talking down to young readers. Adults often love the book as much as children do. It set a new standard for poetry written for the young.
tatian-the-diatessaron-of-tatian-anf-188:
Tatian wove the four Gospels into one smooth narrative around 170. He called the work the Diatessaron, a Greek phrase meaning through four. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers presents the harmony in English.

For centuries the Syriac Church used it as its standard gospel text. Preachers read from its blended story in place of separate gospels. The work thus served both as devotion and as history. It also witnesses what the Gospels looked like in early copies. That value holds for scholars long before the canon was fixed. Few books shaped daily worship in the East as deeply as this one harmony did.
tennyson-idylls-of-the-king-1885:
Alfred, Lord Tennyson worked on Idylls of the King for half a century, publishing the poems in groups from 1859 onward. The complete set of twelve idylls appeared together in 1885. Tennyson, Queen Victoria's poet laureate, drew his Arthurian stories mainly from Malory's medieval romance.

The poems trace Arthur's reign from his coming to his passing. Guinevere's betrayal, Lancelot's divided loyalty, and the wasteful last battle darken the bright beginning. Merlin, Vivien, Gareth, and the Holy Grail each get their own tale. Tennyson used the old legends to ask Victorian questions about faith, duty, and purity. The full cycle is his longest sustained achievement.
tertullian-a-treatise-on-the-soul-holmes:
Peter Holmes translated Tertullian's Treatise on the Soul for the 1885 edition. What is the soul made of, and where does it come from, Tertullian asks. No early Christian writer gave the soul a fuller treatment than this.

He argues that the soul is a real thing with its own substance. It passes, in his view, from parent to child at birth. Greek schools of thought are tested and mostly set aside. His answers shaped Christian views of human nature for a thousand years. Readers meet here the first great Christian psychology, bold in scope and sure in tone on every page.
tertullian-ad-martyras-thelwall-anf-1885:
Thelwall translated Ad Martyras, Tertullian's letter to Christians in prison. The prisoners awaited likely death for confessing their faith. The 1885 edition keeps the short exhortation in plain English.

Your prison, Tertullian tells them, is truly a place of freedom. There they stand free from temptation and free for prayer at last. The coming suffering is framed as a glorious contest to be won. Courage fills every line without a trace of self-pity. Few documents of the persecution age move readers more deeply. In a few pages, fear is recast as honor, and a cell becomes the doorway to a crown.
tertullian-ad-nationes-holmes-anf-1885:
Peter Holmes translated Ad Nationes, Tertullian's address To the Nations, in 1885. The work stands as a companion piece to his greater Apology. Here Tertullian carries the fight straight to the pagans themselves.

He mocks the gods of Rome and their shameful myths with relish. Slanders spread about Christians get sharp and learned answers in turn. Sarcasm is his chief weapon, and he wields it without mercy. The gloves come off in this ancient debate between faiths. Readers who enjoy the Apology will relish the same sharp mind in a freer, ruder mood, sparing no opponent at all.
tertullian-against-hermogenes-holmes-anf:
Holmes translated Against Hermogenes for the 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers. Hermogenes had taught that matter was eternal and never created. Such a claim set a hard limit on the power of God.

Tertullian insists that God made all things from nothing at all. Objection after objection gets a relentless and logical reply. The short book moves fast and wastes no words on mercy. Scholars prize it as a master class in early Christian argument on creation. It also opens a window on the deep debates over God and matter that split the second-century Church into camps.
tertullian-against-praxeas-holmes-anf-18:
Holmes translated Against Praxeas for the 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers. Praxeas had taught that Father, Son, and Spirit were masks of one person. That view, called modalism, threatened the heart of the faith as Tertullian saw it.

His reply forged the very words the West still uses for the Trinity. Three persons, one substance: the Latin terms trinitas, persona, and substantia start here. No other treatise of his may matter more to later centuries. Readers meet the first clear Latin statement of the doctrine in these pages. The words Christians use for God to this day were hammered out in this fierce and brilliant argument.
tertullian-against-the-valentinians-robe:
Alexander Roberts translated Against the Valentinians for the 1885 Fathers. The Valentinians had spun the faith into a vast mythic system. Divine emanations and secret wisdom filled their hidden teaching.

Tertullian answers with mockery as much as with formal argument. He picks their scheme apart piece by piece before the reader's eyes. Each grand claim shrinks until the whole thing looks absurd. The early Church's fiercest mind is also at his most entertaining here. Polemics turn into comedy without losing their bite. Surprisingly, the laughter works: few refutations of a rival school have ever been this fun to read.
tertullian-an-answer-to-the-jews-thelwal:
Tertullian wrote An Answer to the Jews around the year 200. Thelwall's English version appears in the 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers. Jewish and Christian teachers then argued fiercely over the Hebrew scriptures.

Tertullian argues that Christ fulfilled the Jewish prophecies in full. The Church, in his view, inherited the promises made to Israel. Modern readers will find those claims supersessionist, as the v1 notes say. They belong to an age of sharp religious rivalry and deep division. Historians still value the treatise highly. It stands as a major witness to how early Christians defined themselves against the Judaism they came from.
tertullian-appendix-against-all-heresies:
Thelwall translated the Appendix Against All Heresies for the 1885 Fathers. The short piece rides at the end of Tertullian's works in that edition. It sums up the rival teachings that troubled the second-century Church.

Simon Magus, Marcion, and the Valentinians march past in brief review. Each entry states what a group taught and why the Church refused it. The whole serves as a field guide to a bewildering age of belief. Historians treasure the catalog as a snapshot of a Church defining itself. Amid dozens of rival claims, readers see the young faith drawing its borders line by line and name by name.
tertullian-de-fuga-in-persecutione-thelw:
Thelwall translated De Fuga in Persecutione for the 1885 Fathers. Its question faced every believer in the age of the martyrs. Should Christians flee persecution, or stand and face the arrest?

Stand and face it, Tertullian answers without a hint of doubt. Flight, in his view, disobeys the will of God for the confessor. Those who bought safety with bribes or ran from officers draw his scorn. Many will find the standard harsh to the edge of cruelty. Yet the treatise captures the heroic demands of that age, when faith could cost a person home, freedom, and life.
tertullian-of-patience-thelwall-anf-1885:
Thelwall translated Of Patience for the 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers. Tertullian preaches patience here and owns that he is bad at it. That frank confession makes the stern teacher oddly endearing at once.

Patience, he argues, roots every other virtue in the Christian life. Without it there is no faith, no love, and no strength under trial. Persecution tests the virtue hardest, and he writes for people facing it. The fierce controversialist shows a pastor's heart in these pages. He urges his flock toward the hardest virtue of all. Readers who know only his attacks will find a humbler and warmer man at work here.
tertullian-on-baptism-thelwall-anf-1885:
Thelwall translated On Baptism, the earliest full treatise on the rite that survives. Tertullian wrote it to teach what the baptismal water means. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers carries the short foundation work in English.

Why was even Jesus baptized, he asks, if the rite means so little? Hard cases get answers too, like the fate of the unbaptized. Customs of his own day in North Africa fill in the picture. All later Christian writing on the sacrament builds on this stone. Short as it is, the treatise lets readers watch a core practice of the faith take clear and lasting form.
tertullian-on-exhortation-to-chastity-th:
Thelwall translated On Exhortation to Chastity for the 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers. Tertullian directs the plea at widowers who might wed again. One marriage for life, he argues, is the Christian ideal to hold.

His case proceeds with his usual rigor and rare force. Frank words on human weakness startle even seasoned readers of his work. Modern readers may judge the standard severe to the point of harshness. Still, the treatise shows how gravely the early Church treated sexual discipline. It was, in his eyes, a true path of the spirit, and the demand runs through all his late moral writing.
tertullian-on-fasting-thelwall-anf-1885:
Thelwall translated On Fasting for the 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers. Montanist Christians kept longer and stricter fasts than their neighbors. Critics called the practice excessive, and Tertullian rose to defend it.

He argues from scripture and from nature that the body needs discipline. His famous sarcasm then turns on foes who prefer an easy religion. Comfort, he implies, makes poor soldiers in a spiritual war. Short and sharp, the treatise shows how bodily habits became battlegrounds. In the early Church, even meals and fast days could split believers into camps that barely spoke to each other.
tertullian-on-idolatry-thelwall-anf-1885:
S. Thelwall translated Tertullian's On Idolatry for the 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers. Tertullian wrote the broad treatise around the year 200 in North Africa. Its question is stark: how far can a Christian go in a pagan world?

His answer draws the line hard, with no room for half measures. No idols, no star-gazing, no pagan feasts, and no quiet compromises, he rules. Work, trade, and daily custom all come under the ban where idols lurk. The piece shows the early Church wrestling with life inside an empire whose rites honored other gods. Minority faiths still know that hard question well.
tertullian-on-modesty-thelwall-anf-1885:
Thelwall translated On Modesty for the 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers. The Church then debated a hard question of mercy and discipline. Could grave sins after baptism ever be forgiven by the Church?

Tertullian, now a Montanist, answers no for sins of the flesh. He denounces the broader Church's mercy as mere corruption of morals. Anger drives what may be his fiercest late work from first to last. The pain in it is real: a great mind breaks with the Church he helped build. Few documents show the cost of rigor with such force and sorrow combined.
tertullian-on-monogamy-thelwall-anf-1885:
Thelwall translated On Monogamy for the 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers. Tertullian here builds his full case that Christians should marry only once. He wrote the book after joining the strict Montanist movement.

His moral standards visibly harden across these chapters. Second marriage after a spouse's death is treated as a lapse from the ideal. Scripture and church custom are pressed hard into the service of that rule. The book works both as a reasoned case and as a portrait. A brilliant mind pushes its own principles to their limit here, and readers can judge whether the limit holds.
tertullian-on-prayer-thelwall-anf-1885:
Thelwall translated On Prayer, Tertullian's gentle treatise on the Lord's Prayer. It stands as the earliest commentary on the Pater Noster that survives. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers presents the work in English.

Phrase by phrase, Tertullian unpacks the prayer Christ taught his followers. Hallowed be thy name and thy will be done each receive careful thought. The touch is that of a man who prayed the words every day. A softer side of the fierce debater shows through the calm pages. Readers used to his thunder may be surprised. The same pen that scorched heretics could also teach plain believers how to pray.
tertullian-on-the-apparel-of-women-thelw:
Thelwall translated On the Apparel of Women for the 1885 Fathers. Tertullian tells Christian women to dress with plainness and restraint. Gold jewels, styled hair, and fine clothes meant to catch the eye all draw his fire.

Such display springs from worldly pride, he argues at length. It has no place, he holds, among those who serve God. Modern readers will find the tone severe and the rules strict. Even so, historians prize the treatise as a vivid window. It shows daily life, dress, and morals in the Church of the early third century with rare and concrete detail.
tertullian-on-the-flesh-of-christ-holmes:
Holmes translated On the Flesh of Christ for the 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers. Some teachers then claimed that Christ's body was a mere illusion. Against them, Tertullian insists that Jesus had real human flesh.

Born, suffering, and dying in that flesh are all defended at length. His famed paradox rings out across the centuries from these pages. The Son of God died and rose, he writes, certain because it seems impossible. Few lines in early theology are quoted more often than that one. The treatise secured the Church's core belief that God truly became man in history, not in seeming only.
tertullian-on-the-resurrection-of-the-fl:
Holmes translated On the Resurrection of the Flesh as a companion to the Christ treatise. Thinkers of the day found bodily rising crude and hard to credit. Tertullian takes up their scorn in the 1885 Fathers edition.

The same God who made bodies can surely remake them, he argues. Force and scorn mark his case from start to finish. Scripture, nature, and plain reason are all pressed into service. His claim is sharp: salvation takes in the body, not the soul alone. The book remains the classic early Christian statement on the point. Later teaching on the last things builds on the ground he cleared here.
tertullian-on-the-veiling-of-virgins-the:
Thelwall translated On the Veiling of Virgins for the 1885 Fathers. One sharp question drives the short treatise from start to finish. Should unmarried women wear the veil in church, or not?

Tertullian answers yes, with his full force of argument. Scripture, nature, and church discipline are all called as witnesses. Virgins, he holds, should cover their heads like married women do. The case shows how gravely the early Church took modesty and order. Worship was no place for display or loose custom, in his view. Intense and brief, the work comes from the most rigorous moralist of the early centuries.
tertullian-scorpiace-antidote-for-the-sc:
Thelwall translated Scorpiace for the 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers. Its full title promises an antidote for the scorpion's sting. The scorpion, for Tertullian, is the heresy that slighted martyrdom.

Some Christians were arguing that dying for the faith was needless. Tertullian strikes back with a store of scriptural proofs. Confessing Christ before persecutors, he holds, is a believer's highest duty. No escape clause softens the demand in his reading. Fierce and uncompromising, the short work is Tertullian through and through. It shows how the age of persecution prized public courage above safety, comfort, and even life itself.
tertullian-the-apology-anf-1885:
Tertullian wrote his Apology around the year 197 as an open letter to Roman rulers. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers edition carries the famous defense in English. Christians then faced arrest and death for their faith across the empire.

Tertullian demands fair trials and answers the slanders spread against believers. Part legal brief and part thundering sermon, the work blazes with anger and wit. Its best-known line holds that the blood of martyrs is the seed of the Church. No defense of the faith has matched its force since. It forged the language Christians used to face persecution for centuries after his death.
tertullian-the-chaplet-or-de-corona-anf-:
A single act of conscience sparked Tertullian's Chaplet, or De Corona. A Christian soldier refused to wear the formal laurel crown of his rank. The army was scandalized, and many Christians joined in the shock.

Tertullian defends the soldier in this short treatise from the 1885 edition. The only crown a Christian needs, he argues, is the crown of martyrdom. Scripture and custom are weighed with a lawyer's care throughout. Scholars treat the piece as a key text on early Christian views of army service. It lays bare the clash between faith and empire in its sharpest daily form.
tertullian-the-five-books-against-marcio:
Holmes translated Tertullian's Five Books Against Marcion for the 1885 Fathers. Marcion had taught that the stern God of the Old Testament differed from Christ's Father. That split in God himself drew crowds in the second-century Church.

Tertullian spends five books pulling Marcion's system apart. He defends the unity of the Bible from Genesis to the Gospels. The goodness of creation itself stands on trial beside the texts. The result is the longest early Christian attack on a heresy that survives. It also keeps our best record of Marcion's own teaching and canon, fixed while fixing the bounds of sound faith.
tertullian-the-passion-of-the-holy-marty:
R. E. Wallis translated the Passion of Perpetua and Felicitas for the 1885 Fathers. Perpetua, a young Roman noblewoman, kept a diary in prison at Carthage. She and her fellow prisoner Felicitas faced death around the year 203.

In her own voice, Perpetua records visions and her father's pleas. She defies him and holds fast to her confession of Christ. Felicitas gives birth in jail shortly before the day of execution. Few documents of the ancient world feel this close and personal. Many judges call it the most powerful martyrdom account ever written, and its place in this set is secure.
tertullian-the-shows-or-de-spectaculis-t:
Thelwall also translated The Shows, Tertullian's attack on Roman public games. The Latin title is De Spectaculis, and the target is the whole world of Roman amusement. Theater, circus, and the gladiator arena all stand accused in its pages.

Should Christians attend the games at all, Tertullian asks. No, he answers: they are schools of idolatry and cruelty alike. The treatise ends with a famous turn toward the last day. The true spectacle, he promises, will be the Day of Judgment itself. Blistering and unyielding, the work ranks as ancient culture criticism at its most uncompromising and bold.
tertullian-the-soul-s-testimony-thelwall:
Thelwall translated The Soul's Testimony for the 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers. Tertullian calls an unusual witness for the being of God in this short work. His witness is the ordinary human soul itself, pagan or not.

Even pagans cry out O God in moments of sudden terror, he notes. Such cries prove, he claims, that every soul knows its maker by nature. The argument turns on common speech caught in unguarded moments. Clever and brief, the piece ranks among the earliest appeals to shared human experience in Christian defense. It shows Tertullian the lawyer at his most inventive and humane.
tertullian-to-his-wife-thelwall-anf-1885:
Thelwall translated To His Wife, Tertullian's most personal work, for 1885. He writes to his own wife in two short books of counsel. The advice is one few husbands would think to offer a spouse.

If I die first, he tells her, do not marry again. Or at the least, he adds, marry only a fellow Christian. Tender feeling mixes with stern principle on every page. The polemicist steps aside, and the private man comes into view. The books rank among the earliest Christian writings on marriage. Their intimate tone still surprises readers who expect only thunder from his pen.
tertullian-to-scapula-thelwall-anf-1885:
Tertullian addressed To Scapula as an open letter to a Roman governor. Scapula ruled in North Africa and was then persecuting Christians there. Thelwall translated the bold letter for the 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers.

Lawyerly care and prophetic fire mix in Tertullian's warning to the governor. Persecutors of Christians, he says, always come to bad ends in time. Christians pray for the emperor, he adds, even while refusing to worship him. The plea asks in effect for freedom to worship without penalty. Few ancient letters match its courage. It speaks truth to power in plain terms and accepts the risk that came with such speech.
the-didache-teaching-of-the-twelve-apost:
How should a church baptize, pray, fast, and spot a fraud? The Didache, or Teaching of the Twelve Apostles, answers in the earliest church manual we have, from around the year 100. Lost for a millennium, the text was rediscovered in 1873; this edition dates to 1885.

Two ways of life and death open the book, followed by crisp rules for worship and community order. Traveling prophets get tested; freeloaders get exposed. Simple and practical, the manual lets readers watch the first Christians organize their common life. Its eucharistic prayers are among the oldest Christian prayers anywhere. Precious is the word scholars reach for, and it fits.
the-epistle-of-barnabas-1885:
Written around the year 130, the Epistle of Barnabas reads the Old Testament as a Christian book written in code. Food laws become lessons about morals; numbers conceal prophecies of Jesus. The letter appears here in the 1885 edition of early Christian writings.

Its author argues that Israel misread its own scriptures by taking them literally. Circumcision, sacrifices, and feasts all point, for him, toward Christ and the Church. Modern readers may find the method strange, yet some early churches revered the letter as scripture itself. The work shows how the earliest Gentile Christians claimed Israel's heritage for their own story. Few documents reveal that bold act of reading so plainly.
the-lost-continent-pg285: This edition tells the lost continent's tale anew. Atlantis waits. The Tower library holds the full text. It lost again. Seas covered. Myths lived. Readers dreamed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
the-mystery-of-the-yellow-room-pg1685: Gaston Leroux's 1908 locked-room masterpiece: a woman is attacked in a room locked from the inside, and young Rouletabille must solve the impossible crime. The greatest locked-room mystery ever written, ingenious and thrilling. Every detective fan should read it.
the-papers-and-writings-of-abraham-linco: Volume two of Lincoln's writings, 1843-1858: the congressman and the rising lawyer. Speeches and letters trace his growth. The road to greatness, documented. The prairie lawyer finds his voice in these pages, every speech points toward the presidency.
the-renascence-of-hebrew-literature-1743: Nahum Slouschz tells how Hebrew woke from sleep between 1743 and 1885 — poets and thinkers of the Haskalah giving new life to an old tongue. His book was the first to chart this rebirth for scholars. A landmark of Jewish literary history, still cited.
the-science-of-the-mind-applied-to-teach: The Science of the Mind Applied to Teaching, 1885. The teaching science. This book preserves that work. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
theognostus-from-his-seven-books-of-hypo:
Theognostus headed the famed teaching school at Alexandria in the 200s. His seven books of Hypotyposes, or Outlines, covered all Christian doctrine. Only fragments quoted by later writers now survive from that large work.

An 1885 Fathers volume collects the remnants for modern readers. They hint at a bold and speculative cast of theology. Alexandria's school was known for daring thought about God and the world. Scholars mine these scraps for clues to that lost classroom. How did the great school teach before the age of the councils? The fragments give partial answers, and their gaps invite careful study.
theonas-the-epistle-of-theonas-bishop-of:
Bishop Theonas of Alexandria wrote a practical letter to Lucianus. Lucianus served as chief chamberlain in the emperor's own court. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers preserves the counsel in English.

Theonas advises Christians who serve inside a pagan ruler's household. How can they stay faithful while serving a master of another faith? Discretion, loyalty, and quiet firmness mark his answers throughout. The letter works as a guide to survival within the machinery of empire. Its counsel is shrewd without being false to the faith. Few early texts show so clearly how believers held high office before the empire itself turned Christian.
theophilus-of-antioch-theophilus-to-auto:
Bishop Theophilus of Antioch wrote to his pagan friend Autolycus around 180. Book two of that long letter takes up the creation story in Genesis. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers edition presents the text in English.

Greek myths of the gods stand as the rival account in his pages. Theophilus argues that the biblical story is more sensible than those tales. Learning and wit mark his case for one God who made all things. He writes for a friend, not a foe, and the tone stays patient. The book shows how early Christians used reason and scripture together to win a hearing in a pagan world.

Book three closes Theophilus's long letter to Autolycus, his pagan friend. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers edition carries the final part in English. Theophilus now turns from creation to the sweep of human history.

He argues that the Hebrew prophets lived long before the Greek thinkers. If so, Christian teaching rests on older and truer ground than pagan wisdom. Dates and king lists fill pages meant to prove that seniority. The letter as a whole forms one of the earliest full defenses of the faith. Written around 180, it shows a bishop patiently reasoning with a skeptic he plainly likes and hopes to win.
three-distinct-knocks-1785:
The Three Distinct Knocks first appeared in London in 1760 as an exposé of the most antient Free-Masonry. This Dublin reprint of 1785 carried the Irish edition across the water. The book gives the fullest eighteenth-century printed ritual of the three degrees, with the opening and closing of lodges in working order.

Its title names the raps that announce a candidate at the lodge door. Inside, catechisms carry the whole Craft system degree by degree. Irish Masonry had its own strong life, and the Dublin printing served it. Historians rank the Knocks beside Jachin and Boaz among the great exposures. For the ritual as actually worked in the period, few printed sources run fuller.
tob-0085:
Booklets of charms sold under the name of Albertus Magnus, the medieval scholar saint, for hundreds of years. The Egyptian Secrets is the most famous of them, though Albertus never wrote a word of it. Compilers of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries gathered its recipes and spells.

Readers find cures for man and beast, protections against theft and fire, and prayers for luck in love and trade. In America the booklet became a staple of hoodoo and of Pennsylvania powwow practice alike. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. The little book's long career shows folk magic's staying power.
tob-10485:
Benedetto Croce, the Italian philosopher and historian, wrote on five Renaissance-era mystics and thinkers: Eckhart, Tauler, Paracelsus, Boehme, and Bruno. Eugenio Ruggiero translated the work into English. Croce asks what their stress on inner light gave to later thought.

Each figure gets a study that weighs his ideas rather than his marvels. Croce treats mystic experience as a stage in the life of the human spirit, to be understood, not just praised or blamed. The book suits readers who want a clear, critical guide to names often wrapped in fog, by one of Italy's leading minds.
tob-10785:
Herbert Silberer, a pupil of Freud, read alchemy as the unconscious speaking in symbols in Hidden Symbolism of Alchemy and the Occult Arts. Published in 1914, the study was among the first psychoanalytic treatments of mysticism. For Silberer, the philosopher's stone figures the perfected self, and transmutation figures inner transformation.

Working through alchemical texts, emblems, and myths, he argues their strange imagery dramatizes stages of the soul's development. Dreams and fairy tales enter as parallels. Later depth psychology, especially Jung's, would take up similar readings. Readers get a bold early attempt to explain why occult symbolism feels meaningful even to skeptics.
tob-4085:
Yeats published In the Seven Woods in 1903, poems chiefly of the Irish heroic age. Cuchulain, Deirdre, and figures from the old sagas return in taut, harder-edged verse. The dreamy manner of his 1890s work gives way to something sterner, as legend becomes a mirror held up to modern Ireland and its quarrels.

The collection appeared from the Dun Emer Press, tied to the Irish cultural revival Yeats helped lead. Love poems and meditations on change accompany the heroic material, including his response to a changed beloved and a changed country. In the Seven Woods catches a poet mid-transformation, trading twilight for a voice that could face history.
tob-4285:
Budge surveyed Egypt's gods in The Gods of the Egyptians, published in 1904, and volume one opens his great survey. Ra the sun, Osiris the murdered and risen king, and Isis the great mother lead the company of heaven. Texts in translation and many illustrations support the account throughout.

Budge, keeper at the British Museum, wrote from the monuments and papyri in his care. He explains how local gods merged, how myths grew, and how Egyptians prayed. Verified from the 1919 edition, part one of the 1904 classic still serves readers who want the pantheon whole rather than in fragments.
un-ga-res-a-69-85:
Fifty years of space work are marked in Resolution A/69/85, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. Great strides in space science and its uses had let mankind study the far worlds, the Sun, and the Earth itself. The text recalls the chain of space votes back to 1996. It names one body as the sole world stage for joint space work: the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space.

Space work, the text holds, has served the good of all mankind. Its gains run from a deeper grasp of the planets to the web of law that now rules work above the earth. States are urged to keep that work joint and peaceful, as the next half century of space opens.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: The General Assembly's annual text on international cooperation in the peaceful uses of outer space is Resolution 69/85, adopted at its sixty-ninth session in 2014. It endorses the report of the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space on its fifty-seventh session. It urges states to join the space treaties. It presses for action on space debris and near-Earth objects. It notes the UN-SPIDER disaster-response platform. It asks the Committee to keep outer space peaceful and report to the seventieth session.
un-sc-res-1285:
A small observer team watched a disputed Croatian peninsula at the start of 2000. On 13 January 2000 the Council let the Prevlaka observers stay on. Their mission, UNMOP, monitored the demilitarization of the Prevlaka peninsula. Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia both claimed the area. The Secretary-General had reported on the mission at the end of December.

The observers could keep working until 15 July 2000. The Council told both parties to stop breaking the demilitarized regime. It welcomed ideas for confidence-building steps between them. It also urged a negotiated settlement of the Prevlaka dispute itself. The quiet mission helped keep a local quarrel from turning into a wider clash.
un-sc-res-1385:
Sierra Leone diamonds are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1385, adopted unanimously on 19 December 2001. Rough diamonds had funded the rebel war for years. A new certificate scheme now marked legal government exports. The Kimberley Process was building a world-wide version of that check.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council keeps the ban on uncertified rough diamonds for eleven more months from 5 January 2002. Stones certified by the government scheme stay exempt. The text welcomes signs the scheme is cutting the flow of war diamonds. A full review at the end of the period will weigh how far state control reaches over the diamond fields.
un-sc-res-1485:
Western Sahara's mission received a two-month bridge in the spring of 2003. On 30 May 2003 the Security Council extended MINURSO until 31 July 2003. The time was meant for study. The Secretary-General's May report needed closer thought. The Council praised his special representative's work on linked humanitarian issues. Refugee family visits and other trust-building steps fell in that area.

The extension is among the shortest in the mission's history. It kept the ceasefire machinery running while politics caught up. Two months later the Council backed a full peace plan for the territory. That plan forms the core of the next stage of the story. The Council stayed seized of the question throughout.
un-sc-res-1585: Resolution 1585, issued in 2005, adds to the Security Council's long series of formal decisions. The collection keeps it as a Wikisource copy of the official UN record. Reading it, one meets the institution's habits: earlier texts recalled, concern or welcome expressed, then numbered paragraphs that tell governments and officials what to do next.
un-sc-res-1685:
The Golan force was renewed in June 2006 on familiar terms. On 13 June 2006 the Security Council extended UNDOF until 31 December 2006. The Secretary-General had reported on the mission that month. The Council welcomed the force's work on staff conduct. UNDOF was enforcing the zero-tolerance policy on sexual exploitation and abuse. Its personnel had to follow the United Nations code of conduct.

The parties had to carry out resolution 338 without delay. A report on the term was due at its end. It would cover events and steps taken toward 338. The renewal came weeks before war erupted on the nearby Lebanon front. The Syrian line, under UNDOF's watch, stayed quiet through it.
un-sc-res-1785: Resolution 1785 is one of the Security Council's formal acts, kept here in the wording of the UN's official record. The Wikisource transcription preserves the whole instrument: the recitals that frame the problem and the operative paragraphs that answer it. For the governments addressed, those paragraphs were the point; for readers now, they still are.
un-sc-res-1885:
UNMIL was extended as its drawdown slowed on 15 September 2009. The Secretary-General's reports of June and August set out the state of play. Liberia's truth commission had finished its work, offering a path for national dialogue. The army and police were growing more professional. Some drawdown benchmarks, above all on the police and the national security strategy, lagged.

The Council extended UNMIL's mandate until 30 September 2010. The mission was authorized to help Liberia's government prepare the 2011 general elections. Outstanding land and reconciliation questions were flagged for the authorities to settle. The Secretary-General's advice on the mission's further drawdown was endorsed in part, with a free and fair process the guide. His plan to report on the mission's future shape, after talks with the government, was backed. The power to shift troops between UNMIL and the Côte d'Ivoire mission was restated.
un-sc-res-2085:
Northern Mali's capture by armed groups led to Resolution 2085, adopted in December 2012. Islamist fighters and separatists had seized the desert north, and Mali's government asked for help. The Council authorized an African-led force, AFISMA, to take back the region.

The text sets the force's tasks: rebuild Mali's army, retake the north, protect civilians, and create space for elections. It also calls for talks with groups that reject terrorism. Within months, French troops and then a UN mission reshaped the effort, but this resolution was the legal starting gun for intervention.
un-sc-res-385:
Namibia's occupation drew fresh condemnation from the Security Council on 30 January 1976. The Council heard the president of the United Nations Council for Namibia and a senior figure of the South West Africa People's Organization. The World Court had ruled in 1971 that South Africa must withdraw. Pretoria instead kept its rule, its racial laws, and a growing military build-up.

The Council condemned the continued occupation and the discriminatory laws imposed on Namibians. It condemned South Africa's military build-up and any use of Namibia as a base for attacks on neighbors. It demanded an end to the bantustan and homeland policy that split the territory by race. South Africa was faulted for defying resolution 366 (1974) and for schemes meant to dodge free elections. The Council declared that free elections under United Nations supervision across the whole territory were essential so Namibians could decide their own future.
un-sc-res-685:
The Iran-Iraq observer group received its final short renewals in early 1991. On 31 January 1991 the Security Council extended UNIIMOG for one month. The new term ran until 28 February 1991. The Secretary-General had reported on the group days earlier. His recommendation set the one-month term. The observers had watched the ceasefire line since 1988. Their work was nearly done as the Gulf crisis overshadowed the file.

The Secretary-General owed a report during February. It would cover his further consultations on the observers' future. The Council had kept the mission alive in shrinking steps since the war ended. Within weeks the group was withdrawn. Its quiet watch had helped hold a hard-won ceasefire.
un-sc-res-85:
Korea's civilians were suffering badly a month into the war. Offers of help poured in from governments and charities. On 31 July 1950 the Security Council organized the relief effort. It asked the Unified Command to take charge of civilian relief. The command would judge what aid Korea needed. It would also set up the field system for giving that aid out.

All offers of help went through the Secretary-General to the command. The command had to report on its relief work as fitting. United Nations bodies and agencies were asked to assist. The resolution put food and shelter under military coordination. It was the relief counterpart to the war resolutions of June.
un-sc-res-885:
A formal inquiry into attacks on United Nations troops in Somalia was ordered on 16 November 1993. Resolution 837 (1993) had condemned the 5 June 1993 assault on UNOSOM II and called for an investigation. Member states and the Organization of African Unity had proposed an impartial Commission of Inquiry. The Secretary-General had reported twice on the follow-up to the June attack.

The Council authorized the creation of the Commission of Inquiry to investigate armed attacks on UNOSOM II staff that caused casualties. The Secretary-General was asked to appoint the commission at the earliest possible time and to report on its setup. The commission would fix its own procedures under standard United Nations practice. Its members would hold the status of experts on mission. All parties in Somalia were called to cooperate with it fully. The commission had to report its findings through the Secretary-General as soon as it could.
un-sc-res-985:
Resolution 985 recorded the Council's decision on Liberia, adopted unanimously on 13 April 1995. The ceasefire had broken down again. The observer mission could not deploy in full or do its work. Arms kept flowing in despite a total embargo set in 1992.

The Council extends the observer mission, called UNOMIL, until 30 June 1995. The factions are urged to restore the ceasefire under the Akosombo and Accra deals. A new committee of the whole Council will police the arms embargo. It will gather reports from states and propose fixes for breaches. Regional leaders will meet in Nigeria that May to push the peace along.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
A small peninsula at the Bay of Kotor's mouth stayed under UN eyes in 2000. On 13 January, the Council adopted Resolution 1285 without dissent. The Prevlaka peninsula was disputed ground. Croatia and the Yugoslav federation both claimed it. A 1992 deal kept it free of arms under UN watch.

The text lets the observers keep watch until 15 July 2000. Both parties must end breaches of the no-arms regime. They must ease tension and guard safety in the area. The observers must move freely and stay safe. A full mine-clearing program is urged as well. One bright spot is noted with care. Crossing points in the zone moved people and goods in peace.

Diamonds had funded rebels through Sierra Leone's brutal civil war. By late 2001 peace was taking hold, and fighters were disarming. Resolution 1385, adopted unanimously on 19 December 2001, dealt with the gem trade. It extended a ban first imposed in 2000 on uncertified Sierra Leonean rough diamonds.

The ban would run eleven more months from 5 January 2002. Stones certified by Sierra Leone's government stayed exempt. Members welcomed signs that the certificate system was cutting the flow of conflict diamonds. They praised the wider Kimberley Process, a global effort to keep war gems off the market. A fresh review would judge government control over the diamond fields.

For Western Sahara, the long-disputed territory on Africa's northwest coast, Resolution 1485 of 30 May 2003 bought the Council more time. It stretched the mandate of MINURSO, the UN mission created to organize a referendum on the territory's future, by a short period ending on 31 July 2003.

The brief extension had a specific purpose: members wanted to study the Secretary-General's report of 23 May 2003 before deciding the mission's longer course. The text also praised the Secretary-General's special representative for work on humanitarian problems left by the conflict and for supporting aid-agency steps meant to build confidence between the sides.

One week is all that Sudan's advance mission is granted on 10 March 2005. UNAMIS, which had been preparing the ground for a larger operation to support Sudan's new peace agreement, is extended until 17 March 2005. The brief extension kept that preparatory work alive while the Council finished preparing the follow-on mission.

The Golan line stayed still through the spring of 2006. The chief's report of 1 June told of a calm watch. UNDOF's term had weeks to run. The force had held the line since 1974. Resolution 1685 passed on 13 June 2006.

The mandate grew by six months, to 31 December 2006. The old call rang out once more: act on the 1973 text at once. Staff rules fill much of this text. The force must hold the zero-tolerance line on sexual abuse. Troop states must act to bar such acts and punish guilt. A report was due at the term's end. By 2006, these twin themes, the still line and the strict code, had fused in each renewal.

Bosnia and Herzegovina's European Union stabilization force is renewed on 21 November 2007 for a further planned period. The yearly pattern continues: full support for the High Representative, commitment to the 1995 peace agreement, and a Chapter VII authorization for the force that succeeded NATO's SFOR in 2004.

Acting under Chapter VII, states working through the European Union are authorized to keep the force in place under unified command. They may take all necessary measures to enforce the peace agreement's military terms, ensure compliance, and defend the force. The parties are told to respect the force's safety and freedom of movement, and Bosnia's future is restated as lying in meeting its peace and reform duties.

Kenya raised its flag on 12 December 1963, ending British rule. Four days later its UN application was already decided. Resolution 185 was adopted unanimously on 16 December 1963. Some later summaries misdate the text to 1964. The record of the 1084th meeting is clear about the year.

The Council recommended that Kenya be admitted. The General Assembly seated Kenya the same week. Jomo Kenyatta, once jailed by the British, led the new state. Kenya's arrival continued East Africa's entry into the UN. Tanganyika and Uganda had joined just before. The resolution is a single sentence. It still marks the legal close of Kenya's long road from colony to sovereign member.

Resolution 1885, adopted on 15 September 2009, extends the UN Mission in Liberia, UNMIL, into the run-up to the 2011 elections. Liberia's Truth and Reconciliation Commission had finished its work. The army and police were growing more professional, but violent crime, drug trafficking, and slow spots in police benchmarks still worried the Council. Plans for the October 2011 presidential and legislative votes were under study.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends UNMIL until 30 September 2010. It lets UNMIL help with the 2011 elections through supply support and help reaching remote areas. It approves the third drawdown stage, sending home 2,029 soldiers, three attack helicopters, and 72 armored carriers between October 2009 and May 2010. That leaves 8,202 military staff, including 250 guarding the Special Court for Sierra Leone. Free, fair, calm elections are set as a core test for later drawdown.

Terrorist and criminal groups held the north of Mali at the end of 2012, and abuses against civilians were widespread. Mali's transitional authorities had formally asked for an outside force to help win the region back. On 20 December 2012 the Council adopted Resolution 2085, which authorized an African-led mission to Mali.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorized the African-led International Support Mission in Mali, called AFISMA, for an initial year. The mission could take all necessary measures to support Mali's forces and protect civilians. The Council also pressed the transitional leaders to finish a road map to elections. Rebel groups had to break their ties with Al-Qaida-linked groups. Reports on the mission were set every sixty days.

Passed on 5 September 1970, with the United States abstaining, Resolution 285 is one of the shortest texts in the Council's history. Its single operative sentence demands the complete and immediate pullout of all Israeli armed forces from Lebanese territory. Nothing else is asked, explained, or added, which makes the demand itself the entire record of the Council's position that day.

Namibia's blocked freedom drives Resolution 385. The Council passed it by a full vote on 30 January 1976. It heard the head of the UN's Namibia council. It also heard Moses Garoeb, a leader of SWAPO, the freedom movement. The Assembly had ended South Africa's rule over the land in 1966. The World Court said in 1971 that South Africa must leave.

South Africa stayed anyway. The Council restated the UN's legal duty for Namibia. It condemned the hold on the land and the refusal to obey UN rulings. Its core demand was free votes for all Namibians, held under UN watch. That plan, pushed for years, at last brought freedom in 1990.

Resolution 685 was adopted on 31 January 1991, while attention was fixed on the Gulf crisis, and it handles a quieter file: the military observers watching the ceasefire between Iran and Iraq. The observer group, known as UNIIMOG, had patrolled since the two countries stopped fighting in 1988. Its mandate was about to run out.

Following the Secretary-General's advice, the Council extended the group's mandate for a single month, until 28 February 1991. It also asked him to report during February on his talks with both governments about the observer group's future and what he recommended. The tight deadline reflects a mission nearing the end of its useful life as the region's map was redrawn.

War aid for Korea's people took shape in the summer of 1950. The North's attack had left towns wrecked and crowds in flight. Gifts of aid poured in from states and charities. Some plan was needed to sort the flow. Resolution 85 passed on 31 July 1950 by nine votes to none. Yugoslavia held back. The Soviet team was still away in boycott.

The joint UN command in Korea took charge of relief. It would judge what the people needed. It would set the rules for aid on the ground. All gifts were to pass through the chief's hands to the command. UN arms, funds, and aid groups were told to help as asked. News of the relief work had to come back to the Council. Guns had their file; this text built the aid file beside it.

Resolution 885, adopted on 16 November 1993, orders an inquiry into deadly attacks on UN peacekeepers in Somalia. On 5 June that year, gunmen of a Somali faction had ambushed personnel of UNOSOM II, killing dozens. An earlier resolution had condemned the attack and demanded an investigation, and African states in particular had proposed an impartial commission of inquiry.

The Council authorized the commission's creation to investigate the armed attacks that caused the casualties. It asked the Secretary-General to appoint the members as early as possible after sharing his views, and to report on progress. The inquiry fed into arrest warrants and the manhunt politics that consumed the Somalia mission in its final phase.

Liberia's ceasefire had collapsed by the spring of 1995. Resolution 985, adopted unanimously on 13 April 1995, dealt with the fallout. The UN observer mission, UNOMIL, could not deploy fully. Guns kept flowing in despite an arms embargo set in 1992. West African leaders planned a May summit in Nigeria to rescue the peace accords.

Members extended UNOMIL only until 30 June 1995. Liberian factions were told to revive the ceasefire and install the interim Council of State. A new sanctions committee was created to police the arms embargo. It would collect reports of violations and suggest stronger steps. Aid workers and regional peacekeepers had to be protected, the text demands.
various-early-christian-writers-apocryph:
Gospels and acts that missed the Bible fill this apocryphal gathering. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers collects the writings in English. Various hands wrote the pieces across the early Christian centuries.

Infancy gospels tell tales of wonders worked by the child Jesus. Acts of apostles pile marvel upon marvel in their travels. Letters bearing famous names round out the varied set. Early Christians loved reading beyond the bounds of scripture itself. Imaginative, devout, and at times wonderfully strange, the tales reward curiosity. They show the popular faith of the age in a way the formal canon never could.
various-early-christian-writers-memoirs-:
Edessa, the great Syriac Christian city, kept its own proud memories. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers gathers its memoirs with other Syriac records. Together they open a window on the faith east of Rome.

King Abgar's famed letters to and from Jesus lead the legends. Acts of local martyrs tell how the faith first reached the East. Syriac Christianity grew in Semitic soil, apart from the Greek world. Its stories carry an ancient flavor all their own. Scholars prize these records as primary sources for the earliest Syriac Church. They prove the faith had many homes, and many tongues, from its first generations onward.
various-early-christian-writers-remains-:
Fragments of lost Christian writers fill the Remains of the Second and Third Centuries. The 1885 Fathers edition gathers the splinters in English. Papias and Quadratus stand among the names the old notes recall.

Bishops, teachers, and martyrs survive here only in quotation. Later authors cited their words, and citation alone saved them. A vast early literature has otherwise vanished from the earth. Each fragment is a brief voice from the Church's first ages. They speak across a great silence that surrounds them on all sides. Readers who love detective work in history will savor the clues these scraps still offer about lost books.
various-early-christian-writers-the-acts:
Xanthippe and Polyxena star in an early Christian romance of conversion. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers prints their lively acts in English. Xanthippe, wife of a Roman official, hears the apostle Paul preach.

His preaching converts her, and her household begins to change. Her lovely sister Polyxena then suffers a run of wild adventures. Kidnappers seize her, a shipwreck casts her far from home, and rescue follows. Apostolic legend blends with the twists of a Greek novel throughout. The tale counts as popular fiction for ancient Christian readers. Few texts from the age entertain so openly while preaching so plainly.
various-early-christian-writers-the-apoc:
The Apocalypse of Peter ranks as the earliest Christian vision of the afterlife. Peter receives a tour of the world beyond death in its pages. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers preserves the second-century work in English.

Sinners meet punishments fitted to their sins in graphic detail. The righteous enjoy bliss described with equal warmth and color. Such scenes shaped how Christians pictured heaven and hell for centuries. Dante's Inferno stands in this older work's long shadow. Some early churches even weighed the book for the New Testament. Its near miss at canon gives it a special place in the history of Christian hope and fear.

Sedrach dares to question God in this bold ancient dialogue. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers preserves the Jewish-Christian work in English. Suffering, death, and judgment are the hard topics on the table.

Sedrach presses the Almighty with the questions mourners always ask. Why do the righteous suffer, and why must all people die? God answers him directly, and even grants concessions in the debate. Few ancient religious works stage such a daring exchange. A human argues with heaven and is heard with patience. The tale wrestles with faith's hardest questions in the lively form of a face-to-face dispute.

The Virgin Mary herself tours heaven and hell in this Byzantine vision. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers presents the Apocalypse of the Virgin in English. Mary sees the suffering of lost souls with a mother's eyes.

Her heart moves her to plead with her Son for mercy. Intercession becomes the beating heart of the whole tour. The Eastern Church loved the tale and spread it widely. It shows Mary as merciful mediator at her most vivid. Compassion tempers strict judgment throughout the grim scenes. A mother's plea, the story insists, can move even God toward pity for the suffering dead.
various-early-christian-writers-the-decr:
The Decretals gather letters ascribed to the earliest popes. The names run from Clement through bishops of the 300s. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers presents the collection in English.

Most of the letters are now judged later forgeries by scholars. For a thousand years, though, courts cited them as true papal law. They shaped the medieval Church and its claims to wide authority. Forged decretals even fed the great Pseudo-Isidorian collection later on. Historians study the set as prime evidence of a lasting pattern. Power builds its own paper trail, and these pages show that trail being laid with skill.
various-early-christian-writers-the-gosp:
The Gospel of Peter tells the Passion from Peter's own viewpoint. Only a fragment of the ancient gospel now survives. Diggers found the text in Egypt in the 1880s, and the Fathers printed it.

Its risen Jesus emerges from the tomb as a figure of giant size. A cross that speaks follows him out into the morning light. Such wonders set the tale apart from the four church gospels. Scholars still debate how old the work truly is. Its vivid and dramatic passion story shows real power regardless. First Christians clearly pictured the resurrection with awe that burst the bounds of plain report.
various-early-christian-writers-the-narr:
Zosimus journeys to the ends of the earth in this marvelous tale. There he finds the blessed Rechabites living beyond the known world. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers preserves the narrative in English.

The hidden people dwell in a land like paradise itself. Sin has never touched their quiet and ordered common life. Zosimus learns their customs and carries the wonder back with him. Medieval dreams of earthly paradises fed on tales like this one. Lost tribes and blessed isles owe something to its example. Part travel fantasy and part moral vision, the story offers ancient escape with a spiritual heart.
various-early-christian-writers-the-pass:
Court officers at Carthage tried the Scillitan martyrs in the year 180. Seven men and five women from Scilli stood before the Roman governor. The charge was refusal to swear by the genius of the emperor.

The surviving text is the official record of that grim trial. Short questions meet short, dignified answers from the accused. All twelve were beheaded for holding to their confession of Christ. The 1885 Fathers edition presents the transcript in English. History rarely comes rawer than this brief document. It stands as the earliest Christian text to survive from Africa, and among the most moving.
various-early-christian-writers-the-test:
The Testament of Abraham tells how Death came for the patriarch. Abraham, to put it plainly, refused to go with him. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers preserves the beloved tale in English.

Bargaining and trickery fill Abraham's long resistance to his fate. Humor runs warm through scenes that could have been pure dread. At last the old man accepts what no mortal can escape. Tenderness marks his final leave-taking from the world he loved. Ancient readers cherished the story across many retellings. It shows the lighter side of old faith: even its greatest heroes argue with destiny before they bow.

The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs hold twelve dying speeches. Each son of Jacob speaks in turn to his children at death. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers preserves the ancient set in English.

Each patriarch confesses the sin that marked his own life. He then warns his children to shun that same failing. Jewish ethics fill the speeches, with Christian editing layered in. The early Church loved the book and some quoted it as scripture. Part moral handbook and part window, it shows two faiths overlapping. Students of the New Testament prize it for the world of thought that Jesus and his followers shared.
various-early-christian-writers-the-visi:
The Vision of Paul sends the apostle up to the third heaven. Paul tells of such a rising in his own letters to Corinth. The 1885 Fathers edition carries the later vision tale in English.

Torments of the damned unfold before his eyes in stern order. The rest and joy of the saints balance the dreadful scenes. Medieval Christians read, preached, and pictured this work for a thousand years. No other vision of the afterlife shaped their age so deeply. Fears and hopes of common folk live in its pages. Anyone who wants to grasp the medieval mind on death and judgment can start with this famous tour.
various-early-christian-writers-two-epis:
Two ancient letters praise virginity as the highest Christian calling. Later ages ascribed both letters to Clement of Rome. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers presents the pair in English.

Consecrated virgins receive detailed instruction on how to live. Separate, modest lives devoted to prayer are held up as the pattern. Scholars doubt that Clement truly wrote the letters himself. Even so, the texts capture an early mood of the Church. Celibacy stood exalted there in its purest and strictest form. Readers see how a whole way of life grew from the call to give oneself wholly to God.
victorinus-commentary-on-the-apocalypse-:
Victorinus, bishop of Pettau, wrote the oldest surviving notes on Revelation. He died a martyr around the year 304 for his faith. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers carries his commentary in English.

He reads the Apocalypse as a prophecy of the Church under Rome. Struggle with the empire fills his reading of its strange visions. The tone stays vivid and urgent, yet the counsel is often practical. Later readers found his approach steadier than many wild guesses since. The book shows how the first Christian generations grasped their most mysterious text. It guided how believers pictured the end of the age for centuries.
warren-paradise-found-1885:
William Warren, first president of Boston University, placed the cradle of mankind at the North Pole in 1885. Paradise Found argues that the first home of man stood in a warm Arctic land, now lost to ice. Warren was a scholar of wide reading and bold reach.

He draws on myth, geology, and the old tales of a blessed north to build his case. Eden, the Greek Isles of the Blest, and Norse tales all point poleward in his hands. Theosophists took the book up with zeal after his death. It founded the polar line of lost-land thought that still has its heirs.
wellhausen-prolegomena-black-1885:
Julius Wellhausen was a German scholar whose study of the Old Testament changed Bible study for good. His Prolegomena to the History of Israel appeared in German in 1878, and this English version followed in 1885. Sutherland Black and Allan Menzies translated it.

Wellhausen argues that the first five books of the Bible were woven from several older sources by later editors. He traces how Israel's worship moved from free local shrines to one temple and a strict priestly code. He reads law, song, and story as records of changing faith, not as timeless rules. His documentary hypothesis still frames scholarly debate about how the Bible was made.
wilson-congressional-government-1885:
Woodrow Wilson published Congressional Government in 1885, his first book, written as a young scholar. Wilson argues that Congress, not the President, truly governs America. Power sits in committees, whose chairs rule in closed rooms. He contrasts this hidden system with Britain's open cabinet government, which he admires.

The book made Wilson's academic name at once. Later, as President, he revived strong presidential leadership in practice. Critics note that his picture slighted parties and the presidency's tools. Even so, the critique of committee rule remains classic. It is the best entry into Wilson the political scientist. Project Gutenberg's edition keeps it widely read.
